Surat Bara'a (al-Tawba) is Medinan, and it has 129 verses.

It also has other names: Surat al-'Adhab (the Chastising Surah), because it contains mention of repentance (tawba), of the disavowal of hypocrisy (tabriya min al-nifaq), and of the searching out and probing of the condition of the hypocrites, bringing it to light and digging it up, and what disgraces them, disperses them, and crushes them.

That it is well known by these names indicates that it is an independent surah and not part of Surat al-Anfal. The claim that this widespread recognition is restricted to those who hold that it is independent is contrary to what is apparent. The wisdom behind not writing the basmala (tasmiya) at its revelation is that this surah was revealed to lift a security (aman) whose station rejects opening with anything that suggests its continuation, such as mentioning the name of God accompanied by the attribute of mercy. This is what is related from Ibn 'Uyayna (may God be pleased with him). It is not due to doubt over whether the surah is independent or not, as is reported from Ibn 'Abbas (may God be pleased with them both), nor is it due to considering the disagreement that arose among the Companions (may God be pleased with them) on this matter. Moreover, that view leads toward the claim that the basmala is not part of the Qur'an and was written only to separate the surahs, as is reported from the early Hanafiyya (the early followers of the Hanafi school). It also leads toward the claim that its inclusion or omission in the codices depends only on the opinion of those who undertook to compile the Qur'an, without any tawqif (divine determination). There is no doubt that the sound position of the school is that the basmala is a distinct verse of the Qur'an, revealed to separate surahs and for blessing through it, and that no one's opinion has any place in its inclusion or omission. What is followed in this matter is revelation and tawqif. There is also no doubt that it was not revealed here, for otherwise there would have been no possibility of doubt or disagreement regarding its independence. So the cause is either the unity of the two surahs or what we have mentioned. The first is not possible, since otherwise he (ﷺ) would have clarified it, because the need for clarification would have been greatest, given the strength of the evidence for independence: the large number of verses and the long period between the revelation of the two. Since he (ﷺ) did not clarify it, the second alternative is determined, because the absence of explanation from the Lawgiver in a place where explanation is required is itself an explanation of absence.

﴿A disavowal from God and His Messenger, to those with whom you made covenants among the polytheists.﴾

﴿A disavowal (bara'a)﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, and its tanwin is for exaltation (tafkhim). It has also been read in the accusative, meaning: "Hear a disavowal." The "min" in His saying, ﴿from God and His Messenger﴾, is for origin (ibtida'iyya), and it is connected to an omitted element that functions as an adjective for it, in order to give it additional magnification and awe. That is: this is a disavowal initiated from the side of God and His Messenger. The relative clause is ﴿to those with whom you made covenants among the polytheists﴾. The reason the thing from which the disavowal is made was not mentioned, as in His saying, ﴿that God is free of the polytheists﴾ (9:3), is that it is sufficient to rely on what is in the relative clause, since it clearly indicates it, and to avoid repeating the word "min." It has been said that it is a subject (mubtada'), since it is specified by the adjective, and its predicate is "to those..." etc. But what the eloquence of the composition requires is the first view. This disavowal is a new matter whose essence was not known to the addressees, nor the heading of its initiation from God and His Messenger, such that that heading would come out as an adjective for it and be made the primary intended matter. The essential thing in the information is something else: its arrival at those with whom covenants were made. What deserves to be emphasized in conveying is the occurrence of that disavowal (p-40) from His side and its arrival to them. For adjectives, before the addressee knows that they belong to their referents, should be information, and information, after knowing that it belongs to what it is about, should be adjectives, as has been established in its proper place.

It is also read ﴿min Allahi﴾ with a kasra on the nun, on the basis that the original vowel of a moved unvowelled letter is kasra. But the preferred reading is fath, specifically on the lam of definition, because of its frequent occurrence. The 'ahd is a binding covenant confirmed by oath. The address in "'ahadtum" is to the Muslims, and they had made covenants with the polytheists of the Arabs, including people of Mecca and others, with God's permission and the agreement of the Messenger (ﷺ). Then they broke them, except the Banu Damra and the Banu Kinana. So the Muslims were commanded to renounce the covenant with those who had broken it, and they were given a respite of four months so that they could travel wherever they wished. The disavowal is attributed to God and His Messenger, even though it includes the Muslims, shares their ruling, and makes acting upon its requirement obligatory. The covenant, however, was linked only to the Muslims, even though it was with God's permission and the agreement of the Messenger (ﷺ). This was to indicate that its execution and finality are immediate, without depending on the opinion of the addressees, because it is an expression of ending the ruling of security and lifting the danger that the earlier covenant placed upon refraining from attacking the unbelievers. That belongs to the side of God, Mighty and Majestic, because it is a command like other commands that operate according to a wisdom that requires it and a motive that calls for it, and their effects follow from it without depending on anything at all.

The Muslims' participation in its ruling and the obligation to act upon its requirement is only by way of compliance with the command, not that they have any role in completing it or in the consequences of its rulings. As for the covenant, since it is a contract like other lawful contracts, it does not come into being in itself, nor do its rulings follow from it, except through the direct action of the contracting parties in specific forms recognized by the Lawgiver. Therefore, it cannot be conceived as issuing from Him, glorified be He. What issues from Him regarding it is only permission for it, and those who carry it out and take charge of it are the Muslims. It is not hidden that the disavowal relates to the covenant and not to the permission for it. So each of the two is attributed to the one who is its origin. Moreover, in that there is magnification of the matter of the disavowal, awe of its affair, marking the unbelievers with utmost humiliation and abasement, and the ultimate of disgrace and failure, and purification of the court of the Glorified and the Majestic from what might suggest any trace of deficiency or lowliness, may He be exalted far above that.

The inclusion of him (ﷺ) in the first attribution and his exclusion from the second is to exalt his lofty station and to honour his lofty rank in both situations (ﷺ). The choice of the nominal sentence over the verbal one, as if one said: "God and His Messenger have disowned those who..." or something similar, is to indicate its permanence and continuity, and as a means of reaching its awe through the magnifying tanwin, as has been pointed out.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 2:

﴿So travel freely﴾. As-siyaha (travel) and as-sayh mean going about the earth and moving through it with ease, according to what one wills, just as water flows (sāha) by the necessity of its nature. In it there is an indication of complete freedom and enjoyment that is not found in "sīrū" (travel) and its like. The addition of His words, Mighty and Majestic is He, ﴿in the land﴾ is intended to generalize to all its regions, both the abode of Islam and others. The meaning is: permission for them to do this, and leaving them and their own affairs, from preparing for war, or safeguarding their families and wealth, and gaining prestige, or other than that, not an obligation on them to travel in it. The turning of the address away from the Muslims and directing it to them, although the purpose is also achieved with the imperative in the third person form, is for the sake of emphasizing the announcement of the respite, to cut off the pretext of their claiming heedlessness, and to eradicate the root of their excuse of not being prepared. The choice of the imperative form, although this meaning could also be conveyed by way of informing, as if one were to say, for example: "You may travel" or something similar, is to show complete strength and dominance, and disregard for them and their preparation, so it is as if this were a matter demanded of them. The fa' (so) indicates the ordering of the command to travel and what follows it upon what the mentioned disavowal of the treaties implies, on the basis that the first is ordered upon itself, and the second, with both its objects, is ordered upon the title of its being from Allah, the Mighty, not that the first is ordered upon that and the second upon the first, as in His words: ﴿Say: Travel in the land and see﴾ ... etc. It is as if it were said: this is a disavowal necessitating your fighting, so strive to obtain the equipment and means, and exert yourselves in acquiring provisions from every quarter.

﴿Four months. And know that you﴾ by your travelling in the regions of the earth, in breadth and length, even if you ride the back of every difficult and docile mount, ﴿are not able to escape Allah﴾, that is: you will not outrun Him by flight or fortification. ﴿And that Allah﴾: the majestic Name is placed in the position of the pronoun, to cultivate awe and to magnify the matter of humiliation, which is degradation by that which involves disgrace and shame, ﴿will disgrace the disbelievers﴾, that is: will disgrace and abase you in this world by killing and capture, and in the Hereafter by punishment. The choice of the explicit noun over the pronoun is to censure them for disbelief after describing them as polytheists, and to indicate that the cause of the disgrace is their disbelief. It is also permissible that the intended meaning is the class of disbelievers, so that the addressees enter into it by primary inclusion. The "four months" are the sacred months upon the expiry of which fighting was made contingent. It was said: they are Shawwal, Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah and Muharram. It was also said: they are the twentieth of Dhu al-Hijjah, Muharram, Safar, Rabi' al-Awwal, and ten days of Rabi' al-Akhir. They were made sacred because of the sanctity of fighting in them, or because Dhu al-Hijjah and Muharram predominate over the rest. It was said: from the tenth of Dhu al-Qa'dah to the tenth of Rabi' al-Awwal, because the pilgrimage in that year took place at that time because of the intercalation (nasi') practised among them, and then it moved in the following year to Dhu al-Hijjah. This is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Indeed time has returned to its form on the day Allah created the heavens and the earth."

It is narrated that the Prophet ﷺ commanded Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, over the pilgrimage of the year nine, then he sent Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, after him on al-'Adba' to recite it to the people of the pilgrimage. It was said to him ﷺ: "If you were to send it to Abu Bakr?" He ﷺ said: "None shall convey on my behalf except a man from among me." This is because it is the custom of the Arabs that the matter of a covenant and its annulment is not handled on behalf of a tribe except by a man from it. When Ali drew near, Abu Bakr heard the groaning of the camel and halted, and said: "This is the groaning of the camel of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ." When he reached him, he said: "Are you a commander or one commanded?" He said: "One commanded." So they both proceeded. When it was the day before the Day of Tarwiyah, Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, gave a sermon and informed them of their rites. Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, stood on the Day of Sacrifice at the Jamrat al-'Aqabah and said: "O people, I am the messenger of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to you." They said: "With what?" So he recited to them thirty or forty verses, then said: "I have been commanded with four: that no polytheist shall approach the House after this year, that no naked person shall circumambulate the House, that none shall enter Paradise except every believing soul, and that every person with a covenant shall have his covenant fulfilled for him."

﴿And a proclamation from Allah and His Messenger﴾ means a declaration from both of them. The form *fa'āl* here carries the sense of *if'āl*, as *'aṭā'* means *i'ṭā'* (giving). Its grammatical case is like that of *Barā'ah* (disavowal), and the clause is conjoined to a similar clause before it. It says ﴿to the people﴾, meaning all of them, because the proclamation is not restricted to one group over another, unlike the specific *Barā'ah* concerning those who broke their covenants. Rather, it encompasses all the disbelievers in general and the believers as well.

﴿On the day of the greater Hajj﴾ is the day of ʿĪd (the Feast, i.e., the Day of Sacrifice), because on it the Hajj is completed and most of its rites are performed, and because the proclamation took place on it. It is also based on what is narrated: "The Prophet (ﷺ) stood on the Day of Sacrifice at the *Jamarāt* during the Farewell Pilgrimage and said, 'This is the day of the greater Hajj.'"

It is also said that it is the Day of ʿArafah, based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Hajj is ʿArafah." The Hajj is described as "greater" because ʿUmrah is called the "lesser Hajj." Or because the intended meaning of Hajj is what occurs on that day of its rites, for it is greater than the rest of the rites. Or because that Hajj gathered both Muslims and polytheists. Or because on it the might of the Muslims and the humiliation of the polytheists became manifest.

﴿That Allah﴾ means "that Allah" [with the *fath* reading]. It is also read with *kasra* (*inna*), because the proclamation contains the sense of speech. ﴿is free of obligation to the polytheists﴾, meaning those bound by treaty who broke their covenants. ﴿and His Messenger﴾ is conjoined to the pronoun hidden in *barī'* (free), or, in the *kasra* reading, to the place of *inna* and its subject. It is read with *fatḥa* as a conjunction to the subject of *anna*, or because the *wāw* carries the sense of *ma'a* (with), meaning: he is free of them along with him. It is read in the genitive by *jiwār* (attraction of inflection by adjacency), and it is said it is by way of oath.

﴿So if you repent﴾ from polytheism and treachery. This is an *iltifāt* (a shift from third person to second person) for the sake of intensifying the warning and emphasis. The *fā'* marks the sequencing of the conditional clause, which is preceded by the proclamation of disavowal, closed with a severe threat, indicating the softening of their stubbornness and the breaking of their fierce obstinacy. ﴿Then it is﴾, meaning repentance ﴿better for you﴾ in both abodes. ﴿But if you turn away﴾ from repentance, or persist in turning away from Islam and fidelity, ﴿then know that you cannot escape Allah﴾, meaning you will neither outrun Him nor escape Him. ﴿And give tidings to those who disbelieve﴾: this is a shift in address, turning it away from them to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), because the giving of tidings ﴿of a painful punishment﴾, although it is in the manner of mockery, is only fitting for one who is acquainted with the divine secrets.

﴿إلا الَّذِينَ عاهَدْتُمْ مِنَ المُشْرِكِينَ﴾ *(except those of the polytheists with whom you made a covenant)* is a corrective exception (*istidrak*) from the earlier repudiation (*nabdh*), in which fighting was deferred for four months. It is as if it were said: do not give the covenant-breakers more than four months, but as for those with whom you made a covenant and who did not break their pledge, do not treat them like the covenant-breakers by hastening to fight them; rather, fulfil their covenant to them. There is no harm in the intervening clause ﴿وَأذانٌ مِنَ اللَّهِ ورَسُولِهِ﴾ *(and a proclamation from Allah and His Messenger)* ... etc., because it is not wholly foreign to the matter; rather, it is a command to announce that disavowal, as if it were said: and know it. It has also been said that this is a connected exception (*istithna' muttasil*) from the first "polytheists," but this is rejected because the second term then remains general even though both refer to one group. Making it an exception from the second term is refuted by the first remaining in the same way. It has also been said that this is a corrective exception from what is implied in *(fa-sihu)* (so travel freely), i.e.: say to them, "Travel freely for four months," but as for those of them with whom you made a covenant ﴿ثُمَّ لَمْ يَنْقُصُوكم شَيْئًا﴾ *(then they have not fallen short of you in anything)* in the terms of the pact, did not kill any of you, and never harmed you. It is also read with the dotted letter (*al-mu'jama*), i.e. they did not violate your covenant in any way at all. The word ﴿ثُمَّ﴾ *(then)* indicates their steadfastness in their covenant despite the lengthening of the term. ﴿وَلَمْ يُظاهِرُوا﴾ *(and have not supported)*, i.e. did not aid ﴿عَلَيْكم أحَدًا﴾ *(anyone against you)* of your enemies, as the Banu Bakr attacked Khuza'a in the absence of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and Quraysh supported them with weapons. ﴿فَأتِمُّوا إلَيْهِمْ عَهْدَهُمْ﴾ *(then fulfil their covenant to them)*, i.e. discharge it to them in full ﴿إلى مُدَّتِهِمْ﴾ *(until their term)*, and do not surprise them with fighting when the appointed time set for the covenant-breakers has passed, nor treat them as you treat them. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) said: a clan of the Banu Kinana had nine months of their covenant remaining, so he (the Prophet) fulfilled their covenant to them.

﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ يُحِبُّ المُتَّقِينَ﴾ *(Indeed Allah loves the God-conscious)* is a reason (*ta'lil*) for the obligation to comply, and an indication that observing the rights of a covenant is a matter of God-consciousness (*taqwa*), and that treating the faithful and the treacherous alike is incompatible with that, even if the one with whom the covenant was made is a polytheist. (p-43)

**﴿Then when the sacred months have passed﴾**: i.e., have ended. The word is used figuratively from *insilakh* (the stripping off), which is the separation between an animal and its hide. Usually it is attributed to the hide. The meaning is: when the **al-ashhur al-hurum** (the sacred months) have ended and have separated from what they were enveloping and covering, as the hide separates from the sheep, and have been uncovered from it as a veil is lifted from what lies behind it. This is as Abu al-Haytham mentioned, that it is said: "We entered the month of such-and-such" (*ahlalna shahra kadha*), meaning we entered it and put it on. So we add to its garment each night until its half has passed, then we strip it from ourselves part by part, until we have stripped it from ourselves entirely and it has ended. He recited:

*When I strip off the month, I enter upon its like;*
*My stripping off the months and my entering upon them suffice as a killer.*

The reality of this is that time encompasses what is in it of temporal things and envelops them as the hide envelops the animal. Likewise every part of its extended divisions of days, months and years: when it passes, it is as though it has been stripped of what is in it. There is in this a subtle elegance, since it hints that those months were a protection for those treaty-bound polytheists against the harms of the hands of the Muslims. Thus fighting them was tied to their passing. The meaning of "them" (the sacred months) is either only the four months that have passed, and the apparent noun is placed in the position of the pronoun so that it becomes a means of describing them as sacred, emphasizing what the permission to travel freely indicates of the prohibition against harming them, along with greater concern for their status. Or they are, together with what is understood from His saying, ﴿So complete for them their treaty until their term﴾, the remainder of a period left for those who did not break their covenant. On the first view, the meaning of "the polytheists" in His saying ﴿then kill the polytheists﴾ is those who broke their covenant specifically, so fighting the rest is not understood from the expression of the text but from its implication. On the second view, it is understood from the expression, except that the stripping off and what is tied to it of fighting would then occur gradually, not all at once. It is as though it were said: when the appointed time of each group is completed, then kill them. To interpret it as the well-known months that recur every year does not agree with the noble structure of the text. As for the claim that it requires the continuance of the prohibition of fighting in them, since nothing revealed later abrogates it (**naskh**, abrogation), this is not to be taken into account. This is not because it was abrogated by His saying ﴿and fight them until there is no more fitnah﴾, as has been imagined, for that is conjecture about the unseen. If what is meant is what is in Surat al-Anfal, it was revealed after the Battle of Badr, and it is established that the intended ones in His saying ﴿Say to those who disbelieved﴾ ... etc. are Abu Sufyan and his companions, who accepted Islam in mid-Ramadan of the year of the Conquest, the eighth year, whereas Surat al-Tawbah was revealed in Shawwal of the ninth year. If what is meant is what is in Surat al-Baqarah, it too was revealed before the Conquest, as is indicated by what precedes it of His saying ﴿and expel them from where they expelled you﴾, meaning from Makkah, and that was done on the day of the Conquest. How then could what is revealed after it be abrogated by it? Rather, the reason is that the establishment of **ijma'** (consensus) on its abrogation is sufficient in the matter, without any need for its chain of transmission to reach us. It is established that the Prophet (ﷺ) besieged al-Ta'if ten nights before the end of Muharram.

**﴿wherever you find them﴾**: within the sacred area or outside it. **﴿and seize them﴾**: i.e., take them captive; *al-akhidh* is the captive. **﴿and besiege them﴾**: i.e., bind them, or prevent them from roaming the lands.

Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them) said: "Prevent them from reaching the Sacred Mosque."

**﴿and lie in wait for them at every place of ambush﴾**: i.e., every passage and route through which they pass on their journeys. It is in the accusative of place, meaning: watch them and observe them so that they do not pass through it. Its benefit, according to the second interpretation, is to exclude the possibility that "besiege" means the well-known siege.

**﴿But if they repent﴾** from polytheism by faith, after they have been pressed by what was mentioned of killing, capture and besieging, **﴿and establish prayer and give zakat﴾**, confirming their repentance and faith. Mention of these two is sufficient in place of the rest of the acts of worship, because they are the foremost of physical and financial worship. **﴿then let them go their way﴾**: leave them and their affairs, and do not harass them with anything of what has been mentioned. **﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾**: He forgives them what preceded of disbelief and treachery, and rewards them for their faith and acts of obedience. This is the reason given for the command to let them go their way.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 6:

﴿And if any one of the polytheists seeks your protection﴾ This begins the explanation of the ruling concerning those who approach the beginnings of repentance by hearing the words of God Most High and standing before the rites of the religion, following the explanation of the ruling concerning those who repent of disbelief and those who persist in it. It is in the nominative by an implied condition which the apparent text explains, not by the inceptive (ibtida'); because in (in, "if") does not enter except upon a verb.

﴿from the polytheists seeks your protection﴾ after the expiry of the appointed term, i.e., asks you to grant him safe-conduct and to be a protector (jar) for him. ﴿then grant him protection﴾ i.e., give him security, ﴿until he hears the words of God﴾ and reflects upon them, and comes to know the reality of what you call to. The restriction to mentioning hearing is because there is no need for anything else in understanding, since they are people of eloquence (lasan) and fluency (fasahah). And "until" (hatta), whether it is for the limit (li-l-ghayah) or for causation (li-l-ta'lil), relates to what follows it and not to the words of God Most High "seeks your protection," because that would lead to making hatta operate upon a pronoun, which is something hardly committed except out of poetic necessity, as in the verse:

Poem: "By God, no people will find a youth who would hold you back, O son of Abi Yazid."

So it is said, however, the relation of the granting of protection to the hearing of the words of God Most High, in one of the two aspects, necessitates the relation of the seeking of protection also to that, or to what has its meaning among the matters of religion. And what is related from 'Ali - may God be pleased with him - that a man from the polytheists came to him and said: "If a man from among us wishes to come to Muhammad after the expiry of this term to hear the words of God Most High or for a need, will he be killed?" He said: "No; for God Most High says: ﴿And if any one of the polytheists seeks your protection, then grant him protection...﴾" etc. So what is meant by the need in it is the need related to religion, not what includes it and other worldly needs, as his saying "to come to Muhammad" indicates, for whoever comes to him (ﷺ) comes only for matters related to religion.

﴿Then convey him to his place of safety﴾ after his hearing it, if he does not believe, ﴿his place of safety﴾ i.e., his dwelling in which he is secure, which is the abode of his people. ﴿That﴾ meaning: the command of granting protection and conveying him to safety ﴿is because they﴾ are ﴿a people who do not know﴾ what Islam is and what its reality is; or they are an ignorant people, so it is necessary to give them safe-conduct until they understand the truth and they have no excuse at all.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 9, Verse 7**

﴿How can there be a covenant for the polytheists?﴾ This begins the verification of the truth of what preceded concerning the disavowal (al-bara'ah) and its branching rulings, and the clarification of the wisdom that calls for it. The intended "polytheists" are those who broke their covenants, since the disavowal concerns them specifically. The interrogative is one of denial (istifham inkari), not in the sense of denying the reality of the occurrence, as in His saying: ﴿How can you disbelieve in God?﴾ ... and so on, but in the sense of denying that it occurs. This is from the complete verb "to be" (al-kawn al-tamm), and "how" (kayfa) is in a position of accusative (nasb) by analogy with the circumstantial (al-hal) or the adverbial of place (al-zarf).

(p-45) It is also said: it is from the incomplete verb "to be" (al-kawn al-naqis), and "how" is the predicate of "yakunu" (is/can be), placed before its subject, which is "covenant" (ahd), because it requires precedence (al-sadarah). "For the polytheists" is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial (hal) of "covenant"; had it been placed after it, it would have been a qualifier (sifah) of it. Or it is connected to "yakunu," according to those who permit the verbs of incompleteness to govern adverbs of place. "'Inda" (with) is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a qualifier of "covenant," or to itself, since it is a verbal noun (masdar), or to "yakunu" as mentioned before. It is permissible that the predicate be "for the polytheists" with "'inda" as mentioned, or connected to the stability (al-istiqrar) that is attached to "for the polytheists." It is also permissible that the predicate be "'inda Allah" (with God), and "for the polytheists" is either a specification (tabyin), or a circumstantial of "covenant," or connected to "yakunu" or to the stability attached to the predicate. There is no concern about placing the complement of the predicate before the subject, because it is a preposition (harf jarr). "How" in the last two cases is in the accusative by analogy with the adverb of place or the circumstantial, as in the case of the complete verb, and this is preferable, because in denying the establishment of the covenant in itself there is an emphasis that is absent in denying its establishment for the polytheists. This is because its establishment as a relational predicate (al-thubut al-rabiti) is a branch of its establishment as a substantive existence (al-thubut al-'aini), so the negation of the root necessarily entails the negation of the branch entirely. In directing the denial to the manner of the covenant's establishment there is an emphasis that is absent in directing it to its establishment, because every existing thing must necessarily exist in some state or other; so when all the states of its existence are negated, its existence is negated by way of demonstrative proof (al-tariq al-burhani), i.e., in what state (or in which state) does there exist for them a covenant that is worthy of regard?

﴿With God and with His Messenger﴾ — it deserves that its rights be observed and that it be protected until the term is completed, and that they not be attacked in accordance with it by killing or seizing. As for their being secure through it from the punishment of the Hereafter, as has been said, there is no way to consider this at all, since their covenant has no bearing on that security whatsoever. And although it is observed by God and by His Messenger, like the covenant of those who did not break their word. The repetition of the word "'inda" (with) is to signal that it is not taken into account by each of them separately.

﴿Except those﴾ is an exception (istidrak) from the negation understood from the interrogative, which is readily understood to include all who had made covenants. That is: but those ﴿with whom you made a covenant at the Sacred Mosque﴾ — and they are the ones excepted in what preceded. The mention of the covenant being made at the Sacred Mosque is to add clarity about its parties and to indicate the reason for its solemnity. Its place is nominative (raf') by way of inception (ibtida'), and its predicate is His saying: ﴿So as long as they are upright toward you, be upright toward them.﴾ The fa' (so) is because it implies the meaning of a conditional. "Ma" (as long as) is either a verbal particle (masdariyyah) in the accusative by way of the adverbial, with an elided noun (taqdir al-mudaf), meaning: "so be upright toward them for the duration of their uprightness toward you"; or it is a conditional particle in the accusative by way of temporal adverb, meaning: "whatever time they are upright toward you, be upright toward them"; or it is in the nominative by way of inception, with an omitted resumptive pronoun, meaning: "whatever time they are upright toward you in it, be upright toward them in it." It is said: the exception is a contiguous one (muttasil), its place being in the accusative according to the original, or in the genitive by way of apposition (badal) from "the polytheists," and what is meant by them is the category, not a specific known group. Whichever is the case, the ruling of the command to be upright ends with the end of the covenant's term, because their uprightness that was timed to its period, which is the uprightness commanded, is an expression for observing the rights of the covenant. After the expiry of its term there is no covenant and no uprightness, so this becomes the very command that came in what preceded, where it was said: ﴿(Then fulfill for them their covenant until their term)﴾, except that it has here explicitly stated what was not explicitly stated there, although it is certainly taken into account, namely the restriction of the completion commanded to their continuing in the fidelity they had maintained. ﴿Indeed, God loves the righteous﴾ is a reason for the command to be upright, and an indication that carrying out the obligations of the covenant is among the requirements of piety, as has passed.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 8:

﴿How?﴾ is a repetition to express disapproval (istinkar) of what was mentioned earlier, namely that the polytheists should have a covenant worthy of being honoured before Allah, may He be glorified, and before His Messenger (ﷺ). As for what has been said, that it expresses the improbability (istib'ad) of their steadfastness in the covenant, it is as you see, because what is mentioned as a justification (ta'lil) for improbability is itself the very fact of their non-steadfastness in the covenant, not something that calls for it. The disapproval and improbability are repeated only for emphasis and to prepare for enumerating the causes that necessitate them, because of a disruption that intervened between them and what precedes, in terms of connection and proximity. The omission of the verb being disapproved of signals that the mind is present with it and anticipating what would make its disapproval necessary, not merely because it is known, as in the line of verse:

"You two informed me that death is only in the villages,
So how, when here are the hill and the well?"

For this is a justifying cause ('illah musahhahah), not a preponderating one (murajjihah). That is: how can they have a covenant that is valued before Allah, may He be exalted, and before His Messenger (ﷺ)?! ﴿And if they gain the upper hand over you﴾, that is: while their state is that if they gain the upper hand over you, meaning prevail over you, ﴿they will not observe toward you﴾, that is, they will not respect your rights. The original sense of ruqub is looking with the intent of guarding and protecting, and from it comes "raqib" (watcher). It was then used for protection in general. Al-muraqabah is more emphatic than it, as al-mura'ah is. In the negation of ruqub there is an emphasis not found in the negation of its synonyms.

﴿neither kinship nor covenant﴾, that is, an alliance (hilf). It was also said: kinship. And neither a covenant, or a right that would be blamed for neglecting, despite what has preceded from them of emphatic oaths and pledges. The meaning is: the obligation to observe the rights of the covenant on each of the two contracting parties is conditional on the other observing them. So if the polytheists do not observe them, how can you observe them?! Along the lines of the saying of one who said:

"Why would you accept ransom from them when they
Have accepted from us neither silver nor gold?"

It was also said: al-ill is one of the names of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, meaning they do not observe the right of Allah, may He be exalted. It was also said: al-jiwar (protection), and its outcome is alliance, because when they clasp hands and make alliances, they raise their voices with it to publicize it. Since linking the non-observance of the covenant to their gaining the upper hand could suggest that they observe it when they do not have that power, Allah disclosed the reality of their conditions, both manifest and hidden, by way of resumption (isti'naf), and made clear that even in a state of incapacity they have no share in fidelity, and that what they display is flattery (mudahanah), not truce (muhadanah). Thus it is said: ﴿They please you with their mouths﴾, where they display fidelity and friendship, promise you faith and obedience, confirm that with false oaths, and, when their opposite is apparent, offer false excuses. Attributing the pleasing to the mouths signals that their speech is merely words they utter without any corresponding reality in their hearts. ﴿But their hearts refuse﴾ what their speech conveys. ﴿And most of them are defiant﴾, that is, outside obedience, for observing the rights of a covenant is a matter of obedience. They are rebellious, possessing no restraining manliness (muru'ah) and no restraining creed, and they do not conceal themselves as some of those do who avoid treachery and refrain from what would bring about an evil reputation.

﴿They have traded away the signs of Allah﴾ by His signs that command fulfilling covenants and uprightness in every matter, or by all of His signs, so that what has been mentioned enters it by primary inclusion. That is, they abandoned them and took in their place ﴿a small price﴾, meaning something base from the perishable goods of this world, namely their desires and lusts which they followed, or what Abu Sufyan spent of food and distributed among the Bedouins. ﴿So they averted﴾, that is, they deviated and swerved, from ṣadda ṣudūdan (ṣadda), or they turned others away, from ṣadda ṣaddan. The fa' indicates that buying was the cause of this. ﴿from His way﴾, that is, the true religion from which there is no deviation, and the idafa (construct) is for honour; or the way of His Sacred House, since they used to turn away pilgrims and visitors from it.

﴿Indeed, evil is what they used to do﴾, that is, "wretched is what they were doing," or "their continuous deed." The one being dispraised is omitted. It has also been permitted that the word sā'a (ساءَ) remain in its original usage, intransitive, meaning "was ugly" (qabuha), or be transitive with an omitted object, meaning "what they were doing harmed them," or "their deed." And the saying of His, Mighty and Exalted:

(p-47)

The verse, ﴿They do not observe, regarding a believer, either ties of kinship or a covenant﴾, censures them for failing to respect the rights of covenants with believers in general, so there is no repetition. It has also been said that this refers to the Jews, or to the Bedouins mentioned earlier and those who follow their course. As for what has been said, that it is an explanation of Allah's words "they do" (*ya'malun*), or evidence for what is specifically blameworthy, this implies that blame and evil are confined to this conduct of theirs and not to anything else. ﴿And those﴾, the ones described by the evil qualities enumerated, ﴿they are the transgressors﴾, those who exceed the utmost limit of injustice and wickedness.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 11:

﴿Then if they repent﴾ i.e., from what they are upon of disbelief and all other grave sins. The fa' (fa, the particle of consequence) is for indicating that rebuking them for the evil deeds of theirs that have been mentioned is a deterrent from them and a likely cause of repentance, ﴿and establish the prayer and give the zakat﴾ i.e., they commit themselves to both and resolve to maintain them, ﴿then they are your brothers﴾ i.e., then they are your brothers.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿in religion﴾ is related to "your brothers," because of what it contains of the meaning of a verb, i.e., they have what you have and they have what is upon you; so treat them as brothers. In it is a conciliation of them and winning of their hearts beyond which there is no increase. The difference between the answer of this conditional sentence and the answer of the one that came before it, while the condition is the same in both, is because the first was introduced right after the command to kill and its counterparts, so its answer had to be a command of the opposite kind; and this one was introduced after the ruling on them regarding transgression and its like, so its answer must definitely be a ruling of the opposite kind.

﴿And We detail the verses﴾ i.e., We make them clear. What is meant by them is either the verses already mentioned that relate to the states of the polytheists, including the covenant-breakers and others, and their rulings in the two states of disbelief and belief, or all the verses, in which case those verses are included in them as a primary inclusion. ﴿for a people who know﴾ i.e., the rulings contained in them, or for a people who have knowledge. This is an interjection urging reflection upon the rulings embedded within them and adherence to them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 12:

﴿And if they break their oaths﴾ is coordinated with His statement, exalted is He, "But if they repent." That is, if they do not do that, but rather break ﴿their oaths after their covenant﴾, the one confirmed by them, and reveal what is in their hearts of evil, and bring it from potential into action, as His statement, exalted is He, indicates: "And if they gain the upper hand over you, they will not observe any tie of kinship or covenant" ... the verse. Or they persist in the breaking of oaths in which they are, not that they apostatized after faith, as has been said. ﴿And they revile your religion﴾: they disparaged it with explicit denial and disparagement of its rulings. ﴿So fight the leaders of disbelief﴾: that is, fight them. The noble composition has preferred this wording only to announce that by this they became people of leadership and precedence in disbelief, deserving of killing and fighting. It has been said that what is meant by "their leaders" is their chiefs and their champions. Singling them out for mention is either because of the importance of killing them, or to prohibit showing them mercy because they are the likely source of it, or to indicate their complete eradication, for their being killed generally happens after the killing of those below them. It is recited as "a'immata" with both hamzas pronounced in full, according to the original form, but the most eloquent is to render the second one "between between" (bayn bayn, an intermediate pronunciation of the hamza between hamza and the vowel it resembles). (p-48) As for making the ya' explicit, it is a manifest error according to al-Farra' (the grammarian). ﴿Indeed, they have no oaths﴾: that is, in reality, since they do not observe them and do not regard breaking them as something to be feared, even if they utter them with their tongues. The negation has been attached to oaths, like the breaking in what preceded, and not to the covenant confirmed by them, because oaths are the mainstay of pledges. Making the sentence a reason for the command to fight does not agree with its being linked to the breaking and the reviling, because their state in having no oaths in reality after the breaking and the reviling is like their state before that. Taking it to mean that their oaths no longer remain after the breaking and the reviling, although there is no need to explain this, goes against the apparent meaning. Perhaps the better course is to make it a reason for the content of the condition, as if it were said: "If they break and revile, as is expected of them, since they have no oaths in reality for them to refrain from breaking," or for the continuation of the fighting commanded, which is derived from the context of the discourse, as if it were said: "Fight them until they believe, for they have no oaths, until another covenant is made with them." It is also recited with a kasra on the hamza, as a verbal noun meaning the granting of security, that is: there is no way for you to grant them security after that, ever. As for the reverse, as has been said, there is no basis for it, since it implies that their treaty with us is such that the granting of security comes from them, and that is manifestly invalid. Or it may mean Islam, and then its being a reason for the command to fight is problematic, indeed impossible: for if it is taken to mean the absence of Islam absolutely, it has no connection to being the cause of fighting, or of the command to it, just as before the breaking and the reviling. And if it is taken to mean its absence in what is to come, then it does not suit making cessation the limit of fighting in what will follow. So the proper course is to make it a reason for what was mentioned from the content of the condition, as if it were said: "If they break and revile," which is the apparent state of them, since they have no Islam for which they would refrain from breaking the kind of their oaths, or from reviling your religion.

﴿That perhaps they may desist﴾: this is connected to His statement, exalted is He, "So fight." That is: fight them with the intention that they desist. That is, let your aim in fighting be their desisting from the disbelief they are in and from the other grave deeds they commit, not inflicting harm upon them, as is the habit of those who harm.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 13:

﴿Will you not fight﴾ The interrogative hamza (al-hamza, the question particle) that enters on the negation of their fighting is for rebuke and reproach. It indicates urging them to fight, by way of leading them to acknowledge that it has been negated. It is as if this were a matter that cannot be admitted willingly, because of its utter ugliness. So they are driven to it, and they cannot bring themselves to admit it, and so they choose to fight. ﴿a people who broke their oaths﴾ which they swore at the time of the treaty, that they would not assist against them, but they assisted the Banu Bakr against Khuza'ah. ﴿and they plotted to expel the Messenger﴾ from Makkah, when they consulted together about his affair in the Dar al-Nadwa (the Assembly House of Quraysh), as mentioned in His saying, (And when those who disbelieved plotted against you). This would be a censure of them for their earlier crime. It was also said that they are the Jews, who broke the covenant of the Messenger (ﷺ) and plotted to expel him from Madinah. ﴿And they began against you﴾ with hostility and fighting ﴿the first time.﴾ This is because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) first came to them with the Clear Book and challenged them with it, but they turned away from argument, being unable to match it, and resorted to fighting. Or it means they began fighting the Khuza'ah, allies of the Prophet (ﷺ), since assisting the Banu Bakr against them is fighting alongside them.

﴿Do you fear them?﴾ That is: do you fear that some harm from them will befall you, so that you abandon fighting them? He first rebuked them for abandoning fighting them and urged them to it, then he described them with what makes desire for fighting them necessary, and confirms that whoever has these evil qualities deserves not to have his opposition abandoned, and that whoever neglects this should be rebuked. ﴿Allah is more deserving that you fear Him﴾ (p-49) by opposing His command and abandoning the fight against His enemies, ﴿if you are believers.﴾ For the requirement of faith is to restrict fear to Him, the Exalted, and to have no concern for anyone else. In this there is an emphasis of severity that is not hidden.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 14:

﴿Fight them﴾ is an unrestricted command to fighting (tajrid lil-amr bil-qital) after the rebuke for abandoning it, a promise of their victory, of punishing their enemies and humiliating them, and encouragement for them. ﴿Allah will punish them by your hands and disgrace them﴾ through killing and capture, ﴿and give you victory over them﴾, that is: He will make you all prevailing over them, all of them. For this reason, the punishment and the disgrace are mentioned before (the victory) (ukhkhira 'an al-ta'dhib wal-ijza', i.e., the victory is postponed in its mention relative to them). ﴿And He will heal the breasts of a believing people﴾ from among those who did not witness the fighting, and they are Khuza'ah.

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "They are tribes from Yemen and Saba' who came to Makkah and embraced Islam, and they suffered much harm from its people, so they sent to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) complaining to him. He (ﷺ) said: 'Rejoice, for relief is near.'"

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 15:

﴿And He will remove the rage of their hearts﴾ by what they endured of hardships and plots. Allah, glory be to Him, fulfilled all that He had promised them in the most beautiful manner, so His informing the Prophet (ﷺ) of this before it occurred was a great miracle. ﴿And Allah forgives whom He wills﴾ is a new (independent) statement that gives notice of what would happen from some of the people of Makkah in the way of accepted repentance, in accordance with His, exalted is He, will based on profound wisdoms. Thus it came to pass, for some of them embraced Islam and their Islam was sound. It was also read with the accusative (manṣūb), by supposing (an) (anna, "that") to be implied, and the repentance enters into what the command is answered with according to the sense: for fighting, just as it is a cause of breaking their strength and softening their obstinacy, is also a cause of reflecting on their situation and their repentance from disbelief and sins. Because of the difference in the aspect of causation, the construction was altered. And Allah, exalted is He, knows best.

﴿And Allah﴾ — the choice of stating the Divine Name explicitly rather than using a pronoun is to cultivate awe and bring about reverence. ﴿Is All-Knowing﴾ — nothing hidden is concealed from Him. ﴿All-Wise﴾ — He does not act or command except with what contains wisdom and benefit.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 16:

﴿Or did you think﴾ "Am" here is disjunctive (munqati'a), brought to indicate a transition from the preceding rebuke to another. The interrogative hamza of denial (al-hamza al-istifhamiyya al-inkariyya) that accompanies it is a rebuke to them for the supposition mentioned, meaning: "Rather, did you suppose ﴿that you would be left﴾ in the state you are in, and not be commanded to fight, and not be tested with that which would purify you?" The address is either to those among the believers for whom fighting was hard, or to the hypocrites. ﴿While Allah has not yet known those of you who strove﴾ The "wa" is circumstantial (haliyya), and "lamma" is for negation together with expectation (al-nafy ma'a al-tawaqqu'). The intended meaning of the negation of knowledge is the negation of the thing known by way of demonstrative proof (al-tariq al-burhani), since if the scent of existence were detected, it would be known with certainty; so when it is not known, its non-existence is necessarily certain. That is: "Or did you suppose that you would be left while the state is that the sincere among you who strove have not yet been distinguished from others?" The expectation contained in "lamma" alerts that this will come to pass. The purpose of expressing the non-distinction mentioned by the non-knowledge of Allah the Exalted is that what is intended is distinction in terms of it being an object of knowledge and the basis of reward; and there is no mention of the state of those who fall short, because that is far from being included within the will of the Most Generous of the generous.

﴿And did not take﴾ This is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon "jahadu" (strove), falling within the scope of the relative clause (al-sila), or it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from its subject, meaning: they strove while not taking ﴿besides Allah, His Messenger, or the believers, any intimate (waliyja)﴾, that is, a confidant and a person of secrets, the one to whom you reveal what is in your heart of hidden secrets; from "walaj," which means entering. "Besides Allah" is connected to "taking" if it is left in its original state, or it is a second object of it if it is taken to mean "making to flow" (al-taysir).

﴿And Allah is Aware of what you do﴾ That is, of all your deeds. It is read in the third person (ghayba). This is a concluding phrase (tadhyil) that removes what might be suspected from the apparent meaning of His words, "while Allah has not yet known..." etc., or it is an interlocking circumstantial clause (hal mutadakhila) from its subject or from its object. The meaning is: "while Allah has not yet known those of you who strove," and the state is that He knows all your deeds; nothing of them is hidden from Him.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 17:

﴿It is not for the polytheists﴾ That is: it is not valid nor proper for them, in the sense of negating existence and actualization, not negating permissibility, as in His Exalted saying: "Those—it was not for them to enter them except in fear" (Q 2:114), meaning: it did not occur nor was it realized for them ﴿to maintain﴾ the mosques of God, [maintaining them] in a manner that is counted as valid, ﴿the mosques of God﴾, that is: the Sacred Mosque (al-Masjid al-Haram). It is said in the plural because it is the qibla (direction of prayer) of the mosques and their leader (imam), so its maintainer is like the maintainer of them all; or because each side of it, with its differing directions, is a mosque in itself, unlike other mosques, since their sides do not differ in direction. This is supported by the reading in the singular. It is also said: it was not for them to maintain any of the mosques, let alone the Sacred Mosque, which is the foremost of the category (sadr al-jins). This is rejected by the fact that they did not take it upon themselves to maintain the other mosques, nor did they boast of that. Moreover, this interpretation is based on the negation being in the sense of negating permissibility and propriety, rather than negating existence.

﴿bearing witness against themselves to disbelief﴾ That is: by displaying the traces of polytheism, such as setting up idols around the House and worshipping them, for that is a clear testimony against themselves to disbelief, even if they refuse to say "we are disbelievers"—as is reported from al-Hasan, may God be pleased with him. This is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in (ya'muru) [they maintain]. That is: it is impossible that what they call maintenance is the maintenance of the House of God, given their association with what contradicts it and nullifies it, namely the worship of other than Him, Exalted is He, for such worship is not part of maintenance at all. As for what has been said, that the meaning is: it was not proper for them to combine two contradictory matters—the maintenance of the House of God, Exalted is He, and the worship of other than Him, Exalted is He—this does not convey the essence of the intended meaning, for the impropriety of combining two contradictories only requires the negation of one of them, not specifically, and not the negation of maintenance, which is the intended point.

It is narrated that the Muhajirun and the Ansar came upon the prisoners of Badr, reproaching them for polytheism, and 'Ali, may God be pleased with him, began to rebuke al-'Abbas for fighting the Prophet (ﷺ) and severing the ties of kinship, and spoke harshly to him. Al-'Abbas said: "You mention our faults and conceal our virtues." He said: "Do you have virtues?" They said: "Yes; indeed, we maintain the Sacred Mosque, we serve the House, we give drink to the pilgrims, and we ransom the captive." So this verse was revealed.

﴿Those﴾, who claim the maintenance of the mosque and what resembles it of acts of righteousness, together with the disbelief that is in them, ﴿their deeds have become worthless﴾, the deeds in which they take pride, because of the disbelief accompanying them, so they became "scattered dust" (Q 25:23). ﴿And in the Fire they will abide forever﴾ because of their disbelief and their sins. The use of the nominal sentence is for emphasis in indicating eternity, and the adverbial phrase is connected to the predicate, placed before it for emphasis and to observe the rhyme (fasila). Both sentences are resumptive, establishing the earlier negation: the first from the aspect of negating the consequence of reward, and the second from the aspect of negating the averting of punishment.

(p-51) ﴿Innama ya'muru masajida Allah﴾ The discussion regarding the use of the plural form here is as has passed previously, except that the intention of all mosques, and the inclusion of the Sacred Mosque (al-Masjid al-Haram) within that, does not contradict the requirement of the context, for affirmation is not like negation. It has also been read in the singular (al-masjid). The purpose here too is to restrict the realization and existence of the building (of mosques) to the believers, not to restrict its permissibility and fitness; that is, it is only correct and fitting that one should build them with a building that is counted, ﴿[for] whoever believes in Allah﴾ alone, ﴿and the Last Day﴾ with what it contains of resurrection, reckoning and recompense, as the revelation has declared, ﴿and establishes the prayer and gives the zakat﴾ in accordance with what is known of the religion. Thereby the belief in the prophethood of the Prophet (ﷺ) is necessarily included. It has also been said that it is included under belief in Allah alone, since one of the two parts of the testimony of faith (kalimat al-shahada) stands for the whole; that is, only one who combines these scientific and practical perfections builds them. By "building" is meant what encompasses the repair of what has fallen into disrepair, sweeping it, cleaning it, adorning it with carpets, illuminating it with lamps, perpetuating worship and remembrance in it, studying the sciences in it, and the like, and guarding it from what it was not built for, such as worldly talk.

And from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Talk in the mosque devours good deeds as the beast devours grass."

And he (ﷺ) said: "Allah the Exalted said: Indeed My houses on My earth are the mosques, and indeed those who visit them are their inhabitants. Blessed is the servant who purifies himself in his house and then visits Me in My house; it is a right upon the one visited to honour his visitor."

And from him (ﷺ): "Whoever becomes attached to the mosque, Allah the Exalted becomes attached to him."

And he (ﷺ) said: "When you see a man frequenting the mosques, then bear witness to his faith."

And from Anas (may Allah be pleased with him): "Whoever lights a lamp in a mosque, the angels and the bearers of the Throne will continue to seek forgiveness for him as long as its light remains in that mosque."

﴿And fears none﴾ in matters of religion ﴿except Allah﴾, so he acts according to the requirement of His command and prohibition, not taking in the cause of Allah the blame of any blamer, nor the fear of any oppressor. Thus included in it is not fearing at the time of fighting and the like.

As for the natural fear of frightening things, it is not of this category, nor does it fall under obligation and address. It has been said: they used to fear and hope in the idols, so the intention is to negate that fear from them.

﴿Perhaps those﴾ described with those beautiful attributes ﴿will be among the guided﴾ to their goals of Paradise and the various lofty aims it contains. The manifestation of their guidance, together with the noble qualities they possess, in the form of an expectation (fa-'asa / "perhaps"), serves to cut off the hopes of the disbelievers of reaching the stations of guidance and of benefiting from their deeds, through which they reckon themselves to be doing good, and to rebuke them by declaring them to be guided. For if the believers, with these perfections, have their matter lying between "la'alla" and "'asa," then what of the disbelievers, who are as they are and whose deeds are as they are?! In this there is also kindness to the believers, and encouragement for them to give precedence to the side of fear over the side of hope, and a rejection of excusing oneself by (appeal to) Allah the Exalted.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 9, verse 19:**

﴿Do you consider the providing of water for the pilgrims and the maintaining of the Sacred Mosque﴾ — that is, in virtue and in the height of rank — ﴿as [equal to] one who believes in God and the Last Day and strives in the way of God?﴾ The words *siqaya* (providing water) and *'imara* (maintaining/serving the mosque) are verbal nouns (*masdarani*, verbal nouns denoting actions), and it is not conceivable to liken them to concrete entities. Therefore, a genitive construction (*mudaf*) must be understood on one of the two sides, meaning: "Do you consider their people (*ahluhuma*) as [equal to] one who believes in God...?" This is supported by the reading of those who recited (*suqat al-hajj wa-'amarat al-masjid al-haram*, "the providers of water for the pilgrims and the maintainers of the Sacred Mosque") or (*ajataltumuha ka-iman man amana*, "Do you make them like the faith of one who believed?"), and so on.

On both interpretations, the address is either to the polytheists, by way of *al-iltifat* (a shift in grammatical address from the third person to the second), which is what is most apparent from specifying the mention of faith on the side of the thing likened to; or it is to some of the believers who preferred providing water, maintenance and the like over emigration (*hijra*), jihad and their counterparts. The latter is the more suitable, since the refutation of them suffices with a demonstration that they are not equal before God to the second group, and with a statement of the greater rank of the latter before God, in a manner that implies that the former are not entirely deprived. To take the sense of preference as relative to the claim of the unbelievers does not yield much benefit, for if it does not imply that they are not wholly deprived, it does not imply deprivation either. On the first interpretation, it is a rebuke of the polytheists, and its foundation is the denial that they are likened, in terms of their being characterized by the two attributes mentioned, regardless of their polytheism, to the believers in terms of their being characterized by faith and jihad; or the denial that the two attributes mentioned, in themselves, are likened to faith and jihad, setting aside their being accompanied by polytheism. As for considering that they are accompanied by polytheism, as has been said, the context rejects it. How could it not, when the nullification of their deeds by that consideration has already been explained, and that they are as nothing? Then rebuking them after that for likening these two to faith and jihad, and then refuting that with something that implies they are not wholly deprived of the basic virtue, as has been indicated, is something the revealed composition (*al-nazm al-tanzili*) does not support. Had that been intended, there would have been no need to establish the denial of the likening and emphasize it with something else, since nothing is more evidently false than likening the non-existent to the existent.

Thus the meaning is: "Do you consider the people of providing water and maintenance to be in virtue like one who believes in God and the Last Day and strives in His way? Or do you make them, in that respect, like faith and jihad? How far apart are they! For providing water and maintenance, although in themselves they are among the acts of piety and goodness, nevertheless, even if free of defects, are far from being fit to have their people likened to the people of faith and jihad, or themselves likened to the very essence of faith and jihad." This is His, Exalted and Majestic, saying: ﴿They are not equal before God﴾ — that is, the first group is not equal to the second in terms of each of them being characterized by its two attributes. It necessarily follows that there is no equality between the first two attributes and the latter two, because that is the basis of distinction between the two described parties. The predication of non-equality to the described parties is because the more important matter is to explain their difference. The negation and denial here, and what preceded, are directed at equality and likening, even though the claim of those among the polytheists and believers who boast of providing water and maintenance is only superiority, not equality or resemblance, in order to intensify the refutation of them. For the negation of equality and resemblance is, by a stronger argument, a negation of superiority. The sentence is either a resumption (*isti'naf*) to establish and emphasize the aforementioned denial, or it is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) of the two objects of *ja'ala* (to make), with the connecting element being the pronoun. As if it were said: "Do you make them equal to one another while they are differing before Him, exalted is He?"

As for His, Exalted is He, saying: ﴿And God does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾, it is a judgment against them that, together with their wrongdoing through associating partners with God and opposing the Messenger (ﷺ), they are astray in this equating, not guided to the path of knowing the truth and distinguishing the preponderant from the subordinate, and they are wrongdoers in placing each of the two in the position of the other. Within it is further affirmation of the non-equality between them. As for His, Exalted is He, saying:

The Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 9, verse 20:

﴿Those who believed, emigrated, and strove in the way of Allah with their wealth and their lives﴾ is a resumptive sentence (istinaf) explaining the degrees of their excellence, following the statement of non-equality and the misguidance and wrongdoing of the polytheists. It also adds emphasis on emigration (hijrah) and specifies the two types of struggle (jihad), to indicate that these are among the requirements of jihad. It is not that something was considered by way of compensation (tadarruk) that had not been considered earlier. That is: they, by virtue of possessing these praiseworthy attributes, ﴿are greater in rank with Allah﴾, meaning higher in station and more honored than whoever does not possess them, whoever he may be, even if he has attained all other perfections, among which are providing water (siqayah) and maintaining the sanctuary ('imarah).

﴿And those﴾, meaning those described by these excellent qualities, and the sense of distance in the demonstrative pronoun is to indicate the great distance of their rank in elevation, ﴿they are the victorious﴾, those specifically attributed with the great success, or with absolute success, as if the success of others is not success in comparison to theirs. As for the second interpretation, it is a rebuke to those among the believers who prefer providing water and maintaining the sanctuary over emigration and jihad.

It is narrated that 'Ali said to al-'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, after his conversion to Islam: "O uncle, will you not emigrate? Will you not join the Messenger of Allah ﷺ?" He replied: "Am I not in a better position than emigration? I provide water to the pilgrims to the House of Allah and maintain the Sacred Mosque." When this was revealed, he said: "I think I should leave our provision of water." The Prophet ﷺ said: "««Continue in your provision of water, for in it there is good for you.»»"

Al-Nu'man ibn Bashir narrated: "I was at the pulpit of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ when a man said: 'I do not care if I do no deed after providing water to the pilgrims.' Another said: 'I do not care if I do no deed after maintaining the Sacred Mosque.' Another said: 'Jihad in the way of Allah is better than what you have said.' 'Umar rebuked them, may Allah be pleased with him, and said: 'Do not raise your voices at the pulpit of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and it is Friday. But when you have prayed, I will ask the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about what you have disagreed upon.' He entered, and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed this verse."

The meaning: Do you consider the people of providing water and maintaining the sanctuary among the believers in virtue and rank as equal to one who believed in Allah and the Last Day and struggled in His way? Or do you consider the two of them equal to faith and jihad? The faith was not mentioned on the side of the compared item (al-mushabbah), although it is certainly taken into account, relying on the clarity of the matter and to indicate that the basis for denying the comparison is providing water and maintaining the sanctuary, not faith. Its mention was also not omitted on the side of the item compared to (al-mushabbah bihi), in order to strengthen the denial, to remind of the causes of superiority and the foundations of preference, and to indicate the complete inseparability between faith and what follows it. The meaning of non-equality with Allah, Exalted, according to this interpretation, is clear, and likewise the greater rank of the second group.

As for His statement, Exalted: ﴿And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾, what is meant is that He, Exalted, does not guide them to recognize the preferred from the less preferred, and their wrongdoing lies in placing each of the two in the place of the other. It does not mean the absence of guidance absolutely, nor wrongdoing in general. The restriction (qasr) in His statement, ﴿And those, they are the victorious﴾, in relation to the rank of the second group, or to absolute success, is a claim (idda'), as has passed. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 21:

﴿Their Lord gives them good tidings﴾ — it is also read with the lighter form (yubashshiruhum, with the doubled letter unstressed). ﴿of mercy from Him﴾ — great mercy — ﴿and approval﴾ — great — ﴿and gardens﴾ — lofty — ﴿for them, therein﴾ — in those gardens — ﴿is enduring bliss﴾, blessings that will never run out. The mention of the title "Lord" (rubbubiyya) serves to confirm the good tidings given and to nurture the one who receives them.

﴿Abiding therein forever.﴾ That is, in the Gardens. "Forever" (abadan) is an emphasis on the eternity (khulud), to further clarify the intended meaning, since the word may be used to mean a long stay.

﴿Indeed, with Allah is a great reward.﴾ There is no measure for the rewards of this world, or for the deeds that correspond to it, in comparison with it. The sentence is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) that serves as a justification (ta'lil) for what preceded.

(p-54) ﴿O you who believe, do not take your fathers and your brothers as allies﴾ is a prohibition addressed to each individual among those addressed, forbidding him from befriending any single one of the polytheists. This follows from the rule of matching the plural with the plural (*muqābalat al-jamʿ bi-l-jamaʿ*, the grammatical principle of pairing a plural with a plural), which requires that the individuals be distributed among the individuals, as in His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿and the wrongdoers have no helpers﴾. It is not a prohibition on befriending a group of them, since that is understood from the wording by implication (*dalālah*, indication) and not by explicit expression (*ʿibārah*, direct statement).

The verse was revealed concerning the emigrants (*muhājirūn*). When they were commanded to emigrate, they said: "If we emigrate, we will cut off our fathers, our sons, and our clan, our trade will cease, our wealth will perish, our homes will be ruined, and we will be left destitute." So the verse was revealed, and they emigrated. Then a man would be visited by his son, his father, his brother, or some other relative, and he would pay them no heed, would not host them, and would not spend on them. Afterward, they were granted a concession in this matter. It was also said that the verse was revealed concerning the nine men who apostatized and joined Mecca, as a prohibition on befriending them.

From the Prophet (ﷺ): "None of you will taste the sweetness of faith until he loves for the sake of Allah, and hates for the sake of Allah, until he loves for the sake of Allah the most distant of people from him, and hates for the sake of Allah the nearest of people to him."

﴿If they prefer disbelief﴾, that is, they choose it ﴿over faith﴾ and persist in it with such persistence that there is no hope of their ever giving it up at all. The linking of the prohibition on befriending them to this condition is because, before that, they might perhaps lead to Islam through their awareness of the excellences of the religion.

﴿And whoever among you takes them as allies﴾, that is, one of them, as has been indicated. The singular pronoun in the verb is for the sake of observing the wording of the relative pronoun (*alladhī*, "whoever"), and to indicate that each one of them is independent in being characterized by wrongdoing. It does not mean that the intended meaning is the befriending of a single individual. The word *min* (“among”) in His saying, exalted be He, ﴿you﴾ is for the category (*jins*, kind) and not for partitive division. ﴿Then those﴾, that is, those who take them as allies, ﴿they are the wrongdoers﴾, by placing friendship in other than its proper place, as though the wrongdoing of others were no wrongdoing at all in comparison with their wrongdoing.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 24:

﴿Say﴾ is a shift in the mode of address (talwin lil-khitab) and a command to him (ﷺ) to strengthen the believers and to firm up their resolve to refrain from what they were forbidden: taking as allies (muwalat) their fathers and brothers, to make them averse to them and to those who stand in their position among the sons and wives, and to cut their attachments to the adornments and finery of this world, by way of rebuke and warning.

﴿If your fathers, your sons, your brothers, your spouses﴾ He did not mention the sons and wives in what preceded, because taking sons and wives as allies is not customary, unlike love (al-mahabba). ﴿And your kinsfolk﴾, that is, their relatives, derived from al-'ushra (companionship), i.e. al-suhba; it was also said that it is from al-'ashara, for they are a group that returns to a bond like the bond of companionship. It is also read ('asheeratukum wa 'asha'irukum). ﴿And wealth you have acquired﴾, that is, gained; it is described thus to indicate its value in their eyes, since it was obtained by the toil of the hand. ﴿And commerce﴾, that is, goods you bought for trade and profit. ﴿Which you fear will slump﴾ through the passing of the time of their sale due to your absence from Makkah the Honored during the days of the season. ﴿And dwellings you are pleased with﴾, that is, residences in which living delights you, of houses and gardens. The mention of the described attributes serves to announce that the blame for loving the aforementioned (p-55) adornments of the worldly life is not because of ignoring what they contain of the origins of love and the causes of desire for them, and that they, with their various kinds of beauty, are far from being preferred in love over the love of Him, the Exalted, and the love of His Messenger (ﷺ), as in His saying, Exalted and Majestic be He, ﴿What has deceived you concerning your Lord, the Generous?﴾.

﴿More beloved to you than God and His Messenger﴾ with the chosen love (al-hubb al-ikhtiyari) that entails its effect, which is constancy and not separating oneself, not the natural love (al-hubb al-jibilli) from which humans are not free, for it does not fall under the obligation that is bound by capacity. ﴿And striving in His cause﴾: His love is arranged in the same thread as the love of God, Exalted and Majestic be He, and the love of His Messenger (ﷺ), to exalt its status and to alert that it is among what must be loved, let alone hated, and to announce that loving him returns to loving them both, for jihad is an expression for fighting their enemies for the sake of their enmity; so whoever loves them both must love fighting those who do not love them. ﴿Then wait﴾, that is, await ﴿until God brings His command﴾. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that it is the conquest of Makkah. It was also said: it is an immediate or deferred punishment. ﴿And God does not guide the defiant people﴾, those who depart from obedience in allying with the polytheists, or the defiant people in general, so that these enter among them at the first level; that is, He does not guide them to what is good for them. In this noble verse there is a threat from which almost no one escapes except one whom the kindness of his Lord overtakes. And God is the One sought for help.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 25:

﴿Indeed, Allah has given you victory﴾. The address is specifically to the believers, ﴿on many occasions﴾ of battle. The word translated as "occasions" (mawatin, sing. mawtin) means places of encounter and standing positions. What is meant by them are the battles of Badr, Qurayzah, al-Nadir, al-Hudaybiyah, Khaybar, and the Conquest of Makkah. ﴿And on the day of Hunayn﴾ is conjoined to the grammatical position of (fi mawatin) by omitting a genitive-governed noun in one of the two phrases, meaning: "and [the] occasion of the day of Hunayn," or "in the days of many occasions and the day of Hunayn." Perhaps the change of expression (to "the day of Hunayn") is an allusion to the lack of steadfastness that occurred there at the outset of the matter. It has also been said that what is meant by "mawtin" (occasion) is a time, like the killing of al-Husayn. It has also been said that (yawma Hunayn) is in the accusative, governed by a hidden verb conjoined to (nasarakum), meaning: "and He gave you victory on the day of Hunayn."

﴿When your great number pleased you﴾ is a substitute (badal) for (yawma Hunayn), and there is no objection to its being conjoined to the grammatical position of the adverbial phrase, on the basis that there was no great number nor self-admiration in the conjoined-to element, since it is not a requirement of conjunction that the two conjoined elements share what the second is attributed to. Or it is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb: "remember" (udhkur).

Hunayn is a valley between Makkah and al-Ta'if. The battle took place there between the Muslims, who were twelve thousand, ten thousand of whom had witnessed the Conquest of Makkah from among the Emigrants and the Helpers, and two thousand from the Freed (al-Tulaqa'), and between Hawazin and Thaqif, who were four thousand, together with those who joined them from the reinforcements of the rest of the Arabs, and they were a vast multitude. When the two sides met, a man from the Muslims, whose name was Salamah ibn Salamah al-Ansari, said: "We will not be defeated today for lack of numbers." This displeased the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). They fought a fierce battle, the polytheists were routed and left behind their offspring (dhararri), so the Muslims threw themselves upon the spoils.
