The polytheists called out: "O protectors of evil, remember the disgraces!" So they turned back, and the word of self-admiration overtook the Muslims and they were routed. This is His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying: ﴿So their numbers availed you nothing﴾. Ighna' (availing) means giving what removes a need; that is, that great number did not give you anything by which you could remove your need, of the kind of provision (ighna').

﴿And the earth, with all its vastness, became constricted for you﴾, meaning: despite its breadth and expanse. Here "ma" is a verbal-masdar particle, and the "ba'" carries the sense of "ma'a" (with), meaning: you did not find in it any refuge in which your souls could find rest because of the severity of terror, nor did you stand firm in it as one who finds no room in which to stand.

﴿Then you turned back, retreating﴾. It is narrated that "their fleeing reached Makkah, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) remained alone, with none beside him except his uncle al-'Abbas, holding the bridle of his mule, and his cousin Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith, holding its stirrup, while he urged the mule toward the polytheists, saying: 'I am the Prophet, there is no lie; I am the son of 'Abd al-Muttalib.'"

It is narrated that he (ﷺ) would charge against the disbelievers, and they would flee, then they would charge against him, and he would stand firm before them. He did this some ten times. Al-'Abbas said: "I was restraining the mule lest it rush him toward the polytheists." And this single instance suffices as a testimony of truthfulness to his (ﷺ) courage and steadiness of heart, and his being foremost toward distant goals. This was only because he was supported by Allah, the Mighty, the Wise. At that point he said: "O Lord, bring me what You have promised me." He said to al-'Abbas, who had a loud voice: "Shout to the people." So he called out to the Helpers clan by clan, then he called: "O companions of the tree! O companions of the Surah of the Cow!" Whereupon they turned back as one body, saying: "Here we are, here we are!" And this is His, exalted is He, saying:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 26:

﴿Then God sent down His tranquility (sakinah) upon His Messenger﴾. That is: His mercy by which hearts are calmed and at rest, reaching a complete tranquility that entails a near victory. As for absolute tranquility (sakinah) in general, it had already been present in him ﷺ before that as well.

﴿And upon the believers﴾ is a conjunction with "His Messenger," and placing the preposition between the two serves to indicate the difference between them, i.e., the believers who had fled. It was also said: upon those who stood firm with the Prophet ﷺ, or upon all of them, and this is the more fitting view. There is no harm in the existence of the basic tranquility among those who stood firm earlier, and mentioning the attribute of faith serves to indicate that it is the cause of the sending down.

﴿And He sent down hosts you did not see﴾, i.e., with your eyes, as one of you sees another. They were the angels, peace be upon them, who had white marks on them, riding white-and-dark-spotted horses. When the Prophet ﷺ looked at the fighting of the Muslims, he said: "Now it is hot in the oven (hamiya al-watays)." Then he took a handful of dust and threw it toward the polytheists, saying: "May the faces be disfigured," and not one of them remained without his eyes being filled with it. Then the Prophet ﷺ said: "They have fled, by the Lord of the Ka'bah."

They differed about the number of angels on that day: it was said five thousand, it was said eight thousand, and it was said sixteen thousand. As for their fighting as well, it was said they fought, and it was said they did not fight except on the Day of Badr. Their descent was for strengthening the hearts of the believers by casting good thoughts, supporting them thereby, and casting terror into the hearts of the polytheists.

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: A man who was among the polytheists on the Day of Hunayn told me, saying: "When we routed the Muslims, we began driving them. When we reached the rider of the white mule, men with bright faces met us and said: 'May the faces be disfigured! Turn back!' So we turned back, and they mounted upon our shoulders."

﴿And He punished those who disbelieved﴾ with killing, capture and taking of captives. ﴿And that﴾, i.e., what was done to them of what has been mentioned, ﴿is the recompense of the disbelievers﴾ for their disbelief in this world.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 27:

﴿Then Allah relents after that toward whom He wills﴾: that He should relent toward some of them, by a wisdom that requires it; that is, He grants them success in Islam. ﴿And Allah is Oft-Forgiving﴾, who overlooks what has passed from them of disbelief and sins, ﴿Most Merciful﴾, who bestows His favor upon them and rewards them.

It has been related that «some men from them came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), pledged allegiance to him upon Islam, and said: "O Messenger of Allah, you are the best of people and the most righteous of people. Our women and children have been taken captive, and our wealth has been seized." It was said: On that day six thousand souls were taken captive, and camels and sheep were taken in countless numbers. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: «I have what you see. Indeed, the best speech is the truest. Choose either your offspring and your women, or your wealth»." They said: "We do not regard anything as equal to our lineages." The Prophet (ﷺ) stood up and said: «These people have come to us as Muslims, and we gave them the choice between the captives and the wealth, and they did not regard anything as equal to their lineages. So whoever has captives in his possession and is willing to return them, then it is his affair. And whoever is not, let him give us (his share), and it will be a debt upon us until we obtain something and give him its equivalent in its place." They said: "We are content and submit." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, we do not know, perhaps among you there is someone who is not content. So instruct your ʿurafāʾ (tribal chiefs and overseers) to bring that matter to us." Then the ʿurafāʾ reported to him that they were content.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 28:

﴿O you who have believed, the polytheists are only impure (najas)﴾ They are described with the verbal noun (masdar) for emphasis, as if they were the very essence of impurity; or they are possessors of impurity (dhu najas) because of the corruption of their inner selves; or because shirk, which they carry, is in the position of impurity; or because they do not purify themselves, do not perform ghusl, and do not avoid impurities, so impurity clings to them.

From Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him both, that their very persons are impure like dogs and swine. From al-Hasan: whoever shakes hands with a polytheist must perform wudu'. The schools of law (ahl al-madhahib) are opposed to these two opinions. It is also read as (nijs) with a kasrah on the nun and a sukun on the jim, which is a lightened form of najis, like kibd for kabid, as if it were said: the polytheists are an impure kind (jins najis) or an impure sort (darb najis). Most often it occurs as a follower of rijs.

﴿So let them not approach al-Masjid al-Haram﴾ This is a consequence (tafri') of their impurity. The prohibition of approaching is stated for emphasis, or for preventing entry into the Haram. This is the view of 'Ata'. It is said that what is meant is the prohibition of entering in general. It is also said that what is meant is the prohibition of Hajj and 'Umrah, and this is the view of Abu Hanifah, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him. His statement, Mighty and Majestic is He, ﴿after this year of theirs﴾ supports this, for restricting the prohibition to that confines the forbidden matter to a particular time of the year, i.e., they should not perform Hajj or 'Umrah after the Hajj of this year of theirs, which was the ninth year after the Hijrah, when Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, was appointed over the season (al-mawsim). 'Ali's statement, may Allah be pleased with him, when he proclaimed Bara'ah, supports this: "Let no polytheist perform Hajj after this year of ours." According to Abu Hanifah they are not prevented from entering the Haram, the Masjid al-Haram, or all other mosques. According to al-Shafi'i they are prevented from the Masjid al-Haram specifically. According to Malik they are prevented from all mosques. The prohibition of the polytheists from approaching it returns to the prohibition on Muslims enabling them to do so. It is also said that what is meant is that they be prevented from taking charge of the Masjid al-Haram and attending to its affairs, and be removed from that.

﴿And if you fear poverty﴾ That is, destitution resulting from preventing them from Hajj, and the cutting off of what they used to bring to you of provisions and profits. It is read as (a'ilah), taken as a verbal noun like al-'afiyah, or as a circumstantial accusative (hal) 'a'ilah. ﴿then Allah will enrich you out of His bounty﴾ from His giving, or from His favor in some other way. So Allah Almighty sent the sky upon them in abundant rain, by which He multiplied their good and increased their provisions. The people of Tabalah and Jurash embraced Islam, and they carried food and what sustains life to Makkah. That was more beneficial to them than what they feared poverty over, having lost it. Then He opened the lands and spoils for them, and people turned toward them from all corners of the earth.

﴿if He wills﴾ to enrich you. His will follows the wisdom that calls for it. He restricted it with this so that hopes would be cut off from anyone other than Allah Almighty, and because enrichment is not uniform according to individuals, conditions, and times. ﴿Indeed Allah is All-Knowing﴾ of your interests ﴿All-Wise﴾ in what He gives and withholds.

(p-58)﴿Fight those who do not believe in Allah or in the Last Day﴾. He commanded them to fight the People of the Two Books (Ahl al-Kitab) immediately after commanding them to fight the polytheists (mushrikun). He also commanded them to prevent the polytheists from circling around what they used to do of the pilgrimage (Hajj) and the minor pilgrimage (Umrah), without fearing the imagined poverty that might result from cutting off that trade. In the course of this, He alerted them to some of the means of enrichment that were promised in general terms, and guided them to pursue those means, seeking His bounty and asking Him to fulfil His promise. The expression of them by the relative pronoun (al-mawsul, "those who") indicates that what follows in the relative clause is the cause for the command to fight, and that by this cause they are placed in the same category as the polytheists. The Jews say that Allah has a son ('Uzayr), and the Christians are Trinitarians, so they are far from believing in Allah, glorified is He, and from believing in the Last Day, for their knowledge of the conditions of the Hereafter is no knowledge at all. Thus the faith on which they rest is not faith in Him.

﴿And do not forbid what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden﴾. That is, what has been established as forbidden by revelation, whether recited or not (in the Qur'an or otherwise). It has also been said that "His Messenger" refers to the Messenger whom they claim to follow; that is, they oppose the original basis of their abrogated (mansukh, "abrogated by later revelation") religion, both in belief and in practice. ﴿Nor do they adopt the religion of truth﴾, the established religion that abrogates all other religions, which is the religion of Islam. It has also been said that it means the religion of Allah. ﴿From among those who were given the Book﴾, from the Torah and the Gospel. The word "min" here is explanatory (bayaniyyah), not partitive (tab'idiyyah), so that it would not mean that some of them are contrary to what is described. ﴿Until they give﴾, that is, until they agree to give ﴿the jizyah﴾, that is, what has been imposed on them to pay. It is derived from "jaza daynahu," meaning he paid his debt; or because they repay with it the one who has granted them the favour of sparing them from being killed. ﴿With willing submission﴾ is a circumstantial phrase (hal) referring to the pronoun in "yu'tu" (they give). That is, with a willing, compliant hand, meaning as submissive subjects; or "from their hand," meaning handing it over by their own hands, not sending it through the hands of others, and for this reason it is forbidden to appoint an agent for it. Or it means "out of wealth," and for this reason the jizyah is not obligatory on a poor person who is unable to pay. Or it means "under a dominating hand over them," that is, by reason of a hand, meaning being powerless and humiliated. Or it means "as a favour to them," since preserving their lives in exchange for what they pay in jizyah is a great blessing upon them. Or "from the jizyah," meaning cash handed over hand to hand. The goal of fighting is not the act of giving itself, but accepting it, as has been indicated.

﴿And they are humbled﴾, that is, debased. This is done by having the payer bring it himself on foot, not riding, and hand it over while standing, while the one receiving it is seated, and by seizing him by the collar and saying to him, "Pay the jizyah," even if he is in the act of paying it.

The jizyah is taken, according to Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, from the People of the Book without qualification, and from the polytheists of non-Arab peoples (ajam), but not from the polytheists of the Arabs. According to Abu Yusuf, may Allah be pleased with him, it is not taken from an Arab, whether he is a People of the Book or a polytheist, and it is taken from a non-Arab, whether he is a People of the Book or a polytheist. According to al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, it is taken from the People of the Book, whether Arab or non-Arab, and it is not taken from the people of idols (ahl al-awthan) without qualification. Malik and al-Awza'i held that it is taken from all unbelievers.

As for the Majus (Zoroastrians), the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, agreed on taking the jizyah from them, based on the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Treat them as you treat the People of the Book."

It is narrated from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that they once had a book which they studied, then in the morning, their book had been taken away by night and lifted from among them. They also agreed on the prohibition of eating their slaughtered animals and marrying their women, based on the saying of the Prophet ﷺ at the end of the hadith as transmitted: "Except that you may not marry their women nor eat their slaughtered animals."

According to Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, the time for taking it is at the beginning of the year, and it lapses by death or by conversion to Islam. Its amount for a poor person who is able to work is twelve dirhams; for one of middling means, twenty-four dirhams; and for a wealthy person, forty-eight dirhams. The jizyah is not obligatory on a poor person (p-59) who is unable to earn, nor on a decrepit old man, nor a chronically ill person, nor a child, nor a woman.

According to al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, it is taken at the end of the year, one dinar from each person, whether he is wealthy or poor, whether he has earnings or not.

﴿And the Jews said﴾ This is an independent clause, brought in to confirm what has already been mentioned about the failure of the People of the Two Scriptures to believe in God, glorified be He, and their placement by that failure in the same category as the polytheists. ﴿Uzayr is the son of God﴾ This is a subject and predicate (mubtada' and khabar). It has also been read without tanwin (nunation), on the basis that it is a non-Arabic proper name, like Kaʿazir and ʿIzar, and so it is diptote (ghayr munsarif) because of its foreignness and definiteness. As for explaining its unnunated form by the meeting of two unvocalized letters (iltiqa' al-sakinayn), or by treating "son" (ibn) as a descriptive adjective with an omitted predicate, these are forced interpretations that are unnecessary.

It is said that this was the saying of their ancestors, after which it died out, and God, exalted be He, related it from them. The denial of the Jews carries no weight here. It is also said that it was the saying of some of those who were in Medina. Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with both of them, reported that some of them came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), namely Salam ibn Mishkam, Nuʿman ibn Awfa, Shas ibn Qays, and Malik ibn al-Sayf, and they said this.

It is also said that it was said by Finhas ibn ʿAzura, the one who said: "God is poor and we are rich." The cause of this saying was that the Jews killed the prophets after Moses, peace be upon him. So God, exalted be He, lifted the Torah from them and erased it from their hearts. Then ʿUzayr, who was a youth, went out wandering across the earth, and Gabriel, peace be upon him, came to him and said: "Where are you going?" He said: "I am seeking knowledge." So Gabriel made him memorize the Torah, and he dictated it to them from memory, without omitting a single letter. They said: "God would not have gathered the Torah in his breast while he was a youth unless he is His son."

Al-Imam al-Kalbi said: When Bukhtnassar (Nebuchadnezzar) killed all their scholars, ʿUzayr was then a young child, so he considered him insignificant and did not kill him. When the Children of Israel returned to Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), and there was no one among them who could read the Torah, God, exalted be He, sent ʿUzayr to renew the Torah for them, and to be a sign, after He had caused him to die for one hundred years.

It is said that an angel came to him with a vessel containing water and gave him to drink, and so it (the Torah) took shape in his breast. When he came to them and said, "I am ʿUzayr," they denied him. They said: "If you are as you claim, then dictate the Torah to us." So he did. They said: "God, exalted be He, would not have cast the Torah into the heart of a man except because he is His son. Exalted is God far above that, with a great exaltation."

On the authority of Ibn ʿAbbas, may God, exalted be He, be pleased with both of them: The Jews neglected the Torah and acted otherwise than the truth, so God, exalted be He, caused them to forget the Torah and removed it from their breasts. He also lifted up the Ark (al-tabut), so ʿUzayr entreated God, exalted be He, and beseeched Him, and the memorization of the Torah returned to his heart. He then warned his people of it. Then the Ark descended, and they compared what ʿUzayr had recited with what was in it, and they found it identical. So they said what they said.

﴿And the Christians said: the Messiah is the son of God﴾ This too is the saying of some of them. They said it because they deemed it impossible that there could be a child without a father, or because of his doing what he did, such as healing the blind (al-akmah) and the leper and raising the dead, which could only be done by one who is God.

﴿That﴾ is a demonstrative referring to what proceeded from them of the two great claims. The distal form in it (dhalika) indicates remoteness, to signal how far the thing referred to is in its outrageousness and monstrosity.

﴿Their saying with their mouths﴾ This either emphasizes the attribution of the said statement to them and denies any figurative meaning from it, or it indicates that it is a saying devoid of proof, and it is a realization akin to a meaningless utterance that exists only in mouths, without having any counterpart in external reality.

﴿They imitate﴾ That is, in disbelief and monstrosity. It has also been read without the hamza. ﴿the saying of those who disbelieved﴾ That is, their saying resembles—by omitting the first noun in the construct (al-mudaf) and placing the second noun (al-mudaf ilayh) in its position, which takes the nominative case—the saying of those who disbelieved ﴿before them﴾, that is, before them (their time), namely the polytheists who say: "The angels are the daughters of God," or "al-Lat and al-ʿUzza are the daughters of God," not their ancestors as has been said, since there is no multiplicity in the saying that would make the comparison workable. Making it (the comparison) between the two statements of the two groups, while the thing said is the same, adds no distinction.

It is said that the pronoun refers to the Christians, meaning: their saying "the Messiah is the son of God" resembles the saying of the Jews, "ʿUzayr..." etc., because they (the Jews) are older than them. This, too, as you see, requires that the refutation and invalidation expressed by His saying, exalted be He, "That is their saying with their mouths," be restricted to the saying of the Christians.

﴿God destroy them﴾ This is an invocation against all of them for destruction, since whoever God destroys is ruined. Or it expresses wonder at the monstrousness of their saying. ﴿How are they turned away?﴾ How are they diverted from the truth to falsehood, when in fact there is no path to it at all?!

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 31:

﴿They have taken﴾ is an added emphasis confirming their earlier disbelief in God, the Exalted. ﴿Their rabbis﴾, who are the scholars of the Jews. The singular of this word is disputed. Al-Asma'i said: "I do not know whether it is ḥabr or ḥibr." Abu al-Haytham said: "It is with a fatḥa only, and nothing else." Al-Layth and Ibn al-Sikkit used to say: ḥibr and ḥabr are both used for the scholar, whether he is a dhimmi or a Muslim, after having been among the People of the Book. ﴿And their monks﴾, who are the scholars of the Christians from among the people of the monasteries. That is, each of the two groups took its own scholars, not every one of them took every one of the others.

﴿As lords besides God﴾, by obeying them in making lawful what God, the Exalted, has made unlawful and making unlawful what He has made lawful, or by prostrating to them. Similar to this is the naming of following Satan as worship of him, in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿O my father, do not worship Satan﴾, and His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Rather, they used to worship the jinn﴾.

Adi ibn Hatim said: "I came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) with a gold cross around my neck, and at that time I was following a religion called al-Rakusiyya, a group of the Christians. He was reciting Surat Bara'a, and he said: 'O Adi, throw away this idol.' So I threw it away. When he reached His saying, the Exalted: (They have taken their rabbis and their monks as lords besides God), I said: 'O Messenger of God, they did not worship them.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Do they not make unlawful what God has made lawful, and you make it unlawful, and make lawful what God has made unlawful, and you make it lawful?' I said: 'Yes.' He said: 'That is their worship.'"

Al-Rabi' said: I said to Abu al-'Aliya: "How was that lordship among the Children of Israel?" He said: "They would sometimes find in the Book of God, the Exalted, something that contradicted the sayings of the rabbis, so they would take the sayings of the rabbis and leave the ruling of the Book of God." ﴿And the Messiah, son of Mary﴾ is conjoined to ﴿their monks﴾; that is, the Christians took him as a lord to be worshipped, after they had said that he was the son of God, exalted is He far above that by a great exaltation. Specifying the taking (of lords) with him indicates that the Jews did not do this with Uzair. His being placed last in mention, although their taking him as a lord to be worshipped is stronger than mere obedience in the matter of making lawful and unlawful (which is what is meant by their taking the rabbis and monks as lords), is because it is specific to the Christians. Attributing him (ﷺ) to his mother, in terms of her indicating his being a created one, which contradicts lordship, is to announce the complete feebleness of their opinion and to condemn them with the utmost ignorance and foolishness.

﴿And they were not commanded﴾, that is, the state is that those disbelievers were not commanded in their two scriptures ﴿except to worship one God﴾, of great station, who is God, glorified is He and exalted, and to obey His command and not obey the command of another contrary to it, for that undermines His worship, exalted is He. All the heavenly scriptures agree upon this entirely. The Messiah, peace be upon him, has said: ﴿"Indeed, whoever associates with God, God has forbidden him Paradise"﴾. As for obeying the Messenger (ﷺ) and all others whom God, the Exalted, has commanded to be obeyed, that is in reality obedience to God, Mighty and Majestic.

Or: and those whom the disbelievers took as lords, from the Messiah, the rabbis and the monks, were not commanded except to make God, the Exalted, one, so how could they be lords when they too are commanded and made to serve, like them? And it does not undermine this that the lordship of the rabbis and monks was by way of obedience, for specifying worship to Him, exalted is He, is not realized except by specifying obedience also to Him, exalted is He; and since they did not specify it to Him, they did not specify worship to Him, glorified is He.

﴿There is no god but He﴾ is a second attribute of ﴿a god﴾, or a resumptive statement confirming the Oneness. ﴿Glorified is He above what they associate﴾, above associating with Him in worship and obedience.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 32:

﴿They wish to extinguish the light of Allah﴾. The extinguishing of a fire is an expression for removing its flame, which necessarily results in the removal of its light, and not for removing its light directly, as some have said. However, since the purpose of extinguishing a fire that is intended only for its light, such as a lamp, is the removal of its light, the extinguishing of it became an expression for that. Then this usage spread until it became an expression for the removal of light in general, even when it is not of a fire. The secret behind this is that the possibility of removal is confined to its light. By the light of Allah, glorified is He, is meant either His clear proof, which indicates His oneness and His exemption from partners and offspring, or the Mighty Qur'an that declares this, i.e., the People of the Two Books wish to reject the Qur'an and deny it in what it declares of monotheism, of His exemption from partners and offspring, and of the laws, among which are the things they have opposed concerning what is permitted and what is forbidden.

﴿with their mouths﴾: with their false statements that come out of them, without there being any reality to which they correspond or any basis on which they rest, as is related about them. It has been said: the intended meaning is the prophethood of the Prophet ﷺ. It has also been said: their state in what has been mentioned is likened to the state of one who wishes to extinguish a great light spread across the horizons by a breath.

﴿But Allah refuses﴾, i.e., He does not wish, ﴿except that He perfect His light﴾ by exalting the word of monotheism and strengthening the religion of Islam. The exception from a positive statement is valid here, because it carries the meaning of negation, as has been pointed out, since it occurs in opposition to His words, "They wish." In it there is more emphasis and an indication of impossibility that is absent in the negation of wishing, i.e., He does not wish anything except the completion of His light, so that its remaining as it was is included in what is excepted from, let alone its extinguishing. In mentioning the light in the place where a pronoun would be expected, and attributing it to His pronoun, glorified and exalted is He, there is added care for its matter, an honoring of it upon honor, and an indication of the reason for the ruling.

﴿And even if the disbelievers dislike it﴾: the answer to (law, "even if") is omitted, because what precedes it indicates it. The clause is conjoined to a clause before it that is implied, and both are in the position of a circumstantial clause, i.e., Allah does not wish except the completion of His light, even if the disbelievers do not dislike that, and even if they dislike it, i.e., in every supposed state. The first was omitted regularly in this construction, because the second clearly indicates it; for when a thing is realized in the presence of the preventer, it is all the more realized in its absence. Upon this secret turns the emphasis found in the conjunctive particles *in* and *law*, and this has been clarified further many times.

﴿He it is Who sent His Messenger﴾ accompanied ﴿by guidance﴾, that is, the Qur'an, which is a guidance ﴿for the God-fearing﴾, ﴿and the religion of truth﴾, the established one, which is the religion of Islam, ﴿that He may make it prevail﴾, that is, His Messenger, ﴿over all religion﴾, that is, over the people of all the religions. Or [it means] that He may make the true religion prevail over all other religions by abrogating (naskh) them, as wisdom requires. The clause is an explanation and confirmation of the content of the preceding clause. The discussion of His words, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿even though the polytheists dislike it﴾ is as in what preceded, except that describing them with polytheism after describing them with disbelief (p-62) is to indicate that they combined disbelief in the Messenger with disbelief in God.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 34:

﴿O you who have believed﴾ This begins an explanation of the condition of the rabbis (ahbar) and monks (ruhban) in misleading their inferiors, following the explanation of the bad condition of the followers in taking them as lords, obeying them in commands and prohibitions, and following them in what they do and what they leave undone.

﴿Indeed, many of the rabbis and the monks consume the wealth of people unjustly﴾ They take it by way of bribery (rishwah), in exchange for altering the rulings and laws and for making them lenient and permissive. The matter is expressed as "consuming" because it is the greater part of the aim of it, and as a way of disparaging their condition and turning the listeners away from them. ﴿And they avert﴾ people ﴿from the way of Allah﴾, from the religion of Islam, or from the path established in the Torah and the Gospel, toward what they have fabricated and distorted through taking bribes. Or they avert [others] from it by their own selves, through their consuming of people's wealth unjustly.

﴿And those who hoard gold and silver﴾ That is, they gather them and guard them, whether that is by burying them or in some other manner. The relative pronoun may refer either to the many rabbis and monks, in which case it is an intensification in describing them with greed and stinginess with these two (metals), after describing them with what preceded of taking bribes and bribes in falsehoods; or it may refer to the Muslims who hoard and do not spend. The latter is more suitable to His statement, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿and do not spend them in the way of Allah﴾. Thus their arrangement together with the bribe-taking People of the Book is an intensification and an indication that they are a model for them in deserving the announcement of painful punishment. The meaning of spending in the way of Allah here is zakat, based on what is related: "When it was revealed, it weighed heavily upon the Muslims, so Umar mentioned it to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: 'Indeed Allah, Exalted is He, did not prescribe zakat except to purify with it what remains of your wealth.'" And based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whatever its zakat has been paid is not a hoard," meaning, not a hoard for which a threat is made, for the threat is upon it together with not spending in what Allah has commanded spending in.

As for the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever leaves behind gold or silver, he will be branded with it," and similar, the meaning of it is: that whose due (haqq) has not been paid. Based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "There is no owner of gold or silver who does not pay its due from it, except that on the Day of Resurrection, plates of fire will be fashioned for him, and his side, his forehead, and his back will be branded with them."

﴿So give them tidings of a painful punishment﴾ This is the predicate of the relative clause, and the fa' (so) is because it contains the sense of a conditional. It is permissible that the relative pronoun be in the accusative, governed by a verb that it explains, (fa-bashshirhum).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 35:

﴿The day﴾ is in the accusative case (manṣūb, "governed as an object of time"), governed either by (bi-ʿadhābin alīmin) (with a painful punishment), or by an implied verb indicated by that, i.e., "they will be punished," or by (اذْكُرْ) (remember). ﴿It will be heated over them in the fire of Hell﴾, i.e., on the day when the fire, intensely heated, will be kindled over them. Its original form is "the fire will be heated," but the heating was attributed to the fire for emphasis (mubālagha). Then "the fire" was dropped and the verb was ascribed to the prepositional phrase (al-jārr wal-majrūr), to draw attention to the intended meaning. Thus the verb shifted from the feminine form to the masculine form, as you say: "The matter (qiṣṣa) was raised to the governor," and if you drop "the matter," you say: "It was raised to the governor." It was said "over them" (ʿalayhā) although two things are mentioned, because what is meant by them is many dinars and dirhams, as ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Four thousand and below it is expenditure (nafaqa), and above it is treasure (kanz)." The same applies to His words, exalted is He: "and they do not spend it." It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the wealth and treasures, since the ruling is general, and they were singled out for mention because they are the basis of acquiring wealth. Or it refers to silver, and it was singled out because it is closer, and the ruling on it indicates that gold is likewise, or even more so.

﴿So their foreheads, their sides and their backs will be branded with them﴾. This is because their gathering and withholding of it was for seeking eminence through wealth and enjoying delicious foods and splendid clothes. Or because they frowned at the beggar, turned away from him and presented their backs to him. Or because these are the most noble of the visible limbs, for they contain the principal organs, which are the brain, the heart and the liver. Or because they are the roots of the four directions, which are the front of the body, its back, and its two sides.

﴿This is what you hoarded﴾, with an implied "it will be said" (ʿalā irādat al-qawl), ﴿for yourselves﴾, for its benefit, so it became the very cause of its harm and the reason for its punishment. ﴿So taste what you used to hoard﴾, i.e., the evil consequence of your hoarding, or "what you were hoarding." It was also read with the nūn vowelled with ḍamma (takНnizūna, "you hoard," read as tiknizūna with a different vowel pattern).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 36:

﴿Indeed, the number of months﴾ means their number ﴿with Allah﴾ means in His decree, and this (with Allah) is a complement (ma'mul) of it, since it is a verbal noun (masdar). ﴿Twelve﴾ is the predicate of "inna" (indeed). ﴿Months﴾ is a specifying accusative (tamyiz) for emphasis, as in your saying: "I have twenty dinars of gold (ʿindī min al-danānīr ʿishrūna dīnāran)." The intended meaning is the lunar months, since the orbit of the legal rulings revolves around them. ﴿In the Book of Allah﴾ means in the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz), or in what He has ordained and made obligatory. It is a qualifier of ﴿(twelve)﴾, meaning: twelve months established in the Book of Allah. The words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿on the day He created the heavens and the earth﴾ are connected either to what is in the prepositional phrase of the sense of settledness (istiqrar), or to "the Book" considered as a verbal noun. The meaning is: this is a matter established in reality from the time Allah the Exalted created the celestial bodies, the movements, and the times. ﴿Of them﴾ means of those twelve months, ﴿four are sacred﴾ and they are Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah, al-Muharram, and Rajab.

From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) in his sermon at the Farewell Pilgrimage: "Indeed, time has returned to its original form on the day Allah created the heavens and the earth. The year is twelve months, of which four are sacred: three are consecutive, Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah, and al-Muharram, and Rajab of Mudar, which lies between Jumada and Sha'ban." The meaning is that the months returned to what they had been in terms of permissibility and sanctity, and the Hajj returned to Dhu al-Hijjah after they had shifted it from its place through the intercalation (al-nasi') that they had introduced in the Jahiliyyah. The Farewell Pilgrimage coincided with Dhu al-Hijjah, while the pilgrimage of Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) had been before it in Dhu al-Qa'dah.

﴿That﴾ means the prohibition of the four specified and counted months, and the sense of distance in the demonstrative is for magnifying the one referred to, ﴿is the upright religion﴾, the straight religion of Ibrahim and Isma'il (peace be upon them both). The Arabs had held fast to it as an inheritance from them, and they used to glorify the sacred months and dislike fighting in them, to the extent that if a man met the killer of his father or brother he would not harm him. They named Rajab "al-Asamm" and "Munsil al-Asinnah" until they introduced the intercalation (al-nasi') and changed it.

﴿So do not wrong yourselves therein﴾ by violating their sanctity and committing what is forbidden in them. The majority hold that the prohibition of fighting in them has been abrogated (mansukha), and that wronging means committing sins in them, for it is greater in burden, just as committing them in the Sacred Precinct (al-haram) is.

It is related from 'Ata': it is not lawful for people to raid in the Sacred Precinct or in the sacred months unless they are attacked, and that it was not abrogated. The first view is supported by the fact that the Prophet (ﷺ) besieged Ta'if and attacked Hawazin at Hunayn in Shawwal and Dhu al-Qa'dah.

﴿And fight the polytheists all together as they fight you all together﴾ means: collectively. It is a verbal noun from "kaffa 'an al-shay'" (to restrain from something), since the whole is restrained from excess; it is placed in the position of a circumstantial accusative (hal). ﴿And know that Allah is with the God-fearing﴾ means: with you through help and support in what you undertake of fighting. The apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun to praise them for their piety, to urge those falling short in it, and to announce that it is the basis of victory. It is also said that this is good tidings and a guarantee to them of victory because of their piety.

**﴿Indeed, the postponing [of sacred months] is only an increase in disbelief﴾**: *al-nasi'* (the postponement, or intercalation, of the sacred months) is the verbal noun of *nasa'ahu* (نَسَأهُ), meaning he postponed it, with the forms *nasa'an*, *nasa'an* and *nasi'an*, like *massa massan*, *misasan* and *masisan* (مَسَّ مَسًّا ومِساسًا ومَسِيسًا). It is read in all these forms, and it is also read with the hamza changed to a *ya'* and the first *ya'* doubled (نَسِيءُ). When a sacred month came and they were fighting, they made it lawful, and they made another month in its place sacred, until they abandoned the specific months and considered only the number. Sometimes they increased the number of months by making them thirteen or fourteen, so that the time would be wide enough for them and they could make four months of the year sacred. For this reason the specific number was stated in the Book and the Sunnah. That is, the postponing of the sanctity of one month to another month is ﴿an increase in disbelief﴾, because it is making lawful what Allah has made unlawful and making unlawful what He has made lawful. So it is another disbelief added to their disbelief. ﴿By it those who disbelieve are led astray﴾ into an error upon their former error. It is also read in the active voice of the verb, with the action attributed to Allah, the Glorified, meaning: He creates misguidance in them when they engage in its beginnings and causes. This is also the meaning on the first reading. It was said: the ones who lead them astray are then their leaders, and the relative pronoun refers to their followers. It is also read (يَضَلُّ) with a *fatha* on the *ya'* and the *dad*, from *dalla* (ضَلَّ) and *yudhillu* (يُضَلِّلُ), and (نُضِلُّ) with the plural "we" of majesty.

**﴿They make it lawful﴾**, that is, the postponed month, **﴿one year﴾** of the years, **﴿and make sacred in its place another month﴾** from among those that are not sacred. **﴿And they make it sacred﴾**, that is, they observe its sanctity as it was. Describing this as "making sacred" is in view of their making it lawful in the previous year, or because they attributed it to their gods, as will come. **﴿Another year﴾**, if its alteration served none of their purposes.

Al-Kalbi said: The first person to do that was a man from Kinanah called Nu'aym ibn Tha'labah. When the people were about to depart from the pilgrimage season, he would stand and give a sermon, saying: "No one can reverse what I have decided, and I am the one who is not blamed and not refused." The polytheists would say to him: "At your service!" Then they would ask him to postpone for them a month in which they could make changes. He would say: "Indeed, Safar of this year is sacred." If he said that, they would loosen the bowstrings, remove the spearheads and the arrowheads. If he said: "It is lawful," they would fasten the bowstrings, tie the arrowheads and raid.

It was also said: he was Junadah ibn 'Awf al-Kinani, who was obeyed in the pre-Islamic period. He would stand on a camel during the pilgrimage season and call out at the top of his voice: "Your gods have made the sacred lawful for you, so make it lawful." Then in the following year he would stand and say: "Your gods have made the sacred unlawful for you, so make it sacred." It was also said: he was a man from Kinanah called al-Qalammas. One of them said:

*And among us is the postponer of the month, al-Qalammas.*

From Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both): The first to establish the postponement was 'Amr ibn Luhayy ibn Qam'ah ibn Khindif. The two sentences are an explanation of the "misguidance," or a circumstantial clause referring to the relative pronoun, and the governing element is the same as the element governing it.

**﴿So that they may agree﴾**, that is, so that they may conform to **﴿the number of what Allah has made sacred﴾** of the four months. The *lam* is connected to the second verb, or to what is indicated by the two verbs together. **﴿So that they make lawful what Allah has made sacred﴾** specifically, of the designated months. **﴿Their evil deeds were made attractive to them﴾**. It is also read in the active voice, with Allah, the Glorified, as the agent. The meaning is: He made their deeds appealing to their nature and beloved to their souls. It was also said: He abandoned them until they regarded the ugliness of their deeds as good, so they persisted in that.

**﴿And Allah does not guide the disbelieving people﴾** with a guidance that definitely leads to the desired goal. He guides them only to what leads to the goal when they follow the path, but they have turned away from it by their own wrong choice, so they wandered in the bewilderment of error.

O you who have believed, what is [the matter] with you that, when you are told, "Go forth in the way of Allah," you become heavy and cling to the earth? This is a return to urging the believers and steeling their resolve to fight the disbelievers, following a statement of some of their abominable qualities that necessitate this. "What is [the matter] with you?" is an interrogative carrying the meaning of denunciation and rebuke. "When you are told, 'Go forth in the way of Allah,' you become heavy" means: you delayed and held back. Its original form is tathaqaltum (you became heavy), and it has also been read thus. The sense is: "What has come to you?" or "What has come about for you?" Or: "What do you do when the Prophet ﷺ says to you, 'Go forth' (infiru), i.e., set out to the raid in the way of Allah, heavily burdened?" The verb is past in form but present in meaning, as if it were said: "You are becoming heavy." Accordingly, the adverbial of time (idha, "when") is governed by the implied stability (al-istiqrar al-muqaddar) in "lakum" (for you), or by the meaning of the verb indicated by that. It is also permissible that the circumstantial (al-hal) governs it, i.e., "What is [the matter] with you, being heavy when you are told, 'Go forth'?!" It has also been read as "a-thaqaltum" (did you become heavy?) in the interrogative of denunciation and rebuke, in which case the governing element of the adverbial of time is the first [interrogative].

"To the earth" is connected to "athaqaltum" by way of its being construed with the meaning of inclination and adherence (takhmin), i.e., you became heavy, leaning toward the world and its fleeting appetites for a little while, and you disliked the hardships of the raid and its toils, which entail the everlasting journey, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He clung to the earth and followed his desire﴾. Or [it means] to dwelling in your land and your homes. This was at the Expedition of Tabuk, in the ninth year (or tenth year, per the text) after their return from al-Ta'if. They were summoned in a time of hardship, drought and scorching heat, when the fruits of Madinah had ripened and its shade was pleasant, along with the distance of the journey and the multitude of the enemy, so that this was hard upon them. It was said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ did not set out on any expedition he undertook without concealing it by mentioning another destination, except for the Expedition of Tabuk, for he ﷺ made its destination clear to them so that they might prepare for it.

"Are you content with the life of this world" in its deceptions "instead of the Hereafter?" i.e., in place of the Hereafter and its everlasting bliss. "Then the enjoyment of the life of this world" is expressed in the place of the pronoun for the sake of added emphasis, i.e., what is the enjoyment of it and its pleasures "in the Hereafter" i.e., in comparison with the Hereafter "except a little?" i.e., a belittled thing of no account. In describing "the life of this world" with what signals its preciousness and calls for desire for it, and in stripping "the Hereafter" of the like of that, there is an intensification in demonstrating the paltriness and baseness of this world and the greatness and exaltedness of the Hereafter.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 39:

﴿Unless you go forth﴾ i.e., if you do not go forth to what you have been called forth to. ﴿He will punish you﴾ i.e., Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, ﴿with a painful punishment﴾ i.e., He will destroy you with a terrible, dreadful cause, such as famine or the like. ﴿And He will replace﴾ you, after destroying you, ﴿with a people other than you﴾. He described them as being different from you in order to emphasize the threat and to intensify the warning, by indicating a difference in both attribute and essence, which entails complete eradication. That is, a people who are obedient and who prefer the Hereafter over this world, who are not from your children or your relatives, like the people of Yemen and the sons of Persia. In this there is an indication of the intensity of the displeasure that is not hidden (p-66).

﴿And you will not harm Him at all﴾ i.e., your reluctance will not in any way detract from the support of His religion, for He is Self-Sufficient over everything in every respect. It has been said that the pronoun refers to the Messenger (ﷺ), for Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, promised him protection and victory, and His promise is certainly to be fulfilled. ﴿And Allah is over all things Competent﴾, so He is able to destroy you and bring about another people.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 40:

﴿If you do not help him, then Allah has already helped him﴾. That is: if you do not help him, then Allah, who helped him at a time of greater necessity than this occasion, will help him. The answer (jaza') is omitted and its cause (sabab) is put in its place. Or: if you do not help him, then He has already made help for him obligatory, since He helped him in a similar situation, so He will not abandon him in any other.

﴿When those who disbelieved drove him out﴾. That is: they were the cause of his departure, since he (ﷺ) had been permitted to leave when they resolved to expel him. ﴿The second of two﴾ is a circumstantial accusative (hal, a term for a state-describing accusative) from his pronoun (ﷺ). It was also read with the yā' sukūn (a sukun on the ya'), according to the dialect of those who treat the defective noun (nāqiṣ) like the restricted noun (maqṣūr) in its inflection (i'rab, grammatical case endings). The meaning is: one of two, without regard to his (ﷺ) being second. For the meaning of the expressions "third of three," "fourth of four," and the like is: one of these numbers in general, not specifically the third or fourth. For this reason the majority of scholars forbade putting the noun that follows in the accusative, so that one would say "thālith thalāthatan" and "rābi' arba'atan." This was discussed in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Certainly, those who said "Allah is the third of three" have disbelieved﴾ in Surat al-Ma'ida. As for making him (ﷺ) the second of the two because al-Siddiq walked in front of him, and because he entered the cave first in order to sweep it and smooth the cloth, as is mentioned in the reports, this is a forced interpretation (tamahhul) that is unnecessary.

﴿When they were both in the cave﴾ is a substitute (badal, an appositive substitution) for ﴿when He drove him out﴾, a partial substitution (badal al-ba'd), since the intended time is an extended period. The cave (ghar) is a hole at the top of Mount Thawr, a mountain to the south of Makkah at a distance of one hour's walk. They remained in it for three days. ﴿When he said to his companion﴾ is a second substitution, or an adverbial clause of time (zarf) modifying ﴿the second﴾. That is, al-Siddiq. ﴿Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us﴾ with help and protection. The intended meaning of "with" (ma'iyya) is a permanent guardianship in which no trace of grief can approach its possessor. As for the well-known view that "ma'a" is specific to the one who is followed (matbu'), what is meant by the status of being followed (matbu'iyya) in it is being followed in the immediate matter.

It is narrated that "the polytheists came up above the cave, and Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, grew anxious for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and said: 'If one of them looks down today, the religion of Allah will be lost.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'What do you think of two whom Allah is the third of?'" It was also said: "When the two entered the cave, Allah sent two doves, which laid eggs at its base, and the spider, which spun a web over it. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'O Allah, blind their eyes.'" So they kept circling around the cave and did not notice, for Allah had taken their sight away from it. In this there is clear evidence of the high rank of al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, and his early companionship, which is not hidden. For this reason they said: whoever denies the companionship of Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, has disbelieved, because he denies the speech of Allah, glorified and exalted is He.

﴿Then Allah sent down His tranquillity﴾, His security in which hearts find rest, ﴿upon him﴾, upon the Prophet (ﷺ). Its meaning here is that no trace of fear approaches him at all. Or it refers to his companion, since he was the one who was distressed, whereas the Prophet (ﷺ) was at peace regarding his affair. ﴿And He supported him with hosts you did not see﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with ﴿Allah helped him﴾. The hosts are the angels who descended on the day of Badr, the Confederates (al-Ahzab), and Hunayn. It was also said they are the angels whom Allah sent down to guard him in the cave. But the description of them as not seen by the addressees conflicts with this.

His saying, mighty and exalted: ﴿And He made the word of those who disbelieved the lowest﴾, meaning shirk or the call to disbelief. This making is not achieved merely by the rescue, but by killing, capture, and the like. ﴿And the word of Allah﴾, that is, monotheism, or the call of Islam, ﴿is the highest﴾, nothing is comparable to it. The change of style (uslub) indicates that it is in itself thus, that its status does not change and its condition does not alter, unlike other words. For this reason the pronoun of the verb (damir al-fi'l) is placed in the middle. It was also read in the accusative, coordinated with ﴿the word of those who disbelieved﴾. ﴿And Allah is Mighty﴾, who cannot be overcome, ﴿Wise﴾ in His judgment and His management.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 41:

﴿Go forth﴾ is a command in its bare form (tajrid li-l-amr) to go forth (al-nufur), following the reproach for abandoning it and the denunciation of laxity regarding it. His, exalted is He, words ﴿lightly and heavily﴾ are two circumstantial qualifiers (hal) referring back to the pronoun of the addressees. That is: in whatever state you are, whether in ease or hardship, arising from whatever cause, whether from health or sickness, or wealth or poverty, or having few or many dependents, or other matters that fall under the assistance or lack of means, after possibility and capability in general.

As for what has been mentioned in explaining these two words, namely that "lightly" means having few dependents and "heavily" means having many, or that "lightly" means with light weaponry and "heavily" means with heavy weaponry, or riders and foot soldiers, or young and old, or lean and fat, or healthy and sick, it is not meant to restrict the two opposing conditions to the exclusion of the rest without including them.

And from Ibn Umm Maktum, that he said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "Is it obligatory upon me to go forth?" He ﷺ said: "Yes." until there was revealed: ﴿There is no blame upon the blind﴾. And from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, it was abrogated by His, mighty and majestic is He, words: ﴿There is no blame upon the weak, nor upon the sick﴾ ... the verse.

﴿And strive with your wealth and your selves in the way of Allah﴾ is an obligation to fight jihad with both, if possible, and with one of them when it is possible and the other is lacking, to the extent that whoever is supported by both self and wealth fights with both, and whoever is supported by wealth but not self, equips in his place someone whose condition is the opposite of his. Many scholars adopted this view. It was also said that it is an obligation only for the first category. ﴿That﴾, i.e., what has been mentioned of going forth and jihad, and the meaning of distance carried by the demonstrative is to indicate the elevation of its station in nobility. ﴿is better for you﴾, i.e., a great good in itself, or better than what is sought by abandoning it of ease, comfort, abundance of living, and enjoyment of wealth and children. ﴿if you know﴾, i.e., if you know the good, you will know that it is good; or if you know that it is good, since there is no possibility of falsehood in the reports of Allah, exalted is He, then hasten to it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 42:

﴿Had it been﴾ a near gain (ʿaraḍ) and a moderate journey, diverting the address away from them and directing it to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), enumerating the blunders that proceeded from them in word and deed in the manner of reproach, and making clear the baseness of their aspirations and their other vices. That is: had what they were called to been ﴿a near gain﴾ — ʿaraḍ means whatever worldly benefits present themselves to you, i.e., had that been spoils easy to obtain, of near wealth — ﴿and a moderate journey﴾ — having a measure between the near and the far — ﴿they would have followed you﴾ in the expedition, out of desire to win the booty. Making the following conditional on both matters indicates that it would not have come about if only the journey were moderate. ﴿But the distance seemed long to them﴾ — that is, the shuqqah, the distant and arduous stretch that is traversed with hardship. It is also read with the ʿayn and the shīn kasrah.

﴿They will swear﴾ — that is, those who stayed behind from the campaign. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿by God﴾ — either it is connected to (they will swear), or it is part of their own speech, and the saying is intended on both readings. That is: they will swear by God, offering excuses when you return, saying: ﴿If we had been able﴾; or they will swear, saying: by God, if we had been able… etc., that is: if we had had capacity in terms of equipment, or in terms of health, or in terms of both together, as whatever lies they and their pretexts suggested to them. On both interpretations, His saying, exalted is He, ﴿We would have gone out with you﴾ serves in place of the answers of both the oath and the condition together. As for the second, it is evident; as for the first, it is because their saying (if we had been able) is in effect equivalent to: by God, if we had been able; since it is an explanation of His saying, "they will swear by God," and a confirmation of it. The reporting of what would come from them after the return — and it occurred as it was reported — is among the manifest miracles. It is also read ﴿Lawu istaṭaʿnā﴾ with a ḍammah on the waw, likening it to the waw of the plural, as in His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿fatamannawu al-mawt﴾ (so wish for death).

﴿They destroy themselves﴾ — this is a substitute (badal) for ﴿they will swear﴾, since a false oath is a destruction of the self; for this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "A false oath leaves dwellings desolate." Or it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from its doer, i.e., destroying themselves; or from the doer of (we went out): it is brought in the manner of reporting about them, as if it were said: we destroy ourselves, i.e., we would have gone out with you destroying ourselves, as in your saying: "he swore he would do it" in place of "I will surely do it."

﴿And God knows that they are surely liars﴾ — that is, regarding the content of the conditional, and regarding what they claimed implicitly of the non-fulfilment of the antecedent, since they were capable of going out and did not go out.

"ʿAfā Allāh ʿanka" (﴿عَفا اللَّهُ عَنْكَ﴾) is explicit that God Almighty has pardoned the Prophet (ﷺ) for what occurred from him when the hypocrites (al-mutakhallifin) sought his permission to stay behind, offering the excuse of lacking the means, and he granted them permission relying on their oaths and pledges, since these were free from any competing consideration. What he did was leave the better and more excellent course (al-awla wa'l-afdal), which is deliberation and holding back until the matter becomes clear and the situation is revealed.

As for His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Why did you grant them permission?﴾, meaning: for what reason did you grant them permission to stay behind when they pleaded their excuses? This is an elaboration of what was alluded to by the pardon, namely leaving the better course, and an indication that the affairs of the Prophet (ﷺ) should be tied to strong reasons that necessitate them or validate them, and that what they presented by way of excuse and pleading, backed by oaths, could not be a cause for permission before its truthfulness appeared. Both lams are connected to the permission, since they differ in meaning: the first is for causation (ta'lil), and the second is for communication (tabligh). The pronoun in the genitive refers to all who sought permission. The censure is directed at the permission in terms of its encompassing all of them, not in terms of its relation to each individual, since the inability of some of them was established, as His saying, Glorified is He, indicates: ﴿until those who were truthful become clear to you﴾, meaning: regarding what they reported when making their excuse of lacking the means, whether in terms of wealth, or of body, or of both, as each of them conceived there. ﴿And you know the liars﴾ in that matter, so that you treat each of the two groups according to what it deserves. This is an explanation of that "better and more excellent" course and a specification for him (ﷺ) concerning it, for the word "until" (ḥattā), whether it carries the meaning of the lam or of "to" (ilā), cannot be connected to His saying ﴿Why did you grant them permission?﴾, because that would entail that his (ﷺ) granting them permission was either causal or limited by the becoming clear and the knowing; and the question would be directed at him from that standpoint. This is manifestly corrupt, rather it is indicated by what this implies, as if it were said: Why did you hasten to grant them permission? Why did you not deliberate until the matter became clear, as is the demand of prudence?

Qatadah and ʿAmr ibn Maymun said: "Two things were done by the Messenger of God (ﷺ) for which he was not commanded in anything: his granting permission to the hypocrites, and his taking ransom from the captives. So God the Exalted rebuked him, as you hear."

The shift in style, in that he expressed the first group by the relative clause whose predicate is a verb indicating occurrence (ḥudūth), and the second group by the active participle indicating continuity, serves to signal that what appeared from the first group is a truthfulness that is occurrent, concerning a specific matter, and does not qualify them to be counted among the truthful; and that what came from the latter, though it is a lie that is occurrent and related to a specific matter, is nonetheless a matter proceeding according to their constant habit, arising from their deep-rootedness in lying. The expression of the appearance of truthfulness by "becoming clear" (tabayyun), and of what relates to lying by "knowing" ('ilm), is because it is the well-known position that the content of a report is truthfulness, while lying is a rational possibility. So the appearance of its truthfulness is merely the clarifying of that content and the cutting off of the possibility of its contradiction after it had been rationally possible. As for its lying, it is an occurrent matter that the report does not indicate at all, so that its appearance would be a clarification of it; rather it is the contradiction of its content, so what relates to it is a fresh knowledge. Attributing it to his pronoun (ﷺ), not to those known, by building the verb in the passive, together with attributing the clarifying to the first group, is because the intent here is his (ﷺ) knowledge of them and holding them to account by its requirement, unlike the first group, for whom there is no accountability. Whoever did not notice this said: "until it becomes clear to you who among them was truthful in his excuse from among those who lied in it."

The attribution of the clarifying to the first group and the connection of knowledge to the latter, although the basis of attribution and connection primarily and essentially is the attribute of truthfulness and lying as indicated, is because the aim is knowledge of both groups with respect to their being characterized by the two attributes mentioned and treating them according to what each deserves, not knowledge of the two attributes in themselves, or in terms of their subsisting in their described subjects.

Moreover, in opening the address with the glad tidings of pardon, rather than with what would suggest reproach, there is consideration of his (ﷺ) station and care for good conduct in discourse and gentleness in reproof, which is not hidden from people of understanding.

Sufyan ibn ʿUyaynah said: "Look at this gentleness: He began with the pardon before mentioning the one pardoned. He erred and was discourteous, and evil was what he did in what he said and wrote, whoever claimed that the speech is a metonymy for wrongdoing, and that its meaning is: 'You erred and it was evil of you.' Grant that it is a metonymy: is not its preference over explicit mention of the wrongdoing for the sake of softening the address and easing the reproach? And grant that pardon entails error: does it entail that it is of such ugliness and draws such blame as to justify this degree of directness in speaking evil, or to permit the formulation of disapproval by the phrase 'evil is what' which indicates that ugliness has reached a degree at which one is amazed?"

It is not hidden that there was no benefit to the religion in their going out, nor advantage to the Muslims; rather there was in it corruption and disorder, as His saying, Mighty and Majestic, declares: ﴿Had they gone out…﴾ etc. He, Glorified is He, also disliked it, as His saying the Exalted expresses: ﴿But God disliked their being sent forth…﴾ to the end of the verse.

Indeed, it would have been better to delay the permission until their lying became manifest, and they were disgraced before all witnesses, and they were not able to enjoy life in security and ease, nor could they find delight among themselves in having deceived him (ﷺ) and pleased him with falsehoods. Moreover, life did not become wholesome for them, nor did their eyes find comfort, since they were not in security and tranquility, but rather were in fear of their affair being exposed, and so it was.

﴿They do not seek your permission, those who believe in God and the Last Day﴾. This is an alert that it should have been taken as evidence of their state that they seek permission, and that they should not be granted leave. That is, it is not the custom of the believers to seek your permission ﴿to strive (jihad) with their wealth and their selves﴾. The sincere ones (al-khullas) among them hasten to it without waiting for permission, let alone seek your permission to stay behind. Since these people sought your permission to stay behind, that was a sign calling for deliberation regarding their affair, indeed a proof of their hypocrisy. It was said: the object of seeking permission is omitted, and the meaning of His words ﴿to strive﴾ is "out of dislike of striving." Then it was said: the omitted object is staying behind, and the meaning is: the believers do not seek your permission to stay behind out of dislike of jihad. Thus the negation falls upon the condition, and by this the believer is distinguished from the hypocrite. Although this is in itself a hidden matter, not known at the outset, yet since their general conditions point to it, it has been made an evident and established matter. It was said: the matter is jihad itself, that is, the believers do not seek your permission regarding jihad out of dislike of striving, on the basis that seeking permission regarding jihad may sometimes be due to disliking it. But it is not hidden that seeking permission for a thing out of dislike of it is something that does not occur, indeed is not even conceivable. And even if its occurrence is granted, seeking permission due to the cause of dislike is not distinguished outwardly from seeking permission due to the cause of desire. And even if it is granted, what is negated of the believers must be affirmed of the hypocrites, and it is evident that they did not seek permission regarding jihad out of dislike of it, but rather sought permission to stay behind.

﴿And God is Knowing of the God-fearing (muttaqun)﴾. This is a testimony to them of their inclusion in the line of the God-fearing, a promise to them of the most abundant reward, and an affirmation of the content of what preceded, as if it were said: God knows that they are thus. It also indicates that what proceeded from them is motivated by piety (taqwa).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 45:

﴿Only those ask your permission who do not believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾ That is: to remain behind, absolutely, according to the first view, or out of aversion to jihad according to the second. ﴿Those who do not believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾: the restriction of faith to these two in both places is to signal that what motivates jihad, with the expenditure of self and wealth, is nothing but faith in them, for by it the believers are able to exchange the everlasting life and the abiding, eternal bliss for the transient life and the worthless goods. ﴿And their hearts are in doubt﴾: a conjunction upon the relative clause; the choice of the past tense form indicates the certainty and establishment of the doubt. ﴿So they﴾, being ﴿in their doubt﴾ and their suspicion, which is settled in their hearts, ﴿waver﴾: that is, they are bewildered, for wavering is the habit of the bewildered, just as steadfastness is the habit of the one with insight. Expressing it by this is clear enough given its position.

﴿And had they intended the going out﴾ indicates that some of them said, when offering excuses: "We did intend to go out, but we did not make ready for it, and the departure drew so near that preparation was impossible for us." So, as a refutation of them, it was said: had He intended it, ﴿they would have made ready for it﴾, that is, for going out at its time, ﴿a preparation﴾, that is, readiness, of provisions, mounts, weapons, and other things necessary for a journey. It has been read as (ʿuddahu), with the ta' omitted and the noun annexed to a pronoun referring to the going out, as one who said the following did with ʿuddah:

؎ And they failed you in the promise that they had made

That is, ʿuddatahu (its preparation). It has also been read ʿiddatan with a kasra on the ʿayn, and ʿiddahu as an annexed form.

﴿But Allah disliked their being roused﴾, that is, their rising up to go out. It has been said that this is an istidrak (corrective exception, "but") against what is understood from the protasis of the conditional sentence. For the negation of their intention to go out entails the negation of their going out, and Allah's dislike of their being roused entails His holding them back from going out. So it is as if it were said: "They did not go out, but they were held back." Agreement in meaning does not prevent occurrence between the two sides of (lākin, "but") after the difference in the wording, positively and negatively, has been established, as in your saying: "How good he was to Zayd, but he did evil." The more apparent view is that it is an istidrak from the antecedent itself, in the manner of what occurs in the exceptive syllogisms, and the meaning is: (p-71) "Had they intended to go out, they would have made ready for it a preparation. But they did not intend it, because Allah, exalted is He, disliked their being roused, on account of the corruptions in it which will be made clear."

﴿So He held them back﴾, that is, He restrained them through cowardice and sloth, so they held back from it and did not prepare for it. ﴿And it was said: "Sit with those who sit."﴾ This is a figure for Allah, exalted is He, casting the dislike of going out into their hearts, or for the whispering of Satan by the command to sit. Or it is a report of the saying of some of them to others. Or it is the permission of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for them to sit. The intended "those who sit" is either those with valid excuses or others. Whichever it is, it is not free of blame.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 9, verse 47:**

﴿If they had gone forth among you﴾ explains the reason for Allah's disapproval of their setting out. That is, if they had gone forth mixing with you, ﴿they would have added to you nothing﴾, meaning they would have brought you nothing of any kind, ﴿except corruption﴾, meaning ruin and evil. The exception is *mufarragh muttasil* (an exception in which the excluded element is absent, and the exception is connected to the preceding clause). It was also said to be *munqati'* (disconnected), but this is not correct. ﴿And they would have hurried about among you﴾, meaning they would have busied themselves among you with tale-bearing, sowing discord, and corrupting relations between people. It comes from *wada'a al-ba'iru wad'an* (the camel hastened) when it went fast, and *awda'tuhu* (I made it hasten), meaning I drove it to hurry. The meaning is: they would have driven their mounts among you. What is intended is exaggeration in hastening with tale-bearing, because the rider is faster than the walker. It was also read as *wa-la-arqasu* (﴿and they would have galloped﴾), from *raqasat al-naqatu* (the she-camel moved quickly), and *arqastuha* (I made her move quickly). It was also read as *wa-la-awfadu* (﴿and they would have rushed﴾), meaning they would have hastened.

﴿Seeking to cause you discord﴾: they strive to tempt you into dissension among yourselves, by provoking disagreement among you, casting fear into your hearts, and corrupting your intentions. The clause is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) referring back to the pronoun in *awda'u* (they hurried), or it is a resumptive new clause (*isti'naf*).

﴿And among you are those who listen to them﴾, meaning there are tale-bearers who listen to your speech in order to carry it to them, or there are among you weak people who listen to the hypocrites, meaning they obey them. The clause is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the object of *yabghunakum* (they seek you), or from its subject, because it contains pronouns referring to both, or it is a new independent clause. Perhaps they were not, in number and in the manner of corruption, of such a magnitude that their presence would seriously disrupt the affair of jihad among the believers, and the corruption of their going forth was not equal to its benefit. For this reason, wisdom did not require their not going forth, so they went forth with the believers. But since the joining of the hypocrites who stayed behind with them would have entailed total disorder, Allah disapproved of their setting out, so their gathering did not come about, and their corruption was averted.

The reproach concerning the permission given to them to remain behind, although it was certainly established and although their going forth would have included these corruptions, is that if they had stayed behind without permission from him (ﷺ), their hypocrisy would have become manifest among the Muslims from the outset. They would not have been able to mix with them and strive among them with rumours, and they would not have been able to enjoy life until their condition became evident through the striking revealed verses.

﴿And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers﴾, with knowledge encompassing their inner thoughts and outward conduct, and what they did in the past and what may come from them in the future. Placing the apparent noun in the place of the pronoun serves to record their wrongdoing against them, to intensify the threat, and to indicate that the punishment follows from their wrongdoing. Perhaps it includes both groups: the tale-bearers and those who stayed behind.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 48:

﴿Indeed, they had sought discord﴾ — the scattering of your unity and the dispersal of your companions away from you — ﴿before﴾, that is: on the day of Uhud, when ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, the hypocrite (munafiq), withdrew with those who were with him. He had also left behind, with those who were with him, at Tabuk, after he had set out with the Prophet ﷺ as far as Dhu Judda, below the Thaniyyat al-Wada‘ (the Pass of Farewell).

And from Ibn Jurayj, may Allah be pleased with him: they stood in wait for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ at the pass on the night of al-ʿAqaba, and they were twelve men of the hypocrites, intending to assassinate him ﷺ, but Allah, exalted is He, turned them back, rejected and humiliated.

﴿And they devised plots against you﴾ — taqlib al-amr (turning over a matter) is its being turned and manipulated from one aspect to another and its repeated consideration for the sake of planning and striving in deception and stratagem. It is said of a man who is skilled in the various aspects of stratagems: ḥawwal and qullab, meaning: they strove and planned stratagems and schemes against you, and they turned over opinions in order to nullify your affair. It was also read with the lighter (non-doubled) form.

﴿Until the truth came﴾, that is: the victory and the divine support ﴿and the command of Allah became manifest﴾, His religion prevailed and His throne was exalted ﴿while they were averse﴾, the state being that they were averse to that; that is, in spite of themselves. The two verses serve to console the Messenger ﷺ and the believers regarding the staying behind of those who stayed behind, and to clarify what Allah, exalted is He, had hindered them for, to tear away their veils, to expose their secrets and remove their excuses, as a remedy for what might be missed through the hastiness of granting permission, and as an announcement that what was missed through it is not something whose remedy is impossible, to lessen the gravity of the matter.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 49:

﴿And among them is one who says, "Grant me permission [to stay behind]"﴾ in staying behind, ﴿and do not tempt me.﴾ That is, do not cause me to fall into temptation (fitnah), which is sin and wrongdoing. He means: "I will certainly remain behind, whether you grant permission or not, so grant me permission so that I do not fall into sin by opposing you; or do not cast me into destruction, for if I go out with you, my wealth and my dependents will perish, since there is no one to attend to their affairs."

It is said: Al-Jadd ibn Qays said, "The Ansar know well that I am greatly drawn to women, so do not tempt me with the daughters of al-Asfar," meaning the women of the Byzantines. "But I will assist you with my wealth, so leave me be." It was also recited as (وَلا تُفْتِنِّي) from aftanahu, with the same meaning as fatanahu.

﴿Surely, into temptation they have fallen⁠﴾ That is, into its very essence and its most complete instances, the one who is free from the need to be described with the perfection that is truly proper to the noun of genus being specific to it. ﴿they have fallen⁠﴾ not into something other than it, let alone a refuge or a means of escape from it. This is due to what they did: the resolve to stay behind, the audacity of seeking permission in this shameful manner, and remaining seated by the permission that was based upon it and upon their false excuses.

It was also recited with the verb in the singular (فَعَلَ-form), to preserve the wording of "man" (مَن).
