The opening of the sentence with the particle of alerting (أَلَا) together with the fronting of the adverbial phrase indicates that they fell into it while supposing it to be a refuge from temptation, reckoning that temptation is nothing but staying behind without permission. In expressing their being ensnared by falling into temptation, it is presented as a deadly abyss, revealing their plunge into the depths of ruin, to the lowest of the low.

As for His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿And indeed, Hell encompasses the disbelievers﴾, it is a threat against them for what they did, conjoined to the preceding sentence and included under the alerting particle. That is: it will gather them on the Day of Resurrection from every side. The use of the nominal sentence indicates permanence and continuity. Or: it encompasses them now, treating what is about to happen soon as if it had already occurred, or placing the causes of a thing in its place. For the beginnings of the fire's encompassing them, namely disbelief and sins, already encompass them now from all directions, and among these are the temptation they fled from and the temptation into which they fell.

It is also said: those beginnings, taking shape in the forms of deeds and dispositions, are the very fire itself, but this does not appear in this present life; it appears only when they take their true forms in the Hereafter. The word "disbelievers" refers either to the hypocrites, where the use of the apparent noun in place of the pronoun serves to record disbelief against them and to indicate that it is the greatest cause of the aforementioned encompassing, or to all disbelievers, including the hypocrites primarily.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 50:

﴿If good befalls you﴾ in some of your campaigns, ﴿a good thing﴾ of victory and spoils, ﴿it grieves them﴾, that good thing, meaning it causes them distress because of their excessive envy and enmity toward you. ﴿And if misfortune befalls you﴾ in some of them, ﴿a calamity of some severity﴾, ﴿they say﴾ boastfully about what they have done, admiring their own opinions, ﴿"We had already taken our affair"﴾, meaning we had secured what concerned us of the matter, namely withdrawing from the Muslims, holding back from fighting, flattering the disbelievers, and other matters of disbelief and hypocrisy in word and deed, ﴿before﴾, meaning before the calamity struck, at the time of its being averted. By this they indicate that the mentioned conduct is only valued among the disbelievers when it occurs while Islam is strong, not after the calamity has struck. ﴿And they turn away﴾ from the gathering and conversation back to their families, or they turn away from the Prophet (ﷺ), ﴿while they rejoice﴾ at what they did in taking their affair, and at what befell him (ﷺ). The clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the pronoun in "yaqulu" and "yatawallaw," not only to the latter, because joy accompanies both together. The choice of the nominal sentence indicates the continuity of joy. Attributing the distress to the good thing and the gladness to themselves, rather than to the calamity (by saying: "If a calamity befalls you, it will gladden them"), indicates the difference in their two states at the occurrence of distress and gladness: in the first they are compelled, and in the second they are free-choosing.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 51:

﴿Say﴾, as a clarification of the falsity of the belief upon which they built their delight: ﴿"Never will there befall us"﴾ ever. It is also read as (هَلْ يُصِيبُنا) and (هَلْ يُصَيِّبُنا), from the form fa'ala and not from fa'ala, because it is derived from the weak (waw-medial) root; it is said: ṣāba al-sahmu yaṣūbu (the arrow hit its mark), and its derivation is from al-ṣawāb (the correct, the right course).

﴿except what Allah has decreed for us﴾, i.e., what He has ordained for our worldly or otherworldly benefit, of victory over you, or martyrdom leading to everlasting bliss. ﴿He is our Protector (mawlānā)﴾, our helper and the one who manages our affairs. ﴿And upon Allah alone﴾ ﴿let the believers put their trust﴾. Tawakkul (trust in God) is the entrusting of the matter to Allah and contentment with what He has done, even if that comes after arranging the ordinary means. The fa' (in fa-l-yatawakkali) indicates causation. The original form was: "li-yatawakkali al-mu'minūna 'alā Allāh" (let the believers put their trust in Allah). The adverbial phrase was placed before the verb to convey restriction (qaṣr). Then the fa' was added to indicate that He, exalted is He, is deserving of trust placed in Him, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and Me alone, so fear Me﴾. If the sentence is part of the speech commanded to be said, then the placing of the noble Name in the position of a pronoun serves to show blessing and delight in it. If it is directed from Him, exalted is He, as a command to the believers to trust, following His command to the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning what was mentioned, then the command is evident. Likewise the repetition of the command in His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 52:

Because the ruling of the first command is cut off by the second, even though the second is a command in the third-person (absent) form. As for the first mode, the shift is to show the great care given to the matter commanded and to signal the difference in context between it and what was commanded first. Tarabbus (waiting, expectation) means remaining in place while awaiting the arrival of something, whether good or bad. The ba' (ب) is for transitivity (ta'diyah), and one of the two taʼs (التاءين) is elided, i.e., "what are you awaiting for us" (ما تَنْتَظِرُونَ بِنا). ﴿Only one of the two best outcomes﴾, i.e., the two consequences each of which is the best of outcomes, namely victory and martyrdom. This is a kind of clarification of what was left vague in the first answer, and an unveiling of the reality of the situation by informing that what they claim to be harm to the Muslims, namely martyrdom, is more beneficial than what they consider a benefit, namely victory and booty.

﴿And we are waiting for you﴾ for one of the two evil outcomes: either ﴿that Allah will afflict you with a punishment from Himself﴾ (p-74) as He afflicted the destroyed nations before you, the adverbial phrase being a qualifier of (punishment), which is why its governing verb is elided obligatorily; or with a punishment ﴿at our hands﴾, which is killing for disbelief. ﴿So wait﴾: the fa' is fasihah (explanatory), i.e., if the matter is so, then wait for what our end will be. ﴿Indeed we are waiting with you﴾ for what your end will be. So when each of us meets what he awaits, you will witness only what gladdens us, and we will witness only what grieves you.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 53:

﴿Say: Spend [your wealth] in the way of Allah﴾ willingly or unwillingly ﴿طَوْعًا أوْ كَرْهًا﴾ (ṭawʿan aw karhan), both are verbal nouns (maṣdar) that stand in the place of the agent (fāʿil), meaning: willingly or unwillingly. The imperative here carries the sense of a report (khabar), like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Ask forgiveness for them, or do not ask forgiveness for them﴾. The meaning is: you have spent, willingly or unwillingly. ﴿It will never be accepted from you﴾. The structure of the speech, in the form of a command, is for the sake of emphasis (mubālagha) in showing that the two conditions are equal in non-acceptance, as if they were commanded to test the situation, to spend in both states, and then see whether it is accepted from them, so that they witness its non-acceptance. This is a response to the statement of Jadd ibn Qays: "But I will help you with my wealth." Negating acceptance (taqabbul) may mean not taking it from them, or it may mean not rewarding them for it. His saying, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿Indeed, you have been a defiantly disobedient people﴾, that is: rebellious and insolent (ʿātīn mutamarridīn), is an explanation (taʿlīl) for the rejection of their spending.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 54:

﴿And nothing prevented their expenditures from being accepted from them﴾ (it is also read with the yā' of the third person, yuqbala). ﴿except that they disbelieved in Allah and His Messenger﴾. This is an exception from the most general category of things (istithna' min a'amm al-ashya'), meaning: nothing among things prevented the acceptance of their expenditures from them except their disbelief. It is also read (yuqbila) in the active voice, with Allah the Exalted as the agent. ﴿And they do not come to the prayer except while they are lazy﴾, meaning: they do not come to it in any state except the state of being sluggish. ﴿And they do not spend except while they are unwilling﴾, because they do not hope for reward through these two, nor do they fear punishment for neglecting them. As for His, the Exalted's, saying "tawan" (willingly), it means without compulsion from Him, or from the Prophet (ﷺ), not out of desire; or it is a supplementary (fardi) qualifier to widen the scope.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 55:

﴿So let not their wealth nor their children impress you.﴾ Indeed, that is a gradual leading-on (istidraj) of them and a calamity upon them, as His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He, indicates: ﴿Allah only intends to punish them thereby in the worldly life﴾ through the toil they endure in gathering and guarding it, and the hardships and calamities they suffer in it. ﴿And that their souls should depart while they are disbelievers﴾, so that they die as disbelievers, occupied with enjoyment and heedless of consideration of the outcome. Thus that becomes for them a punishment (niqmah) and not a blessing (ni'mah). The root of zahuq (departure) is going out with difficulty.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 56:

﴿And they swear by Allah that indeed they are of you﴾ in religion and Islam, ﴿but they are not of you﴾ in that regard, ﴿but they are a people who are fearful﴾ they fear that what is done to the polytheists will be done to them, so they outwardly profess Islam out of dissimulation (taqiyya), and they reinforce it ﴿(p-75)﴾ with wicked oaths.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 57:

﴿Were they to find a refuge﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) confirming the content of what precedes, namely that they are not of the Muslims, and that their seeking refuge in affiliation with them is only out of taqiyya (dissimulation) under compulsion. The point is that even if they were to find some other refuge, i.e., a fortified place to take shelter in, on a mountaintop, in a castle, or on an island, [they would not stay with you]. The use of the future form in the conditional clause, although the meaning is past, serves to indicate the continuation of their failure to find [such a refuge]. The negated present verb in the place of the past does not categorically indicate the cessation of the continuation of the action, as is apparent; rather it may also indicate the continuation of its negation, according to what the context requires. The meaning of your saying, "If you were to treat me well, I would thank you," is that the absence of thanks is due to the continuing absence of good treatment, not that it is due to the cessation of the continuation of good treatment, since thanks depend upon the existence of good treatment, not upon its continuation, as has been established in its proper place.

﴿or caves﴾ i.e., hollows and caverns in which they might hide themselves. It is also read with a dammah on the mim (مُغاراتٍ read as مُغْرَاتٍ? no: read as maghārāt with ḍamma on the mīm), from aghāra al-rajul, when a man entered the hollow. It is said that it is transitive from ghāra, when one entered the hollow, i.e., places in which they would make their persons and their families flee. It may also be from aghāra al-tha'lab, when the fox ran swiftly, in the sense of places of escape and flight.

﴿or some hiding place (mudda­khal)﴾ i.e., a tunnel into which they would slip and burrow. It is a mufta'al form from entering (al-dukhul). It is also read as (madkhalan) from entering, and (mudkhalan) from causing to enter, i.e., a place into which they cause themselves to enter. It is also read (mutadakhkhalan) and (mundakhalan), from tadakhkhul and indikhal.

﴿they would turn away﴾ i.e., they would divert their faces and proceed. It is also read (lawālaw), i.e., they would take refuge ﴿thereto﴾, i.e., to one of what has been mentioned, ﴿while they rush headlong﴾, i.e., they hurry, with nothing turning them back, from the jamūḥ horse, which is the one that the bridle does not turn. In this there is an indication of the perfection of their defiance and transgression. It is also read (yajmizūna), in the sense of yajmaḥūna, "they rush and run," and from it comes al-jammāza (the ambulance/litter-like conveyance).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 58:

﴿And among them are those who find fault with you﴾ (yalmizuka), with the mim vowelled with a kasra; it is also read with a damma, meaning: they criticise you secretly. It is also read (yulammizuka) and (yulamizuka), for emphasis, ﴿concerning the alms﴾, meaning: concerning their affair and their distribution. ﴿If they are given from them﴾ is an explanation of the corruption of their faultfinding, and that it has no source other than their greed for the goods of this world, meaning: if they are given from them the amount they want, ﴿they are content﴾ with what has occurred of the distribution and approve of it. ﴿But if they are not given from them﴾ that amount, ﴿behold, they are enraged﴾, meaning: they suddenly become angry. Here "idha" (behold/suddenly) takes the place of the response particle "fa" (then) of the conditional.

It is said: the verse was revealed concerning Abu al-Jawaz, the hypocrite, when he said: "Do you not see your companion dividing your alms among the shepherds of the flocks, while claiming that he is just?" It is also said: concerning Ibn Dhi al-Khuwaysira, whose name was Hurqus ibn Zuhayr al-Tamimi, the leader of the Kharijites, who said, when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was dividing the spoils of Hunayn, seeking to win over the hearts of the people of Makkah by lavishing the spoils upon them: "Be just, O Messenger of Allah!" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Woe to you! If I am not just, who then will be just?" It is also said that they are those whose hearts are to be reconciled (al-mu'allafa qulubuhum). The first view is the most apparent.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 59:

﴿And if only they had been content with what Allah and His Messenger gave them﴾, i.e., what the Messenger ﷺ gave them of the alms (ṣadaqāt), being content in their souls with it, even if it was little. The mention of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is for glorification and to draw attention to the fact that what the Messenger ﷺ did was by His command, glory be to Him.

(p-76) ﴿And said, "Allah is sufficient for us. Allah will give us of His bounty, and [so will] His Messenger. Indeed, to Allah we are inclined."﴾ i.e., His bounty and His action toward us and what He has apportioned to us are sufficient for us, after this, as we hope and aspire. ﴿Indeed, to Allah we are inclined﴾ in that He would grant us His bounty. The whole verse is within the scope of a conditional (sharṭ), and the response (jawāb) is omitted because it is evident, i.e., "it would have been better for them."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 60:

﴿Indeed, the charities are only for the poor and for the needy﴾: This begins the establishment of the rightfulness of what the Messenger (ﷺ) did in dividing (the zakat) by specifying its categories, and a refutation of the saying of the gossipers concerning it, and a cutting off of their empty greed, which is based on their corrupt assumption, by showing that they are far from being entitled to it. That is, the genus of charities, which includes its various kinds, ﴿is for the poor and the needy﴾, meaning: it is specifically for these eight categories that come next, and does not go beyond them to others. It is as if it were said: "They are only for them, not for others; so what is it for those who have no connection with them that they should say what they say about them, and what right have they to speak about them and about their divider?" The poor (faqir) is one who has a little, and the needy (miskin) is one who has nothing; this is what is related from Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, though it has also been said the opposite, and each of the two has a basis that supports it. ﴿And those employed to collect them﴾: those who strive in gathering and collecting them.

﴿And those whose hearts are to be reconciled﴾: they are of several types. Among them are nobles of the Arabs whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would win over so that they would embrace Islam, and he would give them a share; and among them are people who embraced Islam while their intentions were weak, so he would reconcile their hearts by giving them generous gifts, such as Uyayna ibn Hisn, al-Aqra' ibn Habis, and al-Abbas ibn Mirdas. And among them are those whose conversion is expected to bring about the Islam of their peers by giving them. Perhaps the first type was given by the Messenger (ﷺ) from the fifth of the fifth, which was his exclusive property. Some have counted among them those whose hearts are reconciled with a portion of it for fighting the disbelievers and those who withhold zakat. The share of these has fallen away by consensus, because that was for increasing the numbers of Islam; when Allah, Mighty and Exalted, strengthened it and raised His word, they became unnecessary.

﴿And for the captives﴾: that is, and for spending on freeing necks, by helping the mukatabun (slaves contracted to buy their freedom) with a portion of it to pay their installments. It has been said: by ransoming captives; and it has been said: by buying slaves from it so that they are freed. Whichever it is, the switch from the preposition "li" (for) is because they are not mentioned under a title that justifies ownership and exclusive entitlement, like those before them; or it is to indicate that their ownership of what they are given is not settled, as in the first two interpretations; or that it is not established at all, as in the last interpretation; or to signal their firm establishment in entitlement to charity, because the preposition "fi" (in) indicates enclosure, showing that they are surrounded by it and are its place and center.

﴿And the debtors﴾: that is, those who incurred debts for themselves in what is not sinful, when they do not have a surplus beyond their debts to meet the nisab. Likewise according to al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him: one who incurred debt to reconcile between people and extinguish strife between two tribes, even if they are wealthy. ﴿And in the cause of Allah﴾: that is, poor fighters, pilgrims, and those cut off from their means. ﴿And the wayfarer﴾: that is, the traveler cut off from his wealth. The repetition of the preposition in the last two is to indicate the greater excellence of these two in entitlement, or because of what was mentioned about their being introduced under a title that does not justify ownership and exclusive entitlement.

These are the categories of charities, so the giver may give his charity to each one of them, or confine it to one category among them, because the "li" (for) indicates that they are destinations from which it does not go out, not that it establishes entitlement. This has been related from Umar, Ibn Abbas, and Hudhayfa, may Allah be pleased with them all. According to al-Shafi'i: it is not permissible except that it be spent on three of those categories.

﴿An obligation from Allah﴾: a emphatic verbal noun for what the beginning of the verse indicates, that is, He prescribed the charities for them as an obligation. It is transmitted from Sibawayh that it is in the accusative governed by an implied verb, meaning: Allah prescribed that as an obligation; or it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the hidden pronoun in the phrase "for the poor," meaning: the charities are due to them in the state of being an obligation, that is, prescribed.

﴿And Allah is All-Knowing﴾ of the conditions of people and the degrees of their entitlement, ﴿All-Wise﴾, who does not do except what wisdom requires of good matters, among which is the delivery of rights to those who deserve them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 61:

﴿And among them are those who harm the Prophet﴾. It was revealed concerning a group of the hypocrites who said about him (ﷺ) what was not fitting. Some of them said: "Do not do it, for we fear that it will reach him and it will fall upon us." Al-Jallas ibn Suwayd said: "We will say whatever we wish, then we will come to him and deny what we said, and swear, and he will believe what we say, for Muhammad is merely an listening ear." This is His saying, mighty and majestic: ﴿and they say, "He is an ear"﴾, meaning: he hears everything that is said without reflecting upon it and distinguishing between what is fitting to accept, by virtue of the signs of truthfulness supporting it, and what is not fitting. They said this because he (ﷺ) did not confront them with the evil of what they did, and he pardoned them out of forbearance and generosity. So they took him to be of sound heart, and said what they said.

﴿Say: "An ear of good for you"﴾. It is of the same type as (a man of truth) in indicating emphasis on excellence and goodness. As if it were said: "Yes, he is an ear, but what a good ear!" It is also possible that the meaning is an ear for what is good and right, and for what it is fitting to hear and accept, and not for anything else. This is indicated by the reading (raḥmatin) in the genitive, in coordination with it, meaning: he is an ear of good and mercy, which hears nothing other than these two and does not accept anything else. It was also read (uḏnun) with a sukun on the dhal in both places, and it was read (uḏunun khayrun) as an attributive or as a second predicate.

His saying, mighty and majestic: ﴿He believes in God﴾ is an explanation of his being an ear of good for them, meaning: he gives credence to God, exalted is He, because of the proofs that have established it for him, which necessitate it. That this is good for the addressees, just as it is good for all the worlds, is not hidden.

﴿And he believes the believers﴾, meaning: he gives credence to them because of the sincerity he knows in them. The lam is extra, to distinguish between the well-known iman (belief) and iman in the sense of submission and confirmation, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Shall we believe you?﴾ ... etc., and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But none believed Moses﴾ ... etc.

﴿And a mercy﴾ is coordinated with (an ear of good), meaning: and he is a mercy, by way of using the verbal noun for the agent, for emphasis. ﴿For those of you who believe﴾, meaning: for those among you who display belief, since he accepts it from them, but not as confirmation of them in that, rather out of gentleness toward them and compassion for them, and he does not expose their secrets nor tear away their veils. The ascription of belief to them by a verbal form after ascribing it to the believers by the form of the active participle, which indicates firmness and continuity, is to signal that their belief is a passing matter that has no permanence.

﴿And those who harm the Messenger of God﴾, by what has been reported of their saying: "He is an ear," and the like. The future form, which indicates that the threat is consequent upon persistence in what they are upon, is an indication of the acceptance of their repentance, as He, exalted is He, made clear in what follows: ﴿If they repent, it will be better for them﴾.

﴿For them﴾, because of what they presume to do of harming him (ﷺ), as the construction of the judgment on the relative pronoun indicates. ﴿A painful punishment﴾. This is a parenthetical statement issued by Him, mighty and majestic, in the manner of a threat, not included under the address. In repeating the predication by affirming a painful punishment for them, and then making the sentence the predicate of the relative pronoun, there is an emphasis that is not hidden. And mentioning him (ﷺ) by the title of Messenger, attached to the Divine Name, is for the utmost glorification and to draw attention to the fact that harming him returns to the sacred presence of Him, mighty and majestic, necessitating complete wrath and anger.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 62:

﴿They swear by Allah to you﴾ The address is specifically to the believers. The hypocrites used to speak with disparagements (of the Prophet), then they would come to them and make excuses to them, and they would confirm their excuses with oaths so that they would excuse them and be pleased with them. That is: they swear to you that they did not say what was conveyed to them of that which causes harm to the Prophet ﷺ. As for staying behind from jihad, it is not included in this excuse. ﴿That they may please you﴾ thereby. The singling out of their seeking to please (you) as the stated purpose, although the principal aim of their intentions is to please the Messenger ﷺ, and he ﷺ accepted that from them and did not refute them, is to signal that this is far from being a means to pleasing him ﷺ, and that he ﷺ did not refute them only out of gentleness toward them and concealment of their faults, not out of contentment with what they did, as has been pointed out.

﴿Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾ That is: more deserving of being pleased. This is only achieved through obedience and following, and fulfilling his ﷺ rights in matters of honour and reverence, in his presence and in his absence. As for the false oaths they have made, they are only pleasing to one whose path of knowledge is confined to reports, until the truth comes and falsehood vanishes. The clause is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in "they swear", meaning: they swear to you in order to please you, while the case is that Allah the Exalted and His Messenger have more right to be pleased than you. That is: they turn away from what concerns them and benefits them, and occupy themselves with what does not concern them.

The singular pronoun in (yurḍūhu) is either to signal that the Prophet's ﷺ pleasure is included within the pleasure of Allah, the Glorified, and pleasing him ﷺ is pleasing Him, the Exalted, by His saying: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has indeed obeyed Allah﴾. Or it is because it is used in place of the demonstrative pronoun that refers to the singular and the plural according to the interpretation of what has been mentioned, as in the saying of Ru'bah:

*In it are lines of black and white, as if on the hide is the streaking of leprosy.*

That is: as if that were not said. What need is there for metaphor after the aforementioned interpretation? We say: were it not for the metaphor, the interpretation would not be possible, because the pronoun does not address anything except the essence of what it refers back to, without addressing any of its attributes, of which being mentioned is one. What addresses these is the demonstrative pronoun. Or it is because it refers to His Messenger, and the statement consists of two clauses, the predicate of the first being omitted because the predicate of the second indicates it, as Sibawayh held, and from this is the saying of the one who said:

*We are with what we have, and you are with what you have, content, and opinions differ.*

Or it refers to Allah, on the basis that what has been mentioned is the predicate of the first clause, and the predicate of the second clause is omitted, as is the view of al-Mubarrad.

﴿If they are believers﴾ Its response is omitted, relying on what precedes it to indicate it. That is: if they are believers, then let them please Allah and His Messenger in the manner mentioned, for they are more deserving of being pleased.

﴿Did they not know﴾, that is, those hypocrites? The interrogative is for rebuke over the enormity they committed while knowing its evil end. It is also read with the letter *tā'* (*Alam tu'lamū*, "Did you not know?"), as an *iltifāt* (shift from third person to second person) to intensify the reproach and rebuke. That is: did they not know, from what they heard from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) of the various kinds of thunderous warnings and admonitions, ﴿that he﴾, that is, the matter, ﴿whoever opposes God and His Messenger﴾? *Muḥādda* (opposition) derives from *ḥadd* (limit), like *mushāqqa* (opposition) derives from *shaqq* (split), and *mu'ādāh* (enmity) derives from *'udwah* (side, flank), meaning that each of those who perform the acts mentioned is in a position other than that of his counterpart. *Man* is a conditional particle whose apodosis is God's words: ﴿then for him is the fire of Hell﴾, with its predicate omitted, that is, "then it is certain that for him is the fire of Hell." It is also read with a *kasra* on the *hamza* (*inna*), in which case the conditional clause is in the nominative position as the predicate of *inna*; together with its predicate it stands in place of the two objects of *ya'lamū* (they know). It has been said that the meaning is: (p-79) "then for him," and that *anna* is a repetition of the first *anna* for emphasis because of the length of separation, not a case of verbal emphasis that would prevent the first from governing. The entry of the *fa'* is like the saying of one who said:

*Indeed the people of Yemen knew that I*
*When I say "amma ba'd," I am its orator.*

It has also been permitted that ﴿then for him﴾ is coordinated with *annahu* and the apodosis of the conditional is omitted; its estimate is: "Did they not know that whoever opposes God and His Messenger will perish, so that for him is..." etc. This was rejected on the ground that such is permissible only when the verb of the condition is in the past tense or is a present verb jussived by *lam*.

﴿abiding therein﴾ is a presumed circumstantial clause (*ḥāl muqaddarah*) from the pronoun in the prepositional phrase, if the beginning of the settling and its occurrence is taken into account in the adverbial phrase; if the absolute settling is taken into account, the matter is evident. ﴿That﴾: reference is made to the mentioned punishment of eternal abiding by "that," to signal the remoteness of its degree in terror and atrocity. ﴿is the great disgrace﴾. *Khizy* is humiliation and abasement accompanied by exposure and remorse, and these are the fruits of their hypocrisy, since they are disgraced before all witnesses when it becomes manifest and the everlasting punishment befalls them. The sentence is a concluding summary (*tadhyīl*) of what preceded.

﴿The hypocrites are wary lest a surah be sent down against them﴾ concerning their affair, for whatever is revealed about them is revealed against them. ﴿A surah telling them what is in their hearts﴾ of hidden secrets, let alone what they used to express among themselves of sayings of disbelief and hypocrisy. The meaning of its "informing them" of what is in their hearts, even though that is known to them, and even though what they feared was the believers' discovery of their secrets, not their own discovery of them, is that it would broadcast the secrets they were concealing, so that they would spread among the people and be heard from men's mouths as public talk. It is as though it were informing them of these things. Or the intended meaning of "informing" is exaggeration in the surah's containing their secrets, as though it knew of their inner states what they did not know, so it informs them of these and censures their ugly deeds.

It has been said: the meaning of ﴿yahdharu﴾ ("is wary") is "let them be wary" (a jussive/imperative sense). It has also been said: the first two pronouns refer to the believers and the third to the hypocrites. Shifting of pronouns is not objectionable when the meaning returns to the same referent once the matter is clear. That is: the hypocrites are wary lest a surah be sent down upon the believers informing them of what is in the hearts of the hypocrites, and exposing their hidden veils.

Abu Muslim (al-Isfahani) said: Their display of wariness was by way of mockery, for when they heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) mention everything and say, "It is by way of revelation," they would deny him and mock him. Therefore it was said: ﴿Say: Mock on﴾, meaning: carry out the mockery, and this is a command of threat. ﴿Indeed Allah will bring forth﴾, meaning: from potentiality into actuality, or from concealment into manifestation, ﴿what you fear﴾, meaning: what you fear of the sending down of the surah, and of your disgraceful deeds and blemishes lurking in your hearts, which will expose you before the people. The emphasis (in the use of "indeed") serves to refute their denial of this, not to dispel their doubt about the occurrence of what they fear, since their wariness is not real in the true sense.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 65:

﴿And if you ask them﴾ about what they said, ﴿they will surely say, "We were only engaging in talk and play."﴾ It is narrated that "he (ﷺ) was traveling on the expedition of Tabuk, and before him was a group of the hypocrites, who were mocking the Qur'an and the Messenger (ﷺ) and saying: 'Look at this man, who wants to conquer the fortresses and palaces of Syria! Far-fetched, far-fetched!' So Allah the Exalted informed His Prophet of that, and he said: 'Hold the caravan back for me.' He came to them and said: 'You said such-and-such.' They said: 'O Prophet of Allah, no, by Allah, we were not in anything concerning your affair or the affair of your companions, but we were in something of what travelers engage in, so that one of us might shorten the journey for another.'"

﴿Say﴾, without paying attention to their excuse, censuring their offenses and treating them as those who admit that the mockery occurred, rebuking them for their errors in the place of mockery: ﴿Was it at Allah, and His signs, and His Messenger that you were mocking?﴾ Here he follows the interrogative particle with the object of mockery. This is not proper unless the mockery is established and confirmed.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 66:

﴿Do not make excuses;﴾ do not occupy yourselves with excusing, which is an expression for wiping out the trace of the sin, for it is known to be false and clearly invalid. ﴿You have indeed disbelieved﴾ you have openly shown disbelief by harming the Messenger (ﷺ) and slandering him ﴿after your belief﴾ after your having professed it.

﴿If We pardon a group among you﴾ because of their repentance and sincerity, or because they refrained from harming and mocking him. It was also read as (إن يَعْفُ, "if He pardons"), with the verb attributed to God, Glorified is He. It was also read in the passive voice, with the verb attached to the adverbial noun (طائفة, "a group") with the verb masculine, and also feminine, going by the meaning, as if it were said: "If a group is shown mercy" ﴿We will punish﴾ with the plural of majesty (نعذب, "We punish"). It was also read with the yā' (يُعَذَّبْ, "he is punished") in the active voice, and with the tā' (تُعَذَّبْ, "it is punished") in the passive voice, attached to what follows it ﴿a group, because they were criminals﴾ persisting in crime, and they are those who did not repent, or who themselves committed it and they are those who did not refrain from it.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: The one who was pardoned was a single man, Yahya ibn Himyar al-Ash'ari (الأشجعي, al-Ash'ja'i in the text). When this verse was revealed, he repented of his hypocrisy and said: "O God, I still hear a verse that makes the skins shiver and the hearts tremble. O God, make my death a killing in Your way, so that no one can say: 'I washed him, I shrouded him, I buried him.'" He was then killed on the Day of Yamama, and none of the Muslims was known to have been slain except that his fall was recognized, apart from him.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 67:

﴿The hypocrite men and the hypocrite women﴾ The mention of the females separately is to announce the completeness of their rootedness in disbelief and hypocrisy. ﴿Some of them are from others﴾ That is: they resemble one another in hypocrisy and in distance from faith, like parts of one and the same person. It has been said: what is intended is the negation that they are among the believers, and the refutation of their oath by God, ﴿Indeed they are surely from you﴾, and an affirmation of the words of the Exalted: ﴿"And they are not from you."﴾

As for the words of the Exalted: ﴿They enjoin what is reprehensible﴾ That is: disbelief and acts of disobedience, ﴿and forbid what is right﴾ That is: faith and obedience. This is a resumed sentence (isti'naf) that affirms the content of what preceded and clarifies the opposition of their state to the state of the believers; or it is a second predicate.

﴿And they withhold their hands﴾ That is: from good deeds and from spending in the way of God, for the grasping of the hand is a metaphor (kinaya) for stinginess. ﴿They forgot God﴾ They neglected His remembrance. ﴿So He forgot them﴾ He abandoned them, withholding from them His mercy and bounty, and forsook them. The expression of this by "forgetting" is by way of correspondence (mushakala). ﴿Indeed the hypocrites, they are the defiantly disobedient﴾ those who are complete in rebellion and defiant wickedness (fisq), which is departure from obedience and stripping away from every good. The use of the explicit noun in place of the pronoun is to increase the affirmation, as in the words of the Exalted:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 68:

﴿God has promised the hypocrites, men and women, and the disbelievers﴾, that is, those who openly declare (their disbelief) (p-81), ﴿the fire of Hell, abiding therein﴾, deeming their abiding therein (as certain), ﴿it is sufficient for them﴾ as punishment and recompense. In this there is evidence of the greatness of its punishment and torment. ﴿And God has cursed them﴾, that is, He has removed them from His mercy and humiliated them. In the manifestation of the Majestic Name there is an indication of the intensity of wrath that is not hidden. ﴿And for them is a lasting punishment﴾, that is, a kind of punishment other than the punishment of the Fire, constant, never ceasing, or: for them is a lasting punishment with them in this world that never leaves them, and it is what they suffer from the toil of hypocrisy in which they are in a constant tribulation, not feeling safe for a single hour from the fear of exposure and the descent of punishment should their secrets be discovered.

﴿كالَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِكُمْ﴾ This is an *iltifat* (a shift from the third person to the second person, a grammatical device, here) for emphasis. The *kaf* (like) is in the nominative position as a predicate, meaning: "You are like those before you from the destroyed nations." Or it is in the accusative position, governed by a deleted verb, meaning: "You did as those before you did."

﴿كانُوا أشَدَّ مِنكم قُوَّةً وأكْثَرَ أمْوالا وأوْلادًا﴾ This is an explanation and clarification of their resemblance to them, and a comparison of their state to the state of those others. ﴿فاسْتَمْتَعُوا﴾ They enjoyed themselves. The *istif'al* form (*istamta'a*) carries a meaning of seeking more and continuing in enjoyment that the *tafa'ul* form (*tamatta'a*) does not carry. ﴿بِخَلاقِهِمْ﴾ with their portion of the pleasures of this world. It is derived from *khalq*, meaning "measure," which is what is measured out for its possessor. ﴿فاسْتَمْتَعْتُمْ بِخَلاقِكم كَما اسْتَمْتَعَ﴾ The *kaf* is in the accusative position as an adjective to a deleted verbal noun, meaning: "enjoyment like the enjoyment of ﴿الَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِكم بِخَلاقِهِمْ﴾ those before you with their portion." This censures the earlier peoples for their enjoyment of their base shares of fleeting appetites, and for their being diverted by them from considering the true consequences and the genuine pleasures. It is a preparation for censuring the addressees by their resemblance to those peoples and their following in their footsteps. ﴿وَخُضْتُمْ﴾ meaning: you entered into falsehood. ﴿كالَّذِي خاضُوا﴾ meaning: like those who (with the *nun* dropped), or like the group who, or like the plunging that they plunged into.

﴿أُولَئِكَ﴾ is a demonstrative referring to those characterized by the enumerated attributes, both the ones compared and the ones they are compared to, and not only to the last group. Otherwise it would follow that the nullification of the works and the loss of the ones compared would be understood only implicitly and not explicitly, and the shift in address would lose its benefit, since the apparent form would then be ﴿أُولَئِكُمْ﴾. The address is to the Messenger of God ﷺ or to everyone fit to be addressed. That is: ﴿أُولَئِكَ﴾ those described by the blameworthy actions mentioned. ﴿حَبِطَتْ أعْمالُهُمْ﴾ It does not mean their enumerated actions, as the use of the demonstrative to refer to them suggests, since the harm of those is clear and needs no explanation. Rather it means their works by which they would have deserved good rewards had they been accompanied by faith. That is, they were lost and nullified entirely, and no effect resulted from them.

﴿فِي الدُّنْيا والآخِرَةِ﴾ by way of reward and honor. As for the Hereafter, this is evident. As for this world, it is because what results from their works in it, such as health, ease, and other things, as indicated by the saying of the Mighty and Majestic: (Whoever desires the life of this world and its adornment, We will pay them their works in it, and they will not be deprived therein), this result is not by way of reward and honor, but by way of *istidraj* (gradual lure).

﴿وَأُولَئِكَ﴾ That is, those described by the nullification of their works in both abodes. ﴿هُمُ الخاسِرُونَ﴾ the complete losers in both abodes, who combine all the beginnings and causes of loss entirely. Their capital, which is their works, has gone to what harmed them and never benefited them at all. Had it gone to what neither harmed nor benefited them, that would have been enough loss for them. The use of the demonstrative in both places is to indicate that the described attributes are the causes of the nullification and the loss. (p-82)

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 70:**

﴿Has there not come to them﴾, i.e., the hypocrites, ﴿the news of those before them﴾, i.e., their report, which is significant, namely what they did and what was done to them. The interrogative (istifham) is for affirmation (taqrir) and warning (tahdhir): ﴿the people of Noah, 'Ad, Thamud, the people of Abraham, and the companions of Madyan﴾, and they are the people of Shu'ayb; ﴿and the overturned cities﴾, the towns of the people of Lot. They were overturned with their people (ii'tafakat bihim), i.e., turned upside down, so that their highest part became their lowest, and they were rained upon with stones of sijjil. It is also said that they are the towns of those who denied, and their overturning (i'tifakuhunna) is the transformation of their conditions from good to evil.

﴿Their messengers came to them with clear proofs﴾: this is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) explaining their report. ﴿It was not God who would wrong them﴾: the fa' is for conjunction with an implied clause that the discourse demands and the structure requires, i.e., they denied their messengers, so God destroyed them, and thus He did not wrong them by that. The choice of what the noble structure has, for the sake of emphasis in declaring the Glorified free from wronging, i.e., it was not proper nor fitting for Him that He should wrong them. ﴿But they were wronging themselves﴾. The combination of the past and the present forms in His words, Exalted and Majestic, ﴿but they were wronging themselves﴾ indicates the continuity of their wrongdoing, since they never ceased exposing themselves to punishment through disbelief and denial. The fronting of the object (taqdim al-maf'ul) is merely for the sake of concern with it, while observing the verse-ending (fasila), without intending to restrict the state of being wronged to them, according to the view of those who do not hold that fronting necessitates restriction. So it is as in His words, Exalted: ﴿And We did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves﴾, without restricting the wronging to the agent or the object. More explanation of this will come in His words, Glorified: ﴿Indeed, God does not wrong people in anything, but people wrong themselves﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 71:

﴿And the believing men and the believing women are allies of one another﴾ This is a statement of the good condition of the believing men and believing women, both in their present state and in their final outcome, following the statement of the ugly condition of their opposites, both in this world and in the next. The expression of the relationship of these (the believers) to one another by "wilayah" (allegiance/alliance), and of the relationship of those (the hypocrites) by "min" (from), which is the connective min, serves to indicate that the relationship of these believers is by way of religious kinship founded upon a covenant, which entails effects such as aid, support and other things; and the relationship of those (the hypocrites) is in accordance with nature and custom.

﴿They enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong﴾ That is, the category of the right (ma'ruf) and the wrong (munkar), which encompass every good and every evil. ﴿And they establish prayer﴾ so they never cease to remember God, Glorified is He; this is in contrast to what preceded in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They forgot God﴾. ﴿And they give zakat﴾, in contrast to His saying, Exalted is He: "and they withhold their hands" ﴿And they obey God and His Messenger﴾ That is, in every command and prohibition. This is in contrast to the description of the hypocrites with complete wickedness and departure from obedience.

﴿Those﴾ is a reference to the believing men and believing women in terms of their being characterized by the virtuous attributes that have preceded. The sense of distance in it (the use of the distal demonstrative) serves to indicate the distance of their rank in excellence; that is: those who are described by the noble qualities that have been detailed. ﴿God will surely show them mercy﴾ That is, He will pour upon them the effects of His mercy, in the form of confirmation and support (p-83) most certainly, for the sin (in sa-yarhamuhum) is emphatic of the occurrence, as in your saying: "I will surely take revenge on you."

﴿Indeed God is Mighty﴾ This is a justification for the promise; that is: He is strong and capable of exalting His allies and subduing His enemies. ﴿Wise﴾ He establishes His rulings on the basis of wisdom, which calls for delivering rights of blessing and of retribution to those deserving of them, from among the people of obedience and the people of disobedience. This is a promise to the believers that includes a warning to the hypocrites, just as what preceded concerning the hypocrites, in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So He forgot them﴾, is a warning to them that includes a promise to the believers, for withholding His gentle favor from them is a gentle favor in regard to the believers.

﴿Allah has promised the believing men and the believing women﴾: this is a detailed account of the effects of His mercy in the Hereafter, following the mention of His mercy in this world. The use of the explicit noun in place of a pronoun serves to reinforce the statement and to indicate that faith is the cause of obtaining what the promise concerns. Not mentioning what preceded, namely enjoining good and other things, signals that these are among its necessary consequences and results. That is, He promised them a promise encompassing each one of them, across their different ranks in excellence, qualitatively and quantitatively.

﴿Gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein﴾: each one of them will certainly attain these gardens. ﴿And pleasant dwellings﴾: that is, He promised some of the distinguished, perfected ones among them dwellings that souls find pleasant, or in which life is pleasant. According to a report, they are palaces of pearls, chrysolite, and red rubies. ﴿In gardens of Eden﴾: these are the most splendid and the most elevated of the places of the Gardens.

From the Prophet (ﷺ): "Eden is the house of Allah which no eye has seen and which has not occurred to the heart of any human being. Only three will dwell in it: the prophets, the truthful (ṣiddīqūn), and the martyrs. Allah, exalted is He, says: 'Blessed is the one who enters you.'"

And from Ibn ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with them both): In Paradise there is a palace called ʿAdan, around which are towers and meadows, and it has five thousand doors, and at each door are five thousand maidens with wide, dark eyes (ḥūr). No one enters it except a prophet, or a truthful one, or a martyr.

And from Ibn Masʿūd (may Allah be pleased with him): it is the innermost part (buṭnān) of Paradise and its center. On this view, ʿAdan is a proper name. It has also been said that it has its linguistic meaning, namely residence and perpetuity. Thus the conjunction returns to the difference and variation of description. It is as if He first described it as being of the kind of the most noble of the known places among them, gardens with flowing rivers, so that their natures would incline toward it at the first striking of their ears. Then He described it as enveloped in pleasant life, free from the impurities of turbidity which the places of this world scarcely ever lack. In it is what the souls desire and what the eyes delight in. Then He described it as a house of residence and steadfastness in the company of the ʿIlliyyūn (the highest ranks), where no decay or change will befall them. Then He promised them what is higher than all of that, saying: ﴿And approval from Allah﴾, that is, and even a small portion of His good pleasure, ﴿is greater﴾, because upon it revolves the attainment of every good and happiness, and by it is linked the gaining of every honor and lordship. Perhaps the reason it was not placed in the same string as the promise, despite its greatness in itself, is that it is realized within every promised thing, and because it is continuous in both abodes.

It has been reported that "He, exalted is He, says to the people of Paradise: 'Are you satisfied?' They say: 'Why would we not be satisfied, when You have given us what You have given no one of Your creation?' He says: 'I will give you something better than that.' They say: 'And what is better than that?' He says: 'I will cause My approval to descend upon you, so I shall never be displeased with you ever again.'"

﴿That﴾ refers to what has been mentioned before, and the sense of distance in it indicates that its rank is far in greatness and magnificence. ﴿That is the great triumph﴾, beyond what people count as triumph from the portions of this world. For, setting aside its perishing, its change, its troubles and its turbidity, it is not, in comparison with even the least of the bliss of the Hereafter, more than the wing of a gnat. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "If this world were worth the wing of a gnat in the sight of Allah, He would not have given a disbeliever a single sip of water from it." How well did the one who said:

Y'Allah, were the whole world to remain for us
and its provision to come to us abundant and easy,
it would not be right for a free person to take pride in it;
so how much less, when it is a enjoyment that vanishes tomorrow.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 73:**

﴿O Prophet, strive against the disbelievers﴾, i.e., those among them who openly show their disbelief, with the sword; ﴿and the hypocrites﴾, with argument and the enforcement of the prescribed penalties (hudud). ﴿And be harsh with them﴾ in that, and let not compassion (ra'fah) for them take hold of you. ʿAṭāʾ said: this verse abrogated (nasakhat, naskh) everything of pardon and forgiveness.

﴿And their refuge is Hell﴾: this is a resumed sentence (jumlah musta'nafah) explaining their ultimate fate following the explanation of their immediate fate. It has also been said that it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāliyyah). ﴿And wretched is the destination﴾: this is a concluding remark (tadhyil) for what precedes it, and the object of the dispraise (al-makhsus bi-l-dhamm) is omitted.

﴿They swear by God that they said nothing﴾. This is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf, a new sentence that resumes the discourse) explaining the offences that came from them, which warrant what preceded it of the command to fight and the harshness toward them, and their entry into Hell. It is narrated that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) remained during the expedition to Tabuk for two months, while the Qur'an was being revealed to him and he was censuring the hypocrites who had stayed behind. Those among them who were with him (ﷺ) heard this. Al-Jalas ibn Suwayd among them said: "If what Muhammad says is true concerning our brothers whom we left behind, who are our lords and nobles, then we are worse than donkeys." 'Amir ibn Qays al-Ansari said to al-Jalas: "Yes, by God, Muhammad is truthful, and you are worse than a donkey." This reached the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he summoned them. Al-Jalas swore by God that he had not said it. 'Amir raised his hand and said: "O God, send down upon Your servant and Prophet the confirmation of the liar and the refutation of the truthful." Then it was revealed. The use of the present form in "yahlifuna" (they swear) either brings the scene before the mind or indicates the repetition of the oath. The plural form in "qalu" (they said), although the speaker was al-Jalas, indicates that the rest of them, by their approval of his statement, became as if they were the speaker.

﴿They have indeed said the word of disbelief﴾. This is what was related just above. The sentence together with what is conjoined to it is a parenthetical clause (i'tiraḍ, an interjected sentence that breaks the flow of the discourse). ﴿And disbelieved after their Islam﴾, that is, they manifested what was in their hearts of disbelief after they had displayed Islam. ﴿And they aspired to what they did not attain﴾: this is the plot to kill the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Fifteen of them agreed to push him (ﷺ) off his mount when he ascended the mountain pass at night. 'Ammar ibn Yasir was holding the halter of his mount, leading it, and Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman was behind it, driving it. While they were thus, Hudhayfah heard the sound of camels' hooves and the clatter of weapons. He turned and saw people with their faces veiled. He said: "Back, back, O enemies of God!" They fled. It is also said that they were the hypocrites, and that they aspired to kill 'Ammar in retaliation for his reply to al-Jalas. It is also said that they intended to crown 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, even though the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was not pleased with that. ﴿And they held against them nothing﴾, that is, they did not disapprove of, nor find fault with, anything, or they did not find anything that would produce their resentment. ﴿Except that God and His Messenger had enriched them from His bounty﴾, glorified and exalted is He. This is because when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) came to Medina, they were in the utmost hardship of living; they did not ride horses and did not obtain booty. Then they were given preference with spoils. A client (mawla) of al-Jalas was killed, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) ordered that his blood-money, twelve thousand dirhams, be paid, and he became wealthy. The exception here is a restricted exception (istithna' mufarragh, an exception whose subject is left unstated and must be supplied from the context) from the most general of the objects (mafa'il) or the most general of the causes ('ilal). That is: they did not disapprove of anything of things except that God had enriched them with it; or they did not disapprove of what they disapproved of for any cause except God's enriching them.

﴿So if they repent﴾ from what they are upon of disbelief and hypocrisy, ﴿it will be better for them﴾ in both abodes. It is said that when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited it, al-Jalas said: "O Messenger of God, God has offered me repentance. By God, I did say it, and 'Amir spoke the truth." So al-Jalas repented, and his repentance was good. ﴿But if they turn away﴾, that is, they persist in what they were upon of turning away and avoiding the religion, or they turn away from repentance after this offer, ﴿God will punish them with a painful punishment in this world﴾ by killing, capture, plunder, and other kinds of punishment, ﴿and in the Hereafter﴾ by the Fire and other forms of retribution. ﴿And they will have in the earth﴾, despite its vastness, the distance of its regions, and the multitude of its inhabitants, which makes it possible to find what is negated by His words, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿any protector or helper﴾ who would rescue them from the punishment through intercession or defence.

(p-85)

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 75:

﴿Among them﴾ is an explanation of the vile deeds of another group among them. ﴿There are those who made a covenant with God: "If He gives us of His bounty, we will surely give charity (taṣṣaddaqanna)"﴾ meaning, we will surely pay zakat (zakah) and other forms of charity (ṣadaqat), ﴿and we will surely be among the righteous (al-ṣāliḥīn)﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: "He means the Hajj." It has also been read with the light nun (nūn al-khafīfah) in both verbs. It was said: "It was revealed concerning Tha'labah ibn Ḥāṭib, who came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: 'O Messenger of God, ask God to grant me wealth.' The Prophet ﷺ said: 'O Tha'labah, a little that you fulfill its right is better than a lot that you cannot bear.' He returned to him and said: 'By the One who sent you with the truth, if God grants me wealth, I will surely give everyone who has a right his right.' So he (ﷺ) prayed for him. He acquired sheep, which multiplied as worms multiply, until Medina became too small for them. He moved to a valley and cut himself off from the congregation and the Friday prayer. The Messenger of God ﷺ asked about him, and it was said: 'His wealth has increased so that a valley cannot contain it.' He said: 'Woe to Tha'labah!' Then he sent two collectors to take the charity. The people met them with their charities, and they passed by Tha'labah and asked him for charity and read to him the book of the Messenger of God ﷺ which contains the obligations. He said: 'This is nothing but a poll-tax (jizyah); this is nothing but a sister of the jizyah.' He said: 'Go back until I consider my opinion.' And that is His saying, Mighty and Majestic:"

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 76:

﴿When He gave them of His bounty, they became miserly with it﴾, i.e., they withheld the right of Allah from it. ﴿And they turned away﴾, i.e., they turned away from obedience to Allah, glorified is He. "When the two of them returned, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to them, before they spoke to him: 'Woe to Tha'labah,' twice, and then it was revealed."

Tha'labah came with the charity, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Allah has forbidden me to accept it from you." So he began throwing dust on his head. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "This is your deed; I commanded you, but you did not obey me." Then the Prophet (ﷺ) passed away. He brought it to Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him), but he did not accept it; and he brought it to 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) during his caliphate, but he did not accept it. He died during the caliphate of 'Uthman (may Allah be pleased with him). It was also said that the verse was revealed concerning him, and concerning Sahl ibn al-Harith, Jadd ibn Qays, and Mu'attib ibn Qushayr. The first view is the most well-known.

﴿And they are turning away﴾: this is an interjectory clause (jumlah mu'taridah), i.e., they are a people whose habit is turning away; or it is a circumstantial clause (haliyyah), i.e., they turned away in their wrongdoing while turning away in their hearts.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 77:**

﴿So He caused them to follow up﴾, i.e., God made the outcome of their action ﴿hypocrisy﴾ firmly established ﴿in their hearts until the Day they meet Him﴾, until the day of their death, on which they meet God Most High, or on which they meet the recompense of their deeds, which is the Day of Resurrection. It was also said: He bequeathed to them miserliness, which resulted in hypocrisy firmly rooted in their hearts, and this does not fit with His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿because they broke what they promised God﴾, i.e., because of their breaking what they had promised God Most High of charity and righteousness.

﴿and because they used to lie﴾, i.e., and because they persisted in lying in all the statements, of which their aforementioned promise is one. Restricting the lying to it would lead to the combination of the past and future verb forms being devoid of excellence, for the causing of the aforementioned consequence by breaking the promise and lying requires attributing it to God, Mighty and Majestic, since there is no sense in these two being causes of the consequence of miserliness resulting in hypocrisy. The verification is that since the particle *fa'* (ف), which indicates sequence and branching, signals the sequential consequence of enduring hypocrisy upon their actions reported about them, namely the covenant to give charity, righteousness, miserliness, turning away, and aversion, and some of these have no part in the stated sequence, such as the covenant itself, the ambiguity in this was removed by specifying what is the pivot in this matter. And God knows best. It was also read with the letter *dhal* (ذ) doubled (shaddah).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 78:

﴿Did they not know﴾ That is: the hypocrites, or those who made a covenant with Allah. It is also read with the second-person ta' (tā'), addressing the believers. So the hamza (alif of interrogation, hamzah) according to the first reading is for denunciation, rebuke and threat, meaning: did they not know ﴿that Allah knows their secret and their private conversation﴾, that is, what they concealed within themselves and what they discussed among themselves of slanders, and calling the charity (ṣadaqah) a jizyah (poll tax), and other such things in which there is no good. The reason for placing the secret before the private conversation will become clear in His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿and you will be returned to the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾.

﴿And that Allah is the Knower of the unseen things﴾, so nothing among things is hidden from Him, to the point that they dared to commit the great offences they committed. The displaying of the name of Majesty (ism al-jalālah, Allah) in both positions serves to instill awe and cultivate reverence; and in the bringing of the knowledge related to their secret and their private conversation in the form of a verb, which indicates occurrence and renewal, and the knowledge related to the many, constant unseen things in the form of a noun, which indicates permanence and intensity, there is a grandeur and eloquence that is not hidden.

And according to the second reading, it serves to confirm the believers' knowledge of this and to alert them that He, exalted is He, will call them to account and recompense them for what He knows of their deeds.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 79:

﴿Those who slander﴾ is in the accusative or nominative case, as a expression of blame (al-dhamm). It is also permissible to read it in the genitive, as a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in ﴿their secret and their private counsel﴾. It has also been read with a ḍammah on the mīm (yalmizūna → ylmzūna is not the reading; rather the reading is with ḍammah on the mīm), which is a dialect form, meaning: they find fault with ﴿those who give charity willingly﴾, i.e., those who volunteer and give freely ﴿from among the believers﴾, which is a ḥāl (circumstantial clause) qualifying "al-muṭṭawwi'īn". The words of the Exalted, ﴿in the charities﴾, are connected to "yalmizūna". It is related that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ urged the people to give charity, and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf came with forty ūqiyyah of gold, and it was said: with four thousand dirhams, and he said: "I had eight thousand; I lent my Lord four thousand and kept four thousand for my dependents." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "May Allah bless you in what you gave and in what you kept." So Allah blessed him, until Tumāḍir, the fourth of his wives, was reconciled for a quarter of the eighth share at eighty thousand. ʿĀṣim ibn ʿAdī gave a hundred wasq of dates. Abū ʿAqīl al-Anṣārī came with a ṣāʿ of dates and said: "I spent my night drawing water with a rope for two ṣāʿ, so I left one ṣāʿ for my dependents and came with one ṣāʿ." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ ordered him to scatter it among the charities, and the hypocrites found fault with them and said: "ʿAbd al-Raḥmān and ʿĀṣim gave only to show off, and Allah and His Messenger are not in need of Abū ʿAqīl's ṣāʿ; rather, he wanted to be mentioned by name so that he would be given from the charities." So this verse was revealed.

﴿And those who find nothing but their effort﴾ is coordinated with "al-muṭṭawwi'īn", meaning: and they find fault with those who find nothing but their capacity. It has also been read with a fatḥah on the jīm, which is the verbal noun of "jahada fī al-amr" when one exerts oneself in it. It has been said that with ḍammah it means capacity (ṭāqah), and with fatḥah it means hardship (mashaqqah).

﴿So they mock them﴾ is coordinated with "yalmizūna", meaning: they ridicule them, and the intended people are the last group. ﴿Allah mocks them﴾ is an announcement of His requiting them for their mockery, and the expression of it in this form is for the sake of mushākalah (correspondence of form). ﴿And for them﴾, meaning: established for them, ﴿is a painful punishment.﴾ The indefiniteness of "ʿadhāb" is for the sake of magnifying and emphasizing, and the nominal form of the sentence indicates continuity.

The phrase ﴿Seek forgiveness for them or do not seek forgiveness for them﴾ is a statement that seeking forgiveness for them and not seeking it are equal, since forgiveness is impossible for them. It is phrased as a command for emphasis in showing that the two are equal, as if the Prophet (ﷺ) were commanded to test the situation by seeking forgiveness at one time and abstaining at another, so that the clear state of the matter would become manifest to him, as in the saying of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Spend willingly or unwillingly; it will never be accepted from you﴾ (9:53), which has already passed.

﴿If you seek forgiveness for them seventy times, Allah will never forgive them﴾ is an explanation of the impossibility of forgiveness after exaggerating in seeking forgiveness, following the explanation of their equality and non-equality. It has been related that "Abd Allah ibn Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, who was among the sincere believers, asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), during the illness of his father, to seek forgiveness for him, and he (ﷺ) did so. Then the verse was revealed, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said, in observance of what is fundamentally the case, that the ranks of numbers are fixed limits whose judgment differs from that of what lies above them: 'Indeed Allah has granted me a concession, so I will add to the seventy.'" Then the verse was revealed: ﴿It is the same for them whether you seek forgiveness for them or do not seek forgiveness for them; Allah will never forgive them﴾. The use of seven, seventy, and seven hundred has become widespread to mean abundance in general, because seven comprises all the categories of number, so it is as if it were the whole number. It was also said that it is the most perfect of numbers, since it combines its meanings. Moreover, six is the first perfect number, because its proper parts are equal: its half is three, its third is two, its sixth is one, and their sum is six; with one added it becomes seven, so it was perfect, since after perfection there is no rank except completeness. Then seventy is the furthest point of completeness, since the units reach their limit in the tens, and seven hundred is the furthest of the limits.

﴿That﴾ refers to the impossibility of forgiving them even after exaggerating in seeking forgiveness. That is, that impossibility is not because your seeking forgiveness is disregarded, but ﴿because they﴾, that is, because ﴿they disbelieved in Allah and His Messenger﴾, with a disbelief that exceeded all bounds, as is indicated by their being described as defiantly disobedient (fasiqun) in the saying of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And Allah does not guide the defiantly disobedient people﴾. Indeed, defiance (fisq) in everything is an expression of rebellion and transgression of its limits. That is, He does not guide them with a guidance that reaches the goal at all, because this contradicts the wisdom upon which the orbit of creation and legislation revolves. As for guidance in the sense of pointing out what leads to the goal, it is certainly realized, but they, through their evil choice, did not accept it, so they fell into what they fell into. This is a concluding statement (tadhyil) confirming the judgment preceding it, for the forgiveness of a disbeliever comes only through abandoning disbelief and turning to the truth, while one who is immersed in it and sealed upon it is far removed from that. In this there is an indication of the excuse of the Prophet (ﷺ) in seeking forgiveness for them, namely that he did not despair of their faith, since he did not know that they were sealed upon error and misguidance. What is forbidden is seeking forgiveness for them after their state has become clear, as will be recited from the saying of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿It is not for the Prophet…﴾ ... the verse.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 81:**

﴿Those who were left behind rejoiced﴾, that is, those whom the Prophet (ﷺ) left behind by granting them permission to remain seated when they asked for leave. Or Allah left them behind by discouraging them, for a hidden wisdom that He knew in that. Or their laziness or hypocrisy left them behind. ﴿In their sitting﴾ is attached to *farika* (rejoiced), meaning: in their sitting and their staying behind from the campaign. ﴿Contrary to the Messenger of Allah﴾ means: after him and after his departure, since he went out and they did not go out. It is said: "He stayed *khilafa al-hayy*," meaning after them, when they departed and he did not depart. This is supported by the reading of those who read *khalfa Rasul Allah* (behind the Messenger of Allah), so its accusative case is as an adverbial of place (*zarf*) governed by *maq'adihim* (their sitting), since there would be no benefit in restricting their rejoicing with that. It was also said that it has the meaning of opposition (*mukhalafa*). This is reinforced by the reading of those who read *khulfa Rasul Allah*, with a dammah on the *kha'*, so its accusative case is as an object of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*), and the governing word is either *farika* (rejoiced), meaning they rejoiced for the sake of opposing him (ﷺ) by sitting, or *maq'adihim* (their sitting), meaning they rejoiced in their sitting for the sake of opposing him (ﷺ). Or it is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*), and the governing word is one of the two mentioned, meaning: they rejoiced while opposing him (ﷺ), or they rejoiced in sitting while opposing him (ﷺ).

﴿And they disliked striving with their wealth and their lives in the way of Allah﴾. This is not merely preferring ease and comfort over obedience to Allah, the Exalted, but comes together with what was in their hearts of disbelief and hypocrisy. Preferring one of two matters can be realized with the slightest inclination toward it, without the other reaching the level of dislike. The noble construction was chosen over saying "and they disliked going out to the campaign" to indicate that striving in the way of Allah, despite being among the greatest of desires and the most noble of aims which the competitors should compete for, is something they disliked, just as they rejoiced in the most vile of vices, which is sitting contrary to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

﴿And they said﴾, that is, to their brothers, to strengthen them in staying behind and sitting, and to counsel one another in evil and corruption. Or to the believers, to discourage them from striving and to forbid what is good, and to reveal some of the excuses that prompted them to what they rejoiced in, of sitting. Thus they combined three of the traits of disbelief and misguidance: rejoicing in sitting, disliking striving, and forbidding others from it.

﴿Do not go forth in the heat﴾, for its intensity cannot be endured. ﴿Say﴾, as a rebuttal to them and a declaration of their ignorance: ﴿The Fire of Hell﴾ which you will enter because of what you have done ﴿is more intense in heat﴾ than the familiar heat you fear and warn people against. So why do you not fear it, and expose yourselves to it by preferring sitting over going forth?

﴿If only they understood﴾. This is a concluding parenthetical statement from Him, glorified and exalted, not included within the speech that was commanded, confirming its content. The answer to "*law*" (if only) is either omitted, meaning: if only they understood that it is so, or how it is, or that their final destination is toward it when they did what they did, or they would have been affected by this admonition. Or it is not intended, with *law* used merely for wishing, which indicates the impossibility of the realization of what follows it, meaning: if only they were among the people of intelligence and understanding, as in the saying of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Say: Look at what is in the heavens and the earth, but signs and warnings avail not a people who do not believe﴾.

﴿So let them laugh a little and let them weep much﴾ This is an informing about their immediate and eventual state: little laughter and much prolonged weeping, which their evil deeds lead to, among which is what was mentioned of joy. The *fa'* (in *fa-l-yadhakū*) indicates causation for what preceded, for the sake of informing about the laughing and weeping that were mentioned, not for the laughing and weeping themselves, since causation cannot be conceived in the first at all. *Qalīlan* and *kathīran* are in the accusative as a verbal noun (*maṣdar*, infinitive-type noun) or as an adverbial accusative of time (*ẓarf*), meaning a little laughter and much weeping, or a little time and a long time. Expressing it in the form of a command serves to indicate the certainty of the occurrence of what is reported, for the command of an obeyed commander is something the one commanded hardly ever fails to carry out. Except that the purpose of the command in the first case is only to convey the description of paucity alone, and in the second, the description of abundance together with the thing described.

It is narrated that the hypocrites (*ahl al-nifāq*) will weep in the Fire for the whole lifetime of this world, their tears never drying up, and they will not enjoy sleep. It is also possible that laughter is a metaphor for joy and weeping for grief, and that paucity is an expression for non-existence and abundance for permanence.

﴿As a recompense for what they used to earn﴾ of the various kinds of sins. The combining of the two forms, the past and the future, indicates a continuous, renewed habit for as long as they were in the world. *Jazā'an* is an object of purpose (*maf'ūl lahu*) for the second verb, meaning "let them weep as a recompense." Or it is a verbal noun whose governing verb has been omitted, meaning they will be recompensed with the much weeping that was mentioned, as a recompense for the sins they earned that were mentioned.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 83:

﴿So if Allah returns you﴾ The fa' (fa) here is for the sequential connection of the command that follows upon what has been explained of their situation. The verb is from ar-raj' in its transitive form (raj'), not the intransitive ruju' (return). That is: if Allah Almighty sends you back ﴿to a group of them﴾, that is, to the hypocrites among those who stayed behind in Madinah, since the staying behind of some of them was due to a genuine excuse alongside their Islam; or to those of the hypocrites who remained behind, some of whom had passed away, or were absent from the city, or some of whom had not sought permission. It is narrated from Qatadah that they were twelve men, and of them it was said what was said.

﴿Then they ask your permission to go out﴾ with you to another campaign after this campaign of yours. ﴿Then say﴾ (as a way of removing them from the register of warriors and distancing their place from the assembly of your companionship): ﴿You will never go out with me, ever, and you will never fight with me against any enemy.﴾ This is a statement in the sense of a prohibition, for emphasis, and it did happen so. ﴿Indeed, you﴾ is the reason for what came before, that is: because ﴿you were pleased with sitting back﴾, that is, from the campaign, and you rejoiced in that ﴿the first time﴾, which is the campaign of Tabuk. ﴿So sit back﴾: the fa' here is for the sequential connection of the command to sit back, by way of punishment, upon what proceeded from them of contentment with sitting back. That is: since you were pleased with sitting back the first time, then sit back hereafter ﴿with those who stay behind﴾, that is, those who lag behind, whose habit is always sitting back and lagging behind. The word has also been read as (al-Khalifin) with a short vowel, so the erasure of their names from the register of the fighters and their being joined with the company of those who stay behind was a punishment for them of the utmost degree. The masculine form of the comparative adjective when it is attached to a feminine noun is the more common usage on people's tongues, for you hardly hear a speaker say: "she is the greatest woman" or "the first time" in the feminine.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 84:**

﴿And do not pray over any of them who has died﴾ is a qualifier (ṣifah) of "aḥad" (any one).
