The past tense is used to draw attention to the certainty that it will happen. ﴿Ever﴾ is connected to the prohibition, meaning: do not supplicate for them or seek forgiveness for them ever. ﴿Nor stand at his grave﴾ means do not stand over it for burial, or for visitation and supplication. It is narrated that "he (ﷺ) used to stand over the graves of the hypocrites and supplicate for them. When the head of hypocrisy, Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, fell ill, he sent to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asking him to come. When he entered upon him, he (ﷺ) said: 'Has the love of the Jews destroyed you?'" He said: (p-90) "O Messenger of Allah, I sent for you so that you would ask forgiveness for me, not so that you would rebuke me." He asked him to shroud him in his inner garment, the one next to his skin, and to pray over him. When he died, his son, who was a believing and righteous man, asked him (ﷺ) to come. He (ﷺ) agreed, as consolation for him and out of consideration for his feelings, and sent his shirt, and he was shrouded in it. When he (ﷺ) was about to pray over him, or had prayed, the verse was revealed."

And from Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "When Abdullah ibn Ubayy died and we placed him to be prayed over, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood up. I said: 'Will you pray over the enemy of Allah, who said on such-and-such a day, "such-and-such," and on such-and-such a day, "such-and-such"?' and I counted his wicked days. The Prophet (ﷺ) smiled, prayed over him, then walked with him and stood at his grave until he was buried. By Allah, he had not stayed long when the verse ﴿And do not pray …﴾ etc. was revealed. After that, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) never prayed over any hypocrite nor stood at his grave." The reason he (ﷺ) was not forbidden from shrouding him in his shirt is that withholding the shirt would have been a likely cause of falling short in generosity. Moreover, it was a recompense for the shirt that he (ﷺ) had given to al-'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, when he was taken captive at Badr. The report is well known.

﴿Indeed they disbelieved in Allah and His Messenger﴾ is the reason (ta'līl) for the prohibition, meaning that seeking forgiveness for the dead and standing at their graves is only for the purpose of improving their condition, and that is impossible for them, since they persisted in disbelief in Allah and His Messenger throughout their lives. ﴿And they died while they were defiant (fāsiqūn)﴾ means: they were rebellious in disbelief, transgressing its bounds, as has been explained regarding the meaning of fisq.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 85:

﴿And let not their wealth or their children impress you.﴾ This is a repetition of what preceded it, and a confirmation of its content by informing of its occurrence. It is also possible that this refers to a group other than the first group. The mention of wealth before children in such contexts, although children are dearer than it, is either due to the general extent of need for it (wealth) in its essence and according to individuals and times, for it is something indispensable for everyone, whether fathers, mothers, or children, at every time and moment, such that whoever has children but no wealth is with his children in hardship and distress; as for children, only one who has reached the stage of fatherhood desires them. Or it is because wealth is the means for the preservation of the self (nafs), and children for the preservation of the species (nawc); or it is because wealth is older in existence than children, since the seminal parts (al-ajza' al-manawiyya) are produced only from nourishment, as will come in surah al-Kahf.

﴿Indeed, Allah intends﴾ by what He has granted them of wealth and children ﴿to punish them with them in this world﴾ because of the hardship they endure and the severe toil they undergo concerning them, ﴿and that their souls should depart while they are disbelievers.﴾ That is: so that they die as disbelievers, through their preoccupation with enjoying them and their distraction from reflecting and contemplating the outcomes.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 86:

﴿And when a surah is sent down﴾ from the Qur'an, and it may also be meant that part of it is [sent down]. ﴿That believe in Allah﴾: "an" (that) here is explanatory (mufassirah) of the meaning of saying and revelation implied in "sending down"; or it is verbal-noun-forming (masdariyyah) with the preposition dropped from it, i.e., "bi-an" (by [saying]) ﴿and strive with His Messenger﴾ for the exaltation of His religion and the elevation of His word. ﴿Those of wealth among them ask your permission﴾, i.e., those possessing bounty, ample means, and capability for jihad by body and wealth. ﴿And they say﴾ is an explanatory conjunction (ʿatf tafsiri) to "they ask your permission", sufficing in place of mentioning what they sought permission for, namely remaining behind (al-qu'ud). ﴿Leave us, that we may be with those who sit [at home]﴾ (p-91) i.e., those who stayed behind from the expedition because of an excuse they had.

"They were content" is a resumptive statement explaining the evil of their conduct and their failure to comply with both commands, even though they did not expressly reject the first, ﴿that they should be with the khawalif﴾, that is, with the women whose lot is sitting still and staying in their homes. Khawalif is the plural of khalifa (the one left behind). It has also been said that the khalifa is one in whom there is no good. ﴿And a seal was set upon their hearts, so they﴾ because of that ﴿do not understand﴾ what is in faith in Allah, obedience to Him in His commands and prohibitions, following His Messenger (ﷺ), and jihad, of happiness, and what is in the opposites of these of wretchedness.

But the Messenger and those who believed with him [believed] in God and in what came to him from Him, the Exalted. This implies that they have no share at all in faith in God, even though they do not openly turn away from it, as they turned away from jihad (struggle in the way of God) by asking permission to stay behind. ﴿They strove with their wealth and their lives.﴾ That is, if these people stayed behind from the expedition, then others who are better than them, and purer in intention and belief, have already set out for it and risen to it. They upheld the matter of jihad in both of its forms, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If these disbelieve in it, We have indeed entrusted it to a people who are not disbelievers in it.﴾

﴿And those﴾, who are described with these noble attributes, ﴿for them﴾, through their aforementioned attributes, ﴿are the good things﴾, that is, the benefits of both abodes: victory and booty in this world, and Paradise and honour in the next. It has also been said that the good things are the maidens (al-hur), as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Therein are good and beautiful [women].﴾ The word is the plural of khayrah, a lightened form of khayyirah (خَيْرَةٍ، تَخْفِيفِ خَيِّرَةٍ). ﴿And those are the successful﴾, that is, those who attain the sought-after goal, not those who obtain some of the perishing portions of fleeting pleasure. The repetition of the demonstrative (those) serves to honour their station and to elevate their rank.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 89:

﴿Allah has prepared for them﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) explaining that they are the successful ones; that is, He has readied for them in the Hereafter ﴿gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever﴾. The phrase ﴿abiding therein﴾ is a predicative circumstantial clause (hal muqaddarah) from the pronoun in the genitive (al-damir al-majrur) and from the governing verb a'adda (prepared). ﴿That﴾ is a demonstrative referring to what is understood from Allah's preparing for them the aforementioned gardens, namely attaining the great honor; ﴿is the supreme triumph﴾, the triumph beyond which there is no other.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 90:

﴿And those who made excuses among the Bedouins came to be given leave;﴾ This begins the explanation of the circumstances of the hypocritical Bedouins, following the explanation of the hypocrites of the people of Madinah. Al-Mu'adhdhirun (those who make excuses) derives from " 'adhdhara fi al-amr" (he fell short in the matter, was negligent and did not exert himself), and its real meaning is that one gives the impression that he has an excuse in what he does while he has no excuse. Or it is al-mu'tadhirun (those who offer excuses), with the ta' assimilated into the dhal and its vowel transferred to the 'ain, and they are those who offer excuses falsely. It has also been read al-mu'dhirun, from al-i'dhar, which is striving in making an excuse and exerting oneself in it. It is said: they were the tribes of Asad and Ghatafan, who said: "Indeed we have dependents, and indeed we are in hardship, so grant us leave to stay behind." It is also said: they were the kinsmen of 'Amir ibn al-Tufayl, who said: "If we go out with you, the Bedouins of Tayy will raid our families and our livestock." So he (ﷺ) said: (p-92) "«Allah the Exalted will suffice me against you."»

It is narrated from Mujahid: a group from Ghifar offered excuses, but Allah, glorified is He, did not accept their excuses. And it is narrated from Qatadah: they offered excuses with falsehood. It has also been read al-mu'adhdhirun, with the 'ain and the dhal both doubled, from ta'adhdhara, meaning i'tadhara (offered an excuse), but this is a lahn (a grammatical/recitational error), since the ta' is not assimilated into the 'ain in the way it is assimilated into the ta', the za', and the sad in al-mutawwi'in (those who volunteer), wa-izzakka (and purified himself), and isssaddaq (and made himself truthful). It is also said: what is meant by them are those who offer excuses with soundness (of reason), and it was interpreted thus for al-mu'adhdhirun and al-mu'dhirun, i.e., those who did not fall short in offering excuses.

﴿And those who lied to Allah and His Messenger sat back.﴾ They are the hypocrites among the Bedouins who neither came nor offered excuses, so it became evident that they lied to Allah and His Messenger in claiming faith and obedience. ﴿Those among them who disbelieved will be struck by a painful punishment.﴾ That is, from among the Bedouins, or from among the excuse-makers, for among them are those who made excuses out of laziness rather than disbelief. ﴿A painful punishment﴾ by killing and capture in this world, and the Fire in the Hereafter.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 91:

﴿There is no blame upon the weak﴾, such as the very old and the chronically disabled, ﴿nor upon the sick﴾, ﴿nor upon those who find nothing to spend﴾ because of their poverty, such as Muzayna, Juhayna, and Banu 'Udhra. ﴿There is no sin (haraj)﴾, meaning no wrongdoing in staying behind, ﴿if they are sincere toward Allah and His Messenger﴾. This is an expression for faith in both of them, obedience to both of them in private and in public, loyalty to both of them in ease and in hardship, and love and hatred for their sake, as a sincere patron (mawla nasih) acts toward his companion.

﴿There is no way (sabil) against the good-doers﴾. This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) confirming the meaning of what preceded it; that is, there is no blame upon them and no path to rebuking them. The particle min (من) here is extra (mazida), for emphasis. Placing "the good-doers" (al-muhsinin) in the position of a pronoun indicates that they are included, by their sincerity toward Allah and His Messenger, among the category of the good-doers. Alternatively, it is a justification for negating blame from them, meaning: there is no path against the category of good-doers, and they are among them. ﴿And Allah is Forgiving, Merciful﴾. This is a concluding clause (tadhyil) that affirms the meaning of what was mentioned, indicating that they still have need of forgiveness, even though their staying behind was due to a valid excuse.

﴿And nor [is there blame] upon those who came to you that you might provide them with mounts,﴾ is a conjunction (ʿaṭf, coordination) with "the doers of good" (al-muḥsinīn), as indicated by His statement, Mighty and Majestic is He, later on: ﴿The only way [against them] is against those who...﴾ to the end of the verse. It was also said: it is a conjunction with "the weak" (al-ḍuʿafāʾ), and they are the weepers: seven men from the Anṣār: Maʿqil ibn Yasār, Ṣakhr ibn Khansāʾ, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Kaʿb, Sālim ibn ʿUmayr, Thaʿlaba ibn Ghanama, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Maʿqil, and ʿUlba ibn Zayd. "They came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: 'We have vowed to go out [to fight], so mount us on leather shoes [or boots] patched and sandals stitched, that we may fight with you.' He ﷺ said: '"I do not find [anything]."' So they turned away while weeping." It was also said: they were the sons of Muqarrin: Maʿqil, Suwayd, and Nuʿmān. It was also said: they were Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī and his companions, may Allah be pleased with them.

﴿You said, "I do not find anything to mount you upon."﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the kāf in (atawka) with the particle qad implied. "Mā" is general, covering what they asked him ﷺ for and other things which are customarily used as mounts. In choosing "I do not find" (lā ajidu) over "I do not have it" (laysa ʿindī), there is a refinement of speech and a soothing of the hearts of the askers, which is not hidden; it is as if he ﷺ were seeking what they asked for continuously, but not finding it.

﴿They turned away﴾ is the response (jawāb) of "idhā." ﴿And their eyes overflow﴾ meaning they flow intensely ﴿with tears﴾ meaning, tears. The "min" here is explicative (bayāniyya) together with its genitive object, in the position of the accusative as a specification (tamyīz). This is more eloquent than "their eye overflows with tears," because it conveys that the eye itself has become an overflowing mass of tears. The clause is circumstantial (ḥāliyya).

As for His statement, Mighty is His name: ﴿grief (ḥazanan)﴾ is in the accusative either as a causal object (ʿilliyya), or as a circumstantial accusative (ḥāliyya), or as a verbal noun (maṣdariyya) for a verb implied by what precedes it, meaning: they overflow out of grief. Grief is attributed to the eye metaphorically (majāzan), like overflowing (al-fayḍ). Or [it means]: they turn away with grief over it, or they are grieved, or they grieve with grief, in which case this clause is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "tafīḍu" (overflow).

﴿So that they do not find﴾ is by omission of a lām connected to "ḥazanan" or to "tafīḍu," meaning: so that they do not find ﴿what they might spend﴾ on buying what they need, since they did not find it with you.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 93:

﴿Indeed, the blame lies﴾ — through rebuke — ﴿upon those who ask your permission﴾ to stay behind, ﴿while they are wealthy﴾ — able to equip themselves for the campaign, along with their soundness of body — ﴿they are content﴾. This is a resumptive clause giving the reason for what preceded, as if it were said: "What is the matter with them that they seek permission while they are wealthy?" So it is said: ﴿they are content﴾ ﴿to be with those who stay behind﴾ — those whose condition is lowliness and baseness. ﴿And Allah has sealed over their hearts﴾, that is: He forsook them, so they became heedless of the grave outcome. ﴿Therefore they do not know﴾ — because of that — ever the peril of what they were content with, and what it entails in the future, just as they did not know the baseness of its condition in the present.

﴿They will make excuses to you﴾ is a resumptive sentence (*istiʾnāf*, a new sentence that resumes the discourse) explaining what they will be intent on when they return to them.

It is narrated that they were some eighty men. When the Prophet ﷺ returned to them, they came to him making excuses with falsehood. The address is to the Messenger of God ﷺ and his Companions, for they were also making excuses to the believers, not to the Messenger of God ﷺ alone. That is: they make excuses to you concerning their staying behind ﴿when you return﴾ from the expedition, ﴿arriving to them﴾. He did not say "to Medina" because it indicates that the basis of the excuse is returning to them, not returning to Medina; so perhaps some of them hastened to make excuses before returning to it. ﴿Say﴾: the restriction of this address to the Messenger of God ﷺ, after its generality previously to his Companions as well, is because answering is his ﷺ function. As for their excuse, it was inclusive of the Muslims in the sense that the return was inclusive of them.

﴿Do not make excuses﴾: that is, do not perform the excuse, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Be silent therein and do not speak to Me﴾ (Q. 23:108). Or: do not make excuses with what you have of pretexts. As for addressing the matter of their excuses being false, His saying, exalted is He, ﴿We will not believe you﴾ does not support it; that is: we will never confirm you in that, ever. This is a causal resumptive sentence (*istiʾnāf taʿlīlī*) explaining the prohibition, built on a question that arose from their side, and dependent upon their claim of truthfulness in the excuse, as if they had said: "Why should we not make excuses?" It was said: "Because we will never believe you," so it would be futile, since the purpose of the one making excuses would not be achieved by it.

His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿God has informed us of your news﴾ is a causal explanation for the absence of belief; that is: we have been informed by revelation of some of your news that is incompatible with belief, of the evil and corruption you have engaged in, which you concealed in your hearts and prepared to be displayed in the guise of excuse, consisting of falsehoods. The use of the first-person plural pronoun in both places is for emphasis in cutting off their hopes of being believed altogether, by showing that their excuses find acceptance with none of the believers at all; for the belief of some of them might lead them to hope for the Messenger's belief as well ﷺ through the believers, and to indicate that their disgrace is among all the believers.

﴿And God will see your deed﴾ in what is to come: whether you will turn in repentance to Him, exalted is He, from the hypocrisy in which you are, or whether you will persist. This seems to be a call to repent and a respite for repentance. The placement of the object of seeing before what is conjoined to its subject, namely His saying, ﴿and His Messenger﴾, is to indicate the difference between the two kinds of seeing and their disparity, and to suggest that the basis of the threat is His knowledge, mighty and majestic is He, of their deeds. ﴿Then you will be returned﴾ on the Day of Resurrection ﴿to the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾ (p-94) for recompense according to what has appeared from you of deeds. The placing of the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun is to intensify the threat, for His knowledge, glorified and exalted is He, of all their deeds, outward and inward, and His encompassing of their conditions, manifest and hidden, is what necessitates a great deterrence.

﴿Then He will inform you﴾ when you return to Him and stand before Him ﴿of what you used to do﴾; that is: of what you used to do in the world continuously, of evil deeds, past and future, on the basis that (*mā*) is a relative pronoun whose returning pronoun is omitted; or, with your continuous deed, on the basis that it is a verbal-noun construction (*maṣdariyya*). The meaning of informing with this is recompensing with it, and the choice of this word over the other is to observe what preceded in His saying, ﴿God has informed us﴾ etc., for what is informed of are the news related to their deeds; and to indicate that they did not know in the world the reality of their deeds, but they will know them on that Day.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 95:

﴿They will swear by Allah to you﴾ is an emphasis upon their false excuses and a confirmation of them. The sin (al-sin) here is for emphasis (li-l-ta'kid). The object of the oath is omitted, but it is indicated by the context, namely what they offered as excuses of falsehoods. The clause is either a substitute (badal) for ﴿they make excuses﴾ or an explanation (bayan) of it. ﴿When you return﴾, i.e., when you turn back (infasaltum) from the expedition, ﴿to them﴾. The meaning of inqilab (return) is turning back and departing, with the added sense of arriving and taking possession. The benefit of restricting their oath to this circumstance is to make clear that it is not meant to repel what the Prophet ﷺ addressed to them in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿"Do not make excuses"﴾ ... and so on; rather, it is an independent command.

﴿So that you may turn away﴾ and overlook ﴿from them﴾, overlooking with approval, so you do not rebuke them or reproach them, as His saying, Exalted is He, makes clear: ﴿"that you may be pleased with them"﴾, ﴿"so turn away from them"﴾. But it is not turning away with approval, as they desire, but turning away with avoidance and abhorrence, as His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He, expresses: ﴿"Indeed they are filth"﴾, for it is explicit that what is meant by "turning away from them" is either avoidance of them because of the spiritual filth within them, or abandonment of reforming them by ceasing reproach, since the purpose of reproach is purification by inducing repentance, and these are filth which does not accept purification, so they are not addressed with it.

His saying, Mighty and Exalted is He: ﴿"And their refuge is Hell"﴾ is either a completion of the justification, for their being among the people of the Fire is one of the motives for avoiding them and a requirement for abandoning their reform through blame and reproach; or it is an independent justification, meaning: the Fire suffices them as reproach and rebuke, so do not burden yourselves with it. ﴿"A recompense"﴾ is in the accusative as an emphatic infinitive (masdar mu'akkid) for a verb of the same root, implied and occurring as a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: they will be recompensed with a recompense; or it is for the content of the preceding sentence, since it definitely conveys the meaning of requital, as if it were said: they will be requited with a requital; ﴿"for what they used to earn"﴾ in the world of various evil deeds. Or it is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu).

﴿They swear to you﴾ is a *badal* (substitution, a grammatical apposition replacing the preceding clause). The sworn-by party is omitted because it is obvious; the meaning is: they swear by Allah, the Exalted, ﴿so that you may be pleased with them﴾ by their oath, and that you continue toward them what you were doing to them. ﴿But if you are pleased with them﴾ in line with what they sought and what you assisted them in, ﴿then surely Allah is not pleased with the defiant people﴾. That is: your pleasure with them will bring them no benefit, because Allah is angry with them, and your pleasure has no effect in the face of His wrath, glorified is He. Placing *al-fasiqin* (the defiant ones) in the place of the pronoun *hum* (they) serves to brand them with having departed from obedience, which deserves the wrath that has befallen them, and to indicate that the ruling extends to whoever shared with them in this. The purpose of the verse is the forbidding of the addressees from being pleased with them and from being deceived by their false excuses, in the most emphatic and forceful manner, since being pleased with one whom Allah, the Exalted, is not pleased with is something that hardly issues from a believer. It has also been said that this was said lest someone suppose that the pleasure of the believers is among the motives for the pleasure of Allah, the Exalted. It is said that they were Jadd ibn Qays, Mu'tib ibn Qushayr, and their companions, and they were eighty hypocrites. So the Prophet ﷺ said to the believers when he arrived in Madinah: "Do not sit with them or speak with them." It has also been said that Abdullah ibn Ubayy came swearing that he would never stay behind him ever.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 97:

"The Bedouins (al-A'rab) are a plural form, but not a plural of 'Arab' (Arabs), as stated by Sibawayh (the early grammarian), so that it would not follow that the plural is more specific than the singular. For 'Arab' refers to this particular people, whether they dwell in the desert (al-badawi) or in towns (al-qura). As for al-A'rab, it is applied only to those who dwell in the desert. For this reason, the relative adjective is formed from the form of the word itself, so it is said: a'rabi (Bedouin). The lexicographers said: a man is 'arabi (Arab), and its plural is al-Arab, just as one says majusi (Magian) and yahudi (Jew), and then the ya' of relation is dropped in the plural, so one says: al-Majus and al-Yahud. And a man is a'rabi, and it is pluralized as al-A'rab and al-A'arib, that is, the people of the desert. ﴿They are more intense in disbelief and hypocrisy﴾ than the people of the settled areas, because of their harshness, the hardness of their hearts, their wildness, and their growing up in isolation from seeing the scholars and conversing with them. This is from the figure of describing a whole category by a characteristic of some of its members, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And man is ever ungrateful﴾, since not all of them are as described, as you will know in detail. ﴿And more likely not to know﴾, i.e., more entitled and more fitting not to know ﴿the limits of what Allah has sent down to His Messenger﴾, because of their distance from his gathering (ﷺ) and their deprivation of witnessing his miracles and observing what descends upon him of the laws within the contents of the Book and the Sunnah. ﴿And Allah is All-Knowing﴾ of the conditions of each of the people of the camel-hair tents and of the settled dwellings, ﴿All-Wise﴾ in what He inflicts upon their evildoers and their good-doers of punishment and reward."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 98:

﴿And among the Bedouins﴾ begins an explanation that the Bedouin category divides into two groups, and that they are not confined to the group previously mentioned, as is apparent from the noble wording, and an explanation of some of the blameworthy traits of these people, which branch off from disbelief and hypocrisy, after an account of their persistence in both. Restricting "the Bedouins" to the aforementioned group alone is possible, even though it is supported by the fact that those whose condition is described are some of them, namely those who are intent on spending from among the hypocrites rather than their poor, or the Bedouins of Asad, Ghatafan and Tamim, as has been said. But this is not supported by what follows in the words of the Exalted: ﴿And among the Bedouins are those who believe﴾ ... etc., for those are certainly not among these, but rather they are of the category, i.e., and of the category of Bedouins, which was described by the description of some of its individuals: ﴿those who take what they spend﴾ of wealth, i.e., they regard what they expend in the way of Allah and give in charity, in appearance only, ﴿as a loss﴾, i.e., a penalty and a necessary deprivation; for they do not spend it seeking reward and hoping for the reward of Allah the Exalted so that it may be a gain for them, but they spend it out of showing off and dissimulation, so it is pure loss. What the form of "taking" implies of choosing and benefiting from what is taken is only with regard to the spender's aim of showing off and dissimulation, not with regard to the expenditure itself, meaning its being a loss.

﴿And they await misfortunes for you﴾. The origin of "dā'irah" (circle, turn of fortune) is that which encompasses a thing, and what is meant by it is the inescapable calamities of time, i.e., they wait for the turns, vicissitudes and reversals of fortune to befall you, so that your victory over them may vanish and they may be freed from what they are afflicted with. ﴿Upon them is the evil turn of fortune﴾: He prayed against them with the like of what they wished for the believers, by way of retort, as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿Their hands are chained﴾ after the Jews' statement of what they said. "Su'" (evil) is originally a verbal noun, then it was applied to every harm and evil, and "dā'irah" was attributed to it as a form of censure, just as one says "a bad man" (rajul su'), because whoever is struck by it blames it. It is from the type of attributing the qualified to its qualifier: it was originally described by the verbal noun for emphasis, then it was attributed to its own attribute, as in the words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Your father was not a man of evil﴾. It has also been said: the meaning of "dā'irah" implies the meaning of "evil", so the construction is one of explanation and emphasis, as they say "the sun of the day" and "the beard of his head". It has also been read with a dammah (ḍamm, i.e., "al-sawʾ" pronounced "sūʾ"), and it means punishment, just as it is called "sayyi'ah" (evil).

﴿And Allah is All-Hearing﴾ of what they say during expenditure that contains no good, ﴿All-Knowing﴾ of what they conceal of corrupt matters, among which is that they await misfortunes for you. In this there is a severity of warning that is not hidden.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 99:

﴿And among the Bedouin﴾ means: of their kind in general, ﴿those who believe in Allah and the Last Day and take﴾ means: take for themselves, by way of selection and storing up, ﴿what they spend﴾ means: what they spend in the way of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿as means of nearness﴾ means: as means (dharā'i', sing. dharī'a, "avenues or means") leading to it. To signify the complete closeness between the two, the spending is treated as if it were the very nearness itself. The plural is in view of the kinds of nearness or their individual instances. It is the second object of "yattakhidh" (takes). The words of the Exalted, ﴿with Allah﴾, are either a description of it or an adverbial complement of "yattakhidh" (takes). ﴿And the prayers of the Messenger﴾ means: as means leading to them, for he (ﷺ) used to invoke blessing and goodness upon those who gave charity and would ask forgiveness for them. For this reason it is recommended that the one who receives the charity invoke blessing upon the giver when taking his charity, but it is not for him to say "prayers" (ṣalāh) upon him as the Messenger (ﷺ) did when he said: ""O Allah, send prayers upon the family of Abu Awfa."" That is his station, so he may bestow it upon whomever he wills. The mention of the attribute of belief in Allah and the Last Day regarding the latter group, although the context is to show the difference between the two groups regarding the matter of taking what they spend, both in state and outcome, and the mention of their taking it as a means to nearness and prayers suffices from explicitly stating that, is for the utmost concern with their faith, showing their being characterized by it, and increasing the care in establishing the distinction between the two groups from the outset. As for the first group, their being characterized by disbelief and hypocrisy is evident explicitly from the context of the noble arrangement.

﴿Unquestionably, it is a nearness for them﴾: a testimony to them from the side of Allah, the Exalted, of the soundness of what they believed and a confirmation of their hope. The pronoun refers to what is spent, and the feminine form is in view of the predicate, along with what has passed of its multiplicity in one of the two ways. The indefiniteness is for magnification, which dispenses with the plural, meaning: a great nearness whose reality cannot be fathomed. In presenting the sentence as nominal and introducing it with the two particles of alerting and affirmation, there is an eloquence that is not hidden. Restricting it to stating that it is a nearness for them is because that is the ultimate goal, and the prayers of the Messenger are among its means.

And the words of the Exalted, ﴿Allah will admit them into His mercy﴾: a promise to them of the encompassing of His vast mercy upon them, and an explanation of the nearness. Just as the words of the Mighty and Exalted, ﴿(And Allah is Hearing, Knowing)﴾, are a warning to the first group following the invocation against them. The "sīn" (sa-) indicates the certainty and absolute establishment of that.

And the words of the Exalted, ﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾: a reason for the certainty of the promise, in the manner of a confirmatory resumption. It has been said: this was about ʿAbd Allah dhu al-Bijadayn and his people. It has been said: about the Banu Muqarrin of Muzayna. It has been said: about Aslam, Ghifar and Juhayna.

And Abu Hurayra (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: ""Aslam and Ghifar, and some of Juhayna and Muzayna, are better with Allah on the Day of Resurrection than Tamim, and Asad ibn Khuzayma, and Hawazin, and Ghatafan.""

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 100:**

﴿And the foremost, the first of the Emigrants﴾ is an explanation of the virtues of the noble among the Muslims, following the explanation of the excellence of a group among them. What is meant by them are: those who prayed towards the two qiblas (*al-Qiblatayn*, the two directions of prayer), or those who witnessed Badr, or those who embraced Islam before the Hijra (emigration to Medina). ﴿And the Helpers﴾ are the people of the First Pledge of 'Aqaba (*Bay'at al-'Aqaba*, the pledges made at the 'Aqaba valley near Mecca), who were seven men, and the people of the Second Pledge of 'Aqaba, who were seventy men. And those who believed when Abu Zurara Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr came to them. It was also read in the nominative (*bi-l-raf'*), as a conjunction with "*al-sabiqun*" (the foremost).

﴿And those who followed them in goodness﴾ means: accompanied by it. What is meant by it is every good quality. They are those who came after the foremost of the two groups, with "*min*" being partitive (*tab'idiyya*), or they are those who followed them in faith and obedience until the Day of Resurrection, in which case what is meant by "*al-sabiqin*" (the foremost) is all the Emigrants and the Helpers, and "*min*" is explanatory (*bayaniyya*). ﴿May Allah be pleased with them﴾ is the predicate (*khabar*) of the subject (*mubtada'*): meaning, Allah is pleased with them by accepting their obedience and approving their deeds. ﴿And they are pleased with Him﴾ through what they attained of His pleasure, which entails all desires in their entirety. ﴿And He has prepared for them﴾ in the Hereafter ﴿gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾. It was also read as "*min tahtiha*" (from beneath them), as in all other occurrences. ﴿Abiding therein forever﴾ without end. ﴿That is the great triumph﴾, beyond which there is no triumph. The sense of distance in the demonstrative pronoun serves to show how far their station is in the ranks of excellence and how great their degree is above the believers among the Bedouin Arabs.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 101:

﴿And among those around you of the Bedouins﴾ This begins the explanation of the condition of the hypocrites of Medina and of those of the Bedouins around it, after the explanation of the condition of the desert-dwelling Bedouins among them; that is: among those around your town ﴿are hypocrites﴾, namely Juhayna, Muzayna, Aslam, Ashja', and Ghifar, who were settled around it. ﴿And among the people of Medina﴾ is conjoined to (among those around you) by a conjunction of a single noun to a single noun.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They have persisted in hypocrisy﴾ may be either a resumptive sentence with no place in terms of i'rab (grammatical position), brought to explain their excess in hypocrisy after explaining that they are characterized by it; or it may be an attribute of the mentioned subject, separated from it by what is conjoined to its predicate; or it may be an attribute of an omitted noun that it has taken the place of, which is a subject whose predicate is "from the people of Medina," as in the saying of the poet:

"I am the son of Jala and the climber of the mountain passes."

The sentence is conjoined to the preceding sentence; that is: and among the people of Medina are a people who have persisted in hypocrisy, meaning: they have become skilled in it, from (marana) so-and-so at his work and (marada) at it when he is accustomed to it and inured to it until it becomes easy for him, and (mahara) in it. However, (marada) is hardly used except for evil. So the persistence in the first two meanings is common to both groups according to the commonality of hypocrisy, and in the last meaning it is specific to the hypocrites of the people of Medina, and this is the more apparent and more fitting, given the mention of the hypocrites of the desert-dwellers first, then the mention of the hypocrites of the Bedouins neighboring Medina, then the mention of the hypocrites of its people. And Allah, exalted is He, knows best.

His saying, exalted is His dignity: ﴿You do not know them﴾ is an explanation of their persistence, that is: you do not know them, but not by their persons, names, and lineages, rather by the mark of their hypocrisy. That is to say, they have reached such a degree of skill in hypocrisy and of refinement in observing dissimulation (taqiyya) and in keeping away from places of suspicion that their condition is hidden from you, despite your high standing and lofty rank in perfect intelligence and true insight. The negation of knowledge concerning them, although it is related to their condition, is an exaggeration in this regard and an allusion to the fact that what they are in of the attribute of hypocrisy, because of its deep-rootedness and firm establishment in them, has become like their essential qualities or their individual characteristics, such that whoever does not know them by that attribute is not considered one who knows them. Interpreting his (ﷺ) lack of knowledge of their persons as his (ﷺ) lack of knowledge after the coming of this explanation, on the basis that he (ﷺ) knows that among them are hypocrites but does not know them by their persons, is contrary to the apparent meaning and is devoid of the exaggeration mentioned.

His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿We know them﴾ is a confirmation of what preceded regarding their skill in the art of hypocrisy; that is, none who is not hidden from anything can have access to their secrets fixed in their hearts, because of their intense concern with concealing unbelief and displaying sincerity. The attribution of knowledge to them, although the intended purpose is to explain its relation to their condition, is as explained in the attribution of its negation to them.

His saying, exalted is His dignity: ﴿We will punish them﴾ is a threat against them and a certainty of their punishment in accordance with what Allah knows of its causes concerning them; and the (sin) is for emphasis. ﴿Twice﴾: from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the Prophet (ﷺ) stood to deliver a sermon on Friday and said: "Go out, so-and-so, for you are a hypocrite; go out, so-and-so, for you are a hypocrite," so he expelled some people and exposed them. This is the first punishment. The second is either killing, or the punishment of the grave. Or the first is killing and the second is the punishment of the grave. Or the first is the taking of zakat, since they regard it as sheer penalty, and the second is the wearing down of bodies and their exhaustion through acts of worship empty of reward. Perhaps the repetition of their punishment is due to the unbelief they carry accompanied by hypocrisy, or to hypocrisy emphasized by persistence in it. It is also permissible that the intended meaning of "twice" is merely multiplicity, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then return your gaze twice﴾, that is, one time after another.

﴿Then they will be returned﴾ on the Day of Resurrection ﴿to a great punishment﴾, which is the punishment of the Fire. In the change of construction, by attributing their earlier punishment to the plural of majesty (nun al-'azama), in accordance with the attribution of the knowledge preceding it, and attributing their return to the later punishment to themselves, there is an indication of the difference between the two in condition: the first is specific to them in occurrence and time, and is undertaken by Him, glorified and exalted is He; the second is general to the generality of disbelievers in occurrence and time, even though the levels of their punishment differ.

﴿And others﴾ is a clarification of the state of a group of Muslims whose resolve in matters of religion was weak. It is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to ﴿hypocrites﴾, meaning: "And among those around you and the people of Madinah are others ﴿who have acknowledged their sins﴾", that is, those who have admitted their failure to join the expedition and their preference for ease over it, and their acceptance of bad company with the hypocrites. They regretted this and did not offer false excuses, nor did they conceal the bad deeds they had committed, unlike the hypocrites, who habitually conceal what is in them and display what contradicts it. The hypocrites offered worthless excuses, reinforced with false oaths, in keeping with their familiar custom.

They were a group of those who had stayed behind, and they tied themselves to the pillars of the mosque when they learned what had been revealed concerning those who stayed behind. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came, entered the mosque, prayed two rak'ahs in accordance with his noble custom, and saw them in that state. He asked about their situation, and it was said: "They have sworn that they will not release themselves until you release them." He (ﷺ) said: "««And I swear that I will not release them until I am commanded concerning them»», " and then it was revealed.

﴿They mixed a righteous deed﴾: this refers to the righteous deeds they had done earlier, such as their going out to previous campaigns and others, and what followed of (p-99) their acknowledgment of their sins in staying behind this time, their self-reproach and their regret over it. Specifying it with "acknowledgment" does not suit "mixing", especially in a form that indicates the two mixed things flow into one another and each is both mixed and mixed with the other. This is also indicated by the substitution of the particle الواو (wāw, "and") with الباء (bāʾ, "with") in His words, ﴿and another bad﴾. For your saying "I mixed the water with the milk" requires that the water be poured onto the milk, not the reverse, whereas your saying "I mixed the water and the milk" means that mixing took place between them without indicating that one of them is specifically the thing mixed with the other. Omitting that indication serves to show that each of them is characterized by both attributes together. In this context, that means each of the two deeds falls upon the other, time after time. "Bad deed" here means the bad deeds they committed, both at the beginning and at the end. It is reported from al-Kalbī that the righteous deed is repentance and the bad deed is sin. It has also been said that الواو here carries the meaning of الباء, as in the idiom "I sold the sheep for a sheep and a dirham," meaning "a sheep for a dirham."

﴿It may be that Allah will relent toward them﴾, that is, accept their repentance, which is understood from their acknowledgment of their sins. ﴿Indeed Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful﴾: He overlooks the bad deeds of the one who repents and bestows His favour upon him. This is the reason for what the word (عسى, "it may be") implies regarding the obligation of acceptance. For it expresses hope, and hope from the Most Generous of the generous is an obligation, and what an obligation it is.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 103:**

﴿Take from their wealth a charity﴾. It is related that when they were released, they said: "O Messenger of Allah, these are our possessions that kept us back from you, so give charity from them and purify us." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I have not been commanded to take anything from your possessions." Then this was revealed.

This is not the obligatory charity (zakat), because he was commanded to take it. It is also related that he (ﷺ) took a third from them and left them two-thirds, so this served as an explanation of the generality (ijmal, a general or unspecified expression) in "charity" (ṣadaqatan). Rather, it is an expiation for their sins, as indicated by the words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿to purify them﴾, that is, from what they had soiled themselves with of the filth of staying behind. The "ta'" is for address, and the verb is in the jussive mood, since it is a response to the imperative. It has also been read in the nominative (marfu'), in which case it is a circumstantial clause (ḥal) from the pronoun of the addressee in "take," or an attribute (ṣifah) of "charity," with the "ta'" being for address, or for the charity. The returning pronoun in the first case is omitted, relying on what follows it. It has also been read as "tuṭhirahum," from "aṭharahu," with the same meaning as "ṭahharahu."

﴿and purify them thereby﴾, with the "ya'" affirmed. It is the predicate of an omitted subject, and the clause is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in the imperative or in its response, meaning: "while you purify them thereby," that is, you cause their good deeds to grow through that charity to the ranks of the sincere, or their wealth grows, or you go to great lengths in purifying them. This is according to the jussive reading of "tuṭahhirhum." As for the nominative reading, whether the "ta'" is for address or for the charity, and likewise if the first clause is made a circumstantial clause from the pronoun of the addressee, or an attribute of the charity in both cases, the second is conjoined to the first, as a circumstantial clause or an attribute, without any need to posit an omitted subject, in order to account for the entry of the "waw" into the circumstantial clause.

﴿And pray for them﴾, that is, bestow your kindness upon them through supplication and asking forgiveness for them. ﴿Indeed your prayer﴾ (it has also been read as "ṣalawatika," in the plural, in consideration of the multiplicity of those prayed for) ﴿is a comfort for them﴾, through which their souls find rest, their hearts are reassured, and they are confident that He, glory be to Him, has accepted their repentance. The clause is a justification for the command to pray for them. ﴿And Allah is All-Hearing﴾, who hears what proceeds from them of confession of sin, repentance, and supplication, ﴿All-Knowing﴾ of what is in their hearts of regret and grief over what they neglected, and of sincerity in repentance and supplication. Or: All-Hearing, who answers your supplication for them, All-Knowing of what wisdom requires. In that case the clause is a concluding remark (tadhyil) to the justification, confirming its content. And according to the first, it is a concluding remark to the two preceding verses, confirming what is in them.(p-100)

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 104:

﴿Did they not know﴾. It is also read with the taa' (tā', "do they not know" addressed to the second person). The pronoun is either referring to those who repented, in which case it confirms what preceded concerning the acceptance of their repentance, the purification of the charity, and its being a means of purifying and cleansing them (tazkiyah), and it establishes that and settles their hearts by declaring that the one who takes charge of accepting their repentance and receiving their charities is God, glorified is He, even though the taking, the purifying and the cleansing were attributed to him ﷺ. That is: did those penitents not know ﴿that it is God who accepts repentance﴾ that is sincere and pure, ﴿from His servants﴾ who are sincere in it, and who overlooks their misdeeds, as the word "from" (ʿan) makes clear. By "His servants" is meant either those penitents, and placing the apparent noun in the place of the pronoun indicates that worship is the cause of its acceptance; or all the servants, and they are included in this primarily.

﴿And takes the charities﴾: that is, He accepts their charities, on the basis that the lām (definite article) is a substitute for the genitive (i.e., "their charities" is replaced by "the charities"), or that the genus of charities, under which their charities fall primarily, is intended. That is: He is the one who takes charge of accepting repentance and taking charities and what is connected with them of purification and cleansing, even though you are the one who directly handles them outwardly. In this there is, by way of establishing what has been mentioned and raising the status of the Prophet ﷺ, following the pattern of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who pledge allegiance to you, they are only pledging allegiance to God﴾, what is not hidden.

﴿And that God is the Relenting, the Merciful﴾: this is an emphasis on what it is conjoined to, and an increase in establishing what it establishes, with an added meaning not present in it. That is: did they not know that He is the one exclusively singled out for attaining the utmost limit of accepting repentance and mercy, and that this is a continuous practice of His and a constant matter? The two clauses are in the accusative position governed by "they know", each of them standing in place of its two objects.

As for the second interpretation, that it refers to the believers other than the penitents: it has been narrated that when the first group was forgiven, they said: "Those who repented, were they not with us yesterday, not spoken to and not sat with? What is their state?" Then this was revealed.

That is: did they not know the qualities of the penitents that call for honour, drawing near, joining the ranks of the believers, and being received with good acceptance and companionship? This is an encouragement for them to repent and give charity.

And His saying, exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 105:

﴿And say: "Work"﴾. This is an addition that encourages them to do righteous deeds, of which repentance is a part, and it is also for the earlier ones (the believers who had already repented), to keep them steadfast in what they are upon. That is, say to them, after the matter of repentance has become clear to them: "Do whatever deeds you wish." Its outward meaning is permission and choice, while its inner meaning is encouragement and warning. His saying, mighty and majestic is He, ﴿Then Allah will see your deeds﴾, that is, whether good or bad, is a reason for what precedes it and an emphasis on the encouragement and the warning. The particle "sa" (sin) is for emphasis. ﴿And His Messenger﴾ is coordinated with the Exalted Name, and its being placed after the object is to indicate the difference between the two seeings. ﴿And the believers﴾. In the report: «If a man worked inside a rock that has no door and no window, his deed would come out to the people, whatever it might be.» The meaning is that your deeds are not hidden from them, as you have seen and as has become clear to you. Then, if the intended meaning of "seeing" is its literal sense, the matter is evident. If it is intended to mean its consequence in terms of reward, good or bad, then it is specific to the worldly, such as the manifestation of praise, commendation, good remembrance, honor, and similar rewards and their opposites.

﴿And you will be returned﴾, that is, after death, ﴿to the Knower of the unseen and the seen﴾. The placing of the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun is for magnifying the matter and cultivating awe, which is not hidden. The reason for mentioning the unseen first, over the seen, due to the vastness of its realm and the greater weight it carries over the seen, needs no explanation. It was said: the existents that are absent from the senses are causes, or like causes, for the sensible existents, and knowledge of causes is a cause for knowledge of effects, so knowledge of the unseen must precede knowledge of the seen.

And from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "The unseen is what they conceal of deeds, and the seen is what they manifest," as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He knows what they conceal and what they disclose﴾. The priority in this case is to establish that the relation of His all-encompassing knowledge to the secret and the public is one and the same, in the most eloquent and emphatic manner, and not to suggest that His knowledge, glorified is He, of what they conceal is prior to His knowledge of what they disclose. How could it be otherwise, since His knowledge, glorified is He, of His objects of knowledge is exalted above being by way of the acquisition of an image; rather, the existence of each thing and its realization in itself is knowledge in relation to Him, exalted is He. In this sense, the situation does not differ between what is manifest and what is latent. Or it is to signal that the rank of the secret precedes the rank of the public, since nothing is made public except that it is, or its near or distant beginnings are, concealed in the heart beforehand. Thus the attachment of His knowledge, exalted is He, to it in its first state precedes its attachment to it in its second state.

﴿Then He will inform you﴾ following the return, which is an expression for the matter extending to the Day of Resurgence, ﴿of what you used to do﴾ before that in the worldly life. What is meant by the informing about that is the recompense according to it: if good, then good; if bad, then bad. Thus it is a promise and a warning.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 106:**

﴿And others﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with the previous "others," meaning: and among those who stayed behind from the people of Medina and those around it from the Bedouins are other people, not the confessing ones mentioned, ﴿deferred﴾. It is also read as (مُرْجَئُونَ), from arjaytuhu and arjaʾtuhu, meaning: I delayed it. From this comes the Murji'a (a theological school whose adherents do not affirm with certainty that repentance will be accepted). ﴿Until God's command﴾ concerning their matter. Ibn ʿAbbas (may God be pleased with both of them) said: they were Kaʿb ibn Malik, Murara ibn al-Rabiʿ, and Hilal ibn Umayya, who did not hasten to repentance and apology as Abu Lubaba and his companions did, by binding themselves to the pillars, and by showing grief, distress and regret over what they had done. So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) detained them and forbade his companions from greeting them and speaking to them. They were among the people of Badr, yet they were shunned. People differed about their matter: some said, "They are ruined," and others said, "Perhaps God will forgive them." Thus they were, in their view, ﻿deferred to God's command, most high. ﴿Either He will punish them﴾ if they remain in the state they are in, and it was said: if they persist in hypocrisy, but this is not so, for those mentioned are not among the hypocrites. ﴿Or He will relent toward them﴾ if their intention becomes sincere and their repentance is valid. The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: of them, these are either punished or pardoned. It was also said: ﴿others﴾ is a subject (mubtadaʾ), ﴿deferred﴾ is its adjective (ṣifa), and this clause is its predicate (khabar). ﴿And God is All-Knowing﴾ of their conditions, ﴿All-Wise﴾ in what He does to them of deferment and what follows it. It is also read (وَاللَّهُ غَفُورٌ رَحِيمٌ), meaning: ﴿and God is Most Forgiving, Most Merciful﴾.

﴿وَالَّذِينَ اتَّخَذُوا مَسْجِدًا﴾ is coordinated (*'atf*, conjunction) with what precedes it, meaning "and among them are those who...". Alternatively, it is in the accusative (*nasb*) by way of censure (*dhamm*). It was also read without the conjunction *wa*, since it is then a separate account standing on its own.

﴿ضِرارًا﴾ means "for the purpose of harming the believers." It is in the accusative in one of several ways: as an object of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*); as a second object of "*ittakhadhu*" ("they took"); as an emphatic verbal noun (*masdar mu'akkid*) for an implied verb in the circumstantial accusative (*hal*), meaning "they harm by this, a harming"; or as a verbal noun used in the sense of an active participle (*bi-ma'na al-fa'il*) functioning as a circumstantial accusative from the pronoun in "*ittakhadhu*", meaning "harming the believers."

It is reported that the clan of Bani 'Amr ibn 'Awf, when they built the Mosque of Quba, sent to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ asking him to come to them and lead them in prayer in their mosque. When he did so, their brothers, the Bani Ghanm ibn 'Awf, envied them and said: "We will build a mosque and send to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ so that he may pray in it." Abu 'Amir the monk would also pray in it when he came from Syria. He is the one whom the Messenger of Allah ﷺ named "the Corrupt" (*al-Fasiq*). He had said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ on the day of Uhud: "I do not find a people who fight you except that I will fight you alongside them." He continued doing this until the day of Hunayn. When Hawazin were defeated that day, he fled to Syria and sent to the hypocrites: "Prepare whatever strength and weaponry you can, for I am going to Caesar and will come back with troops, and I will expel Muhammad and his companions from Madinah." So they built a mosque beside the Mosque of Quba, and they said to the Prophet ﷺ: "We have built a mosque for the one who is ill, the one in need, the night that is rainy, and the winter. We would love for you to pray in it for us and to invoke blessing for us." He ﷺ said: "I am on the verge of a journey and occupied with affairs; when we return, if Allah the Exalted wills, we will pray in it." When he ﷺ returned from the expedition of Tabuk, they asked him to come to the mosque, and so this verse was revealed to him. He then summoned Malik ibn al-Dukhshum, Ma'n ibn 'Adi, 'Amir ibn al-Sakan, and Wahshi, and said to them: "Go to this mosque whose people are wrongdoers, and demolish it and burn it." They did so, and he ordered that its site be made into a dunghill where carrion and refuse would be thrown. Abu 'Amir the Corrupt died in Syria, at Qinnasrin.

﴿وَكُفْرًا﴾ means: strengthening the disbelief they were concealing.

﴿وَتَفْرِيقًا بَيْنَ المُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ means: dividing the believers, who used to gather together to pray at the Mosque of Quba, so that it overflowed with them. They therefore wanted them to scatter, so that their word would be divided.

﴿وَإرْصادًا﴾ means: preparing, waiting, and watching for ﴿لِمَن حارَبَ اللَّهَ ورَسُولَهُ﴾, namely the corrupt monk, that is, for his sake, until he comes and prays in it and gains dominance over the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

﴿مِن قَبْلُ﴾ is connected to "*ittakhadhu*" ("they took"), meaning: they took it before they became hypocrites by staying behind, since they had built it before the expedition of Tabuk. Alternatively, it is connected to "*harab*" ("fought"), meaning: he fought both of them (Allah and His Messenger) before the taking of this mosque.

﴿وَلَيَحْلِفُنَّ إنْ أرَدْنا﴾ means: "We did not intend by building this mosque except ﴿إلا الحُسْنى﴾", that is, except the good quality, which is prayer, the remembrance of Allah, and providing space for those who pray; or, except the good intention.

﴿واللَّهُ يَشْهَدُ إنَّهم لَكاذِبُونَ﴾ means: in their oath that they swear.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 108:

﴿Do not stand﴾ for prayer ﴿in it﴾, in that mosque, in the manner they invited you to, ﴿ever. A mosque founded﴾, i.e., whose foundation was built, ﴿upon piety﴾. It means the mosque of Quba', which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) founded and in which he prayed during the days he stayed at Quba'. These days were Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday, and he left on Friday. It has also been said that it is the mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in Medina.

And on the authority of Abu Sa'id (may Allah be pleased with him): I asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about the mosque founded upon piety. He took a pebble, struck it on the ground, and said: "Your mosque here is the mosque of Medina." The lam (in the phrase ﴿لَمَسْجِدٌ﴾) is either the lam of initiation (lam al-ibtida', an emphatic particle) or the lam of an omitted oath (qasam mahdhuf), i.e., "By Allah, it is a mosque." On both readings, ﴿mosque﴾ (masjidun) is the mubtada' (grammatical subject), and what follows it is its ṣifah (descriptive attribute). The words ﴿from the first day﴾ mean from the days of its founding, and they are connected to ﴿founded﴾ (ussisa). The words ﴿more deserving that you stand in it﴾, i.e., for prayer and the remembrance of Allah the Exalted, are its khabar (predicate). The words ﴿in it are men﴾ form a new independent clause explaining his worthiness, since he (ﷺ) stood in it; it is a ḥāl (circumstantial clause) from the standpoint of the state, after the explanation of his worthiness with respect to the place. Alternatively, it is another ṣifah of the subject, or a ḥāl from the pronoun in ﴿in it﴾. In every case, it asserts and confirms that the mosque deserves that he stand in it. The meaning of it being "more deserving" is that it is truly deserving of him, since there is no deservingness at all in the Mosque of Harm (masjid al-Ḍirār). It is expressed with the comparative form (ṣīghat al-tafḍīl) because of its excellence and perfection in itself; or the preference is in the deservingness, covering what is so by the builders' claim and by those who share their belief, and this latter is the more fitting reading in view of what will come later.

﴿They love to purify themselves﴾ from sins and blameworthy traits, seeking the pleasure of Allah the Glorified. It has also been said: from major impurity (janabah), so that they do not sleep in that state. ﴿And Allah loves those who purify themselves﴾, i.e., He is pleased with them and draws them near to His presence, as a lover draws near to his beloved.

It has been said: when this verse was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) walked, and the Muhajirun were with him, until he stood at the door of the mosque of Quba'. There the Ansar were sitting. He said: "Are you believers?" The people were silent. He repeated it, and 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "O Messenger of Allah, they are indeed believers, and I am with them." He (ﷺ) said: "Are you content with the decree?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Will you be patient in affliction?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Will you be thankful in ease?" They said: "Yes." He (ﷺ) said: "Believers, by the Lord of the Ka'bah!" Then he sat down, and said: "O assembly of the Ansar, Allah the Mighty and Majestic has praised you. What do you do at wudu' and when relieving yourselves?" They said: "We follow the excrement with the three stones, then we follow the stones with water." The Prophet (ﷺ) then recited: ﴿In it are men who love to purify themselves﴾. It is also read as (an yaṭṭahharū) with idgham (assimilation of the two identical letters). It has been said that the verse is general, covering purification from all impurities, and they used to follow the urine's trace with water.

And on the authority of al-Hasan (may Allah be pleased with him): it is purification from sins through repentance. It has also been said: they love to purify themselves through the expiating fever that removes their sins, so they all came down with fever.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 109:

﴿Is one who founded his building﴾ is read in the active form with the accusative (ﷺ, no: the verb is in the active voice with a nasb/accusative object). It is also read in the passive voice with the nominative. It is read as (ʾusus bunyānihi) in the construct form, the plural of asās. Asās, with fatḥa or kasra, is the plural of ussun. It is also read as (asāsu bunyānihi), the plural of ussun, and as (ussu bunyānihi). This is a resumptive sentence (jumla mustaʾnafa) that explains the superiority of the men mentioned from among the people of the mosque of harm (masjid al-ḍirār). The hamza is for denial (al-inkār), and the fāʾ is for coordination (al-ʿaṭf) upon an implied element. The meaning is: after he knew their condition, is one who founded the building of his religion ﴿upon piety from God and good pleasure﴾, that is, upon a firm foundation, which is piety from God and seeking His pleasure through obedience. By piety is meant its second degree, which is guarding oneself against everything that makes one sinful, whether by an act or an omission. It is also read as (taqwan) with tanwīn, the alif being for the extension (al-ilḥāq) and not for the feminine. ﴿Is it better, or one who founded his building﴾: leaving out the pronoun is to signal that the two buildings differ in essence, and also differ in description and attribution. ﴿upon the brink of a crumbling precipice﴾. Al-shafā is the edge and the rim. Al-jurf is what the torrent has carried away, that is, it has uprooted it and dug out what is beneath it, so that it remains weak and tends to collapse. Al-hār is the one that is ready to fall, split and inclined to collapse, from hāra yahūru and yahāru, or hāra yahīru, whose lām was moved before its ʿayn, so it became like ghāz and rām. It is also said that its ʿayn was deleted irregularly (iʿtibāṭan), that is, without a cause, so the aspects of inflection (wujūh al-iʿrāb) applied to its lām.

﴿So it collapsed with him into the fire of Hell﴾: what they built the matter of their religion upon is likened to this in its falsity and the speed of its being wiped out, by what has been mentioned. Then it is developed further (rushshiḥa) by its collapse into the fire, and it is placed in opposition to good pleasure, as an alert that founding that upon something which protects one from the fire and leads one to good pleasure and its requirements, the least of which is Paradise, is different from founding this upon what is about to fall into the fire moment by moment, and then their final destination is there without doubt. It is also read as (jurfin) with a sukūn on the rāʾ.

﴿And God does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾: that is, to their own harm, or those who place things in other than their proper places. (p-104) That is, He does not guide them to what contains their salvation and their welfare with a guidance that necessarily entails it. As for indicating to them what guides them, if they seek guidance by it, that is established without any doubt.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 110:**

﴿Their building which they built will never cease to be a source of doubt in their hearts﴾. Al-bunyan is a verbal noun (masdar) used in the sense of the passive participle (maf'ul), and its qualification by the relative pronoun "alladhi" (which), whose clause is its verb "built," serves to indicate the manner of their building it and its foundation upon the weakest base and the feeblest foundation, and to indicate the cause of the ruling. That is: their mosque will not cease to be built and demolished.

﴿A source of doubt in their hearts﴾: that is, a cause of doubt and suspicion regarding the religion, as if it were itself the doubt. As for the situation of its building, it is evident, because their withdrawal from the believers and their gathering in a separate assembly, in which they manifest what is in their hearts of the traces of unbelief and hypocrisy, and in which they plan their affairs and consult about them, and some of them convey to others what they have heard of the secrets of the believers, increases them in doubt and suspicion regarding the religion. As for the situation of its demolition, it is because what was in their hearts of evil became firmly established by it, and its effects and rulings multiplied; or it caused doubt regarding their affair, since their hearts became weakened, namely their belief that their affair was hidden from the believers, because after the building they manifested more of their affair than they had been manifesting before that, at the time of their mixing with the believers, and their opinions of themselves became evil. So when their building was demolished, that weakness increased and grew stronger, and they became doubtful as to whether the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would leave them in the state they had been in before, or would order their killing and the plundering of their wealth. Al-Kalbi said: the meaning of "rayba" (doubt) is grief and remorse. Al-Suddi, Habib, and al-Mubarrad said: the demolition of their building remains a sore and rage in their hearts.

﴿Unless their hearts are cut to pieces﴾: it is from the tafa''ul form with the deletion of one of the two taa's, that is: unless they are cut to pieces (tataqatta'a) ﴿their hearts﴾ into pieces and divided into parts such that they no longer retain any capacity for perception. The supplying of "qita'an" (in pieces) is an exception from the most general of times or the most general of states, and its position is accusative as an adverbial of time. That is: their building will remain a source of doubt at all times or in every state, except at the time their hearts are cut to pieces, or in the state of their hearts being cut to pieces; then they will be relieved of it. As long as their hearts are intact, the doubt remains within them. This is a depiction of the impossibility of the removal of doubt from their hearts. It is also permissible that the intended meaning is the literal cutting of them at the time of their killing, or in the graves, or in the Fire. It was read as "tuqatta'" in the passive form of the tafil form, and in the active form of it addressing the Prophet ﷺ, that is: unless you (yourself) cut their hearts by killing. It was also read in the passive of the triliteral, masculine and feminine, and read "ila an tuqatti'a qulubahum" and "ila an tuqatta'a qulubuhum" in the second person; and read "wa law qutti'at qulubuhum" with the verb in the passive attributed to their hearts, and "wa law qatta'ta qulubahum" in the second person addressed to the Messenger ﷺ or to everyone fit to be addressed. It has also been said: unless they repent a repentance by which their hearts are cut to pieces with regret and sorrow over their negligence.

﴿And Allah is All-Knowing﴾ of all things, of which what has been mentioned of their states is part ﴿All-Wise﴾ in all His acts, of which His command concerning them is part.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 111:

﴿Indeed, Allah has purchased from the believers their lives and their properties﴾ is an exhortation for the believers to engage in jihad (struggle in the way of Allah), by explaining its excellence right after describing the state of those who stayed behind from it. This is stressed in a manner that cannot be exceeded, in that Allah's acceptance from the believers of their lives and their properties, which they expended in His way, and His rewarding them by setting Paradise against them as the price, is expressed through the purchase, by way of the subsidiary metaphor (al-isti'arah al-tab'iyyah). Then the thing sold, which is the principal and the aim of the contract, is made to be the believers' lives and properties, while the price, which is the means in the transaction, is Paradise. The matter was not reversed by saying: "Allah has sold Paradise to the believers in exchange for their lives and their properties," in order to indicate that the aim of the contract is Paradise, and that what the believers expended against it of lives and properties is a means to it, signalling the complete care bestowed upon them and upon their properties. Then He did not say "for Paradise," but rather it was said: ﴿that for them is Paradise﴾, emphasizing the establishing of the price's reaching them and its being specific to them, as if it were said: "for Paradise, which is established for them and specific to them."

As for what is said, that this is in praise of the believers, in that they expended their lives and properties merely upon the promise, due to their complete trust in His promise, and that the completion of the metaphor depends upon this (for if it were said "for Paradise," it would be possible that the purchase is literal, since it is suitable for being a consideration, unlike a promise of it), then this is worthless. This is because the basis of the indication of the promise in the noble construction is not that it is a nominal clause introduced by *anna* (that), for that has nothing to do with indicating the future, but rather it is Paradise, whose existence in this world is impossible. And even if that were granted, the consideration would be the Paradise that was promised, not the promise of it.

﴿They fight in the way of Allah﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf), but not to explain what the purchase is for, nor to explain the purchasing itself, because their fighting in the way of Allah is not Allah's purchasing from them their lives and properties; rather it is their expending of them in that. Rather, it explains the sale that the mentioned purchase requires, as if it were said: "How do they sell their lives and properties for Paradise?" So it was said: "They fight in the way of Allah," and this is their expending of their lives and properties toward Allah, may He be glorified, and exposing them to destruction.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so they kill and are killed﴾ explains that fighting in the way of Allah is the expending of the self, and that the one who fights in His way is expending it, even if he remains safe and victorious. The predication in the two verbs is not by way of stipulating that both be combined, nor stipulating that one be attributed with either of them absolutely; rather it is by way of describing the whole by the state of some. Fighting is realized from the whole whether both verbs occur, or one of them occurs from some of them, or from some of them. Indeed, it is realized even if neither of them proceeds from them, just as when fighting (mudaraba) occurs but no killing occurs from either of the two combatants, or when fighting does not occur either. Then jihad is realized by mere resolve, readiness, and increasing the numbers.

The placing of the state of killing (al-qatiliyyah) before the state of being killed (al-maqtuliyyah) is to indicate that there is no difference between them in being instances of fighting being an expending of the self. It was also read with the passive voice verb placed first, in consideration of martyrdom being a familiar notion in this context, and to indicate their disregard for death in the way of Allah, may He be exalted, and rather that death is more beloved to them than safety, as was said regarding them:

*They do not rejoice when their spears attain a people, and they are not frightened (or humiliated) when they are attained.*
*The spear-thrust does not cease except in their throats,*
*and for them, from the watering-places of death, there is no averting.*

It was also said: in "they fight... etc.," there is the meaning of a command, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and strive in the way of Allah with your properties and your selves﴾.

﴿a promise binding upon Him﴾ is an emphatic infinitive (masdar mu'akkid) for what the price being deferred indicates. ﴿true﴾ is an adjective of *wa'dan* (a promise). The prepositional phrase is a circumstantial clause (hal) from it, because if it had been delayed it would have been an attribute of it. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿in the Torah and the Gospel and the Qur'an﴾ is connected to an omitted element that occurred as it is affirmed in the Qur'an.

﴿And who is more faithful to his covenant than Allah?﴾ is a parenthetical clause (i'tirad) confirming the content of what precedes it, namely the truth of the promise, in the manner of exaggeration regarding His being, may He be glorified, more faithful to the covenant than every faithful one. This is because breaking a promise is something that hardly proceeds from noble creatures, though its occurrence from them is possible. How then with the presence of the Creator, the Self-Sufficient, free from all worlds, may His majesty be exalted? The composition of the structure, although it is in denial that anyone could be more faithful to the covenant than Him, the Exalted, without addressing the denial of equality or its negation, nevertheless the intended meaning, by a consistent purpose, is the denial of equality and its absolute negation. Thus when it is said: "Who is more generous than so-and-so?" or "There is none more excellent than him," what is definitively meant is: he is the most generous of every generous one and the most excellent of every excellent one.

﴿So rejoice﴾ is a shift to direct address (iltifat), as an honour upon an honour for them, and an increase of their joy upon joy. Al-istibshar is the display of happiness. The *sin* in it is not for requesting (as in *istawqada* and *awqada*). The *fa'* (so) indicates the sequencing of the rejoicing, or the command to it, upon what precedes it, i.e.: since it is thus, then be delighted with the utmost delight and rejoice with the greatest joy for what you have attained of Paradise. It was said: ﴿with your sale﴾ although the rejoicing at it is with regard to its leading to Paradise, because the intended meaning is to encourage them toward jihad, which is expressed as a sale. The contract was not mentioned under the title of purchase, because that is from the side of Allah, may He be glorified, not from their side, and encouragement is only in what is completed from their side.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿which you have sold﴾ is for further affirmation of their sale, and to indicate that it is different from all other sales, for it is a sale of the perishable for the everlasting, and because both of the two exchanges belong to Him, glorified and exalted is He.

From al-Hasan, may Allah be pleased with him: "Selves: He created them; and properties: He provided them."

It was narrated that when the Ansar gave their pledge to him (ﷺ) at al-'Aqabah, 'Abdullah ibn Rawahah, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Stipulate for your Lord and for yourself whatever you wish." He (ﷺ) said: "I stipulate for my Lord that you worship Him and do not associate anything with Him, and I stipulate for myself that you protect me from what you protect your own selves from." They said: "If we do that, what will we have?" He said: "For you is Paradise." They said: "The sale has profited; we will not cancel it, nor ask for its cancellation."

A Bedouin passed by the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while he was reciting it, and said: "Whose speech is this?" He said: "It is the speech of Allah, mighty and majestic." He said: "A sale, by Allah, that is profitable; we will not cancel it, nor ask for its cancellation." So he went out to the raid and was martyred.
