﴿And that﴾, i.e., Paradise, which was made the price in exchange for what they expended of their lives and properties, ﴿is the great triumph﴾, beyond which there is no greater triumph. What is in that of the meaning of distance indicates the remoteness of the status of the one referred to and the sublimity of his rank in perfection. It is permissible that this refers to the sale which they were commanded to rejoice in, and that this is made as if it were itself the great triumph, or is made a triumph in itself. The sentence, according to the first view, is a concluding statement (tadhyil) for the noble verse, and according to the second, it is an affirmation of the content of His saying, exalted is He: "So rejoice."

The Repentant (al-Tā'ibūn) is in the nominative case as a laudatory epithet (al-madḥ, praise), meaning: they are the repentant ones, namely the believers already mentioned. This is supported by the reading with the *yā'* (i.e., *al-Tā'ibīna*) in the accusative as a laudatory epithet. It is also permissible for it to be in the genitive, as an attribute (ṣifah) of "the believers." The nominative is also permitted as the subject (mubtada'), with the predicate omitted, meaning: the repentant are also among the people of Paradise, even if they did not fight (in jihad). This is like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And to each God has promised the best (reward)﴾. It is also permissible for its predicate to be His saying, the Exalted, *al-ʿĀbidūn* (The Worshippers), and what follows it is a predicate after a predicate, meaning: the truly repentant from disbelief are those who combine these excellent qualities, namely those who are sincere in the worship of God, the Exalted, ﴿the Praisers﴾ for His blessings, or for what befalls them of ease and hardship, ﴿the Wanderers﴾, meaning the fasting ones, based on his saying (ﷺ): "The wandering (siyāḥah) of my community is fasting," with which they are compared, because fasting restrains one from desires, or because it is a spiritual discipline by which one reaches the discovery of the hidden aspects of the dominion and the realm of the unseen. It was also said: they are the wanderers in jihad and in the pursuit of knowledge. (p-107)

﴿the Bowers, the Prostrators﴾ in prayer, ﴿those who enjoin what is right﴾ with obedience and faith, ﴿and those who forbid what is wrong﴾, namely from polytheism and sins. The conjunction (ʿaṭf) here serves to indicate that the two conjoined items are as one quality. As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and the Guardians of God's limits﴾, meaning: concerning what He has made clear and specified of the realities and the laws, in action and in conveying them to people and enjoining them upon it, so that it is not supposed that it is restricted to one of the two aspects.

﴿And give good tidings to the believers﴾, meaning: those described with the qualities mentioned. Placing "the believers" in the position of their pronoun is to draw attention to the fact that the essence of the matter is faith, and that the complete believer is one who is like this. The object of the good tidings is omitted, to indicate that it is beyond the bounds of description. And in specifying the address to the first group, there is a display of additional care for their matter, through encouragement and consolation.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 113:

﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe﴾ in God alone, that is: it is not valid for them, according to the command of God, Mighty and Majestic, and His wisdom, nor is it proper ﴿to ask forgiveness for the polytheists﴾ through Him, glorified is He, ﴿even if they were﴾ — that is, the polytheists — ﴿of near kin﴾, that is: those who are their relatives. The response to "even if" (law) is omitted, because what precedes it indicates it, and the sentence is conjoined to another sentence before it that is omitted by a regular ellipsis, as is clarified in His words, Exalted is He, "and even if the disbelievers dislike it" and its like.

It is narrated that when death approached his uncle Abu Talib, the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "O uncle, say a word by which I may argue on your behalf before God." He refused, so the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I will not cease to ask forgiveness for you as long as I am not forbidden from it." Then the verse was revealed.

It is also said: when he (ﷺ) conquered Makkah, he went out to al-Abwa, visited the grave of his mother, then stood weeping and said: "I asked my Lord for permission to visit my mother's grave and He permitted me, and I asked Him for permission to ask forgiveness for her and He did not permit me," and He revealed to me the two verses.

﴿From after what has become clear to them﴾, that is: to the Prophet (ﷺ) and the believers, ﴿that they﴾, that is: the polytheists, ﴿are the companions of the Blazing Fire﴾, by dying in disbelief, or because revelation came down that they would die upon that.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 114:

﴿And the seeking of forgiveness by Abraham for his father was not⦆ by his saying: ("﴿Forgive my father﴾"), i.e., by your granting him guidance to faith and leading him to it, as is indicated by the justification given in His saying: ﴿Indeed, he was among the astray.﴾ The sentence is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) brought to affirm what preceded it and to repel what appears, on the surface, to be a contradiction. It was also read as (وَما اسْتَغْفَرَ إبْراهِيمُ لِأبِيهِ, "And Abraham did not seek forgiveness for his father") and as (وَما يَسْتَغْفِرُ إبْراهِيمُ, "And Abraham does not seek forgiveness"), as a narration of a past state. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿except from a promise﴾ is an exceptive clause with its anterior element omitted (istithna' mufarragh) from the most general of the causes, meaning: the seeking of forgiveness by Abraham, peace be upon him, for his father Azar did not arise from any thing except from a promise ﴿that he had made﴾ by Abraham, peace and blessings be upon him, ﴿to him﴾, i.e., to his father. It was also read thus, in His saying: ﴿I will surely seek forgiveness for you﴾ and His saying: ﴿I will ask my Lord to forgive you﴾, based on hope in his faith due to the non-clarity of his real state; otherwise, he would not have promised him. It is as if it were said: The seeking of forgiveness by Abraham for his father was not except from a promise based on the non-clarity of his state, as is indicated by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿But when it became clear to him﴾, i.e., to Abraham, by being revealed to him that he was persistent in disbelief and would never believe. It was said: by his dying in disbelief. The first is more suitable given His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿that he was an enemy of Allah﴾, for describing him with enmity is something that the state of death does not allow. ﴿He disassociated himself from him (p-108)﴾, i.e., he kept himself far from seeking forgiveness for him and fully distanced himself from him. In it there is an emphasis that is not present in (تَرَكَهُ, "he left him") and similar expressions.

﴿Indeed, Abraham was ʾawwāh, forbearing.﴾ ʾAwwāh means one who sighs greatly, and it is a metaphor for perfect tenderness and softness of heart. ﴿Forbearing﴾ means patient toward harm and trial. This is a resumptive clause explaining what motivated him, peace and blessings be upon him, to the seeking of forgiveness that proceeded from him. In it is an indication that Abraham, peace and blessings be upon him, was ʾawwāh and forbearing, and therefore what proceeded from him of seeking forgiveness before clarification proceeded from him. So it is not permissible for others to take him as a model in that. It is also an affirmation of the obligation to abstain from it after clarification, since he, peace and blessings be upon him, disassociated himself from him after clarification, and he, being of perfect tenderness of heart and forbearance, must be more than others in abstention and disassociation. As for the claim that seeking forgiveness before clarification, if it were not forbidden, would not have been excepted from the emulation of him in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿except the saying of Abraham to his father: "I will surely seek forgiveness for you"﴾, it has been verified in surah Maryam, by the permission of Allah, Exalted is He.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 115:

﴿And it is not the case that Allah would send astray a people﴾ That is: it is not part of His custom to describe them as astray from the path of truth and to apply His rulings to them.

﴿after He had guided them﴾ to Islam, ﴿until He makes clear to them﴾ through revelation, explicitly or by indication, ﴿what they should guard against﴾ That is: what must be guarded against of the prohibitions of the religion, so that they refrain from what they have been forbidden. As for before that, what proceeds from them is not called error (dalal), and they are not held accountable for it. So this is, as it were, a consolation for those who sought forgiveness for the polytheists before that. And in it is evidence that the heedless person is not obligated to do what reason alone cannot independently know.

﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing of all things﴾ This is a reason for what preceded. That is: indeed He, exalted is He, is Knowing of all things, among which is their need for an explanation of the ugliness of what reason cannot independently know, so He makes that clear to them, as He has done here.

Indeed, to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, without any partner in it. ﴿He gives life and causes death; and you have no guardian or helper apart from Allah.﴾

When He forbade them from asking forgiveness for the polytheists, even if they were close relatives, and this implied total disavowal of them, He made clear to them that Allah the Exalted is the owner of every existing thing, the one who manages its affairs and the one who prevails over it. No help or guardianship can come to them except from Him, the Exalted, so that they turn to Him with their whole being, disavowing everything else and intending none but Him.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 117:

﴿Indeed Allah turned in forgiveness to the Prophet﴾ Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: it refers to the pardoning of his (the Prophet's) granting permission to the hypocrites to stay behind from him. ﴿And the Emigrants and the Helpers﴾. It has been said: this concerns the lapses that had proceeded from them on the Day of Uhud and the Day of Hunayn. It has also been said: the purpose is to show the excellence of repentance, and that there is no believer who does not stand in need of it, even the Prophet ﷺ, because of what proceeded from him in some circumstances of leaving what is better (tark al-awla). ﴿Who followed him﴾, and did not stay behind from him, nor neglected any of his commands, ﴿in the hour of hardship﴾. That is, at its time; the expression "hour" is used to increase its definiteness. It refers to their condition during the expedition to Tabuk: they were in hardship regarding the mount, as ten men would take turns riding a single camel; and regarding provisions, they took with them rotten dates, weevil-infested barley, and rancid ghee; the severity reached such a point that two men shared a single date, and at times the group would suck on it so that they could drink over it the water that had changed in taste; they were in hardship regarding water, to the point that they slaughtered the camels and squeezed their dung; and it was a time of severe heat, of drought, famine and extreme straitness. The describing of the Emigrants and the Helpers with what has been mentioned of their following him, peace and blessings be upon him, in such degrees of hardship, serves to emphasize the need for repentance: for if that did not render them independent of it, then others are all the more in need of it and more deserving of it.

﴿After the hearts of a group of them had nearly swerved﴾. This is an explanation of the extreme severity and its reaching a point beyond which there is no limit, namely that some of them were on the verge of inclining to stay behind from the Prophet ﷺ. In "kada" (nearly) there is a pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n), or a pronoun referring to the people, to which the pronoun in "minhum" refers. It was also read with the verb feminine, and it was read: "after the hearts of a group of them had swerved", meaning the lagging-behind believers such as Abu Lubaba and their like.

﴿Then He turned in forgiveness to them﴾. This is a repetition for emphasis, and an alert that He turns to them because of what they endured of hardship. The meaning is that He turned to them for their steadfastness. ﴿Indeed He is toward them Kind and Merciful﴾. This is a resumptive explanatory clause, for the attribute of kindness and mercy is among the motives for repentance and pardon. It is permissible for the first to refer to the removal of harm and the second to the bestowal of benefit, and for one of them to pertain to the former (past) and the other to the latter (what follows).

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 9, verse 118:**

﴿And [He turned in mercy] to the three who were left behind﴾. That is: Allah turned in mercy to the three whose matter was deferred from the matter of Abu Lubabah and his companions, since their excuse was not accepted as theirs had been, and their case was not decided in any way until revelation came down concerning them. They were Ka'b ibn Malik, Hilal ibn Umayyah, and Murarah ibn al-Rabi'. It is also read as (khallafu) [with the verb in the form that means "they caused to remain behind"], meaning: they left behind the fighters in Medina; or [it is derived] from (fasadu) [they became corrupt], from al-khalifah (the one left behind) and khuluf al-fam (a change in the mouth's odour). It is also read as (ʿala al-mukhallafin) [meaning "upon those left behind"]. The first reading is the most suitable, because His saying, ﴿until, when the earth became narrow for them﴾, is the limit (ghayah) of the act of leaving behind, and only the first meaning fits it. That is: they were left behind, and their matter was deferred until the earth became narrow for them ﴿despite its vastness﴾, that is, despite its breadth and expanse, because the people turned away from them and cut off dealings with them. This is a figure of speech for extreme bewilderment, as if no one could settle in it and no dwelling could give them rest. ﴿And their souls became narrow for them﴾: that is, when they returned to themselves they found no peace in anything, because of the absence of comfort and joy and the dominance of loneliness and bewilderment. ﴿And they realised that there is no refuge from Allah except in Him﴾: that is, they knew that there is no refuge from His wrath except by seeking His forgiveness. ﴿Then He turned to them﴾: that is, He granted them the ability to repent ﴿so that they might repent﴾; or He sent down the acceptance of their repentance so that they would become among those who repent often, and He returned to them with acceptance and mercy again and again so that they would remain steadfast in their repentance. ﴿Indeed Allah is the Accepting of repentance﴾, the one who goes to the utmost in accepting repentance in quantity and quality, even if the sins are many and grave, ﴿the Merciful﴾, the one who bestows upon them favours of every kind, despite their deserving the various forms of punishment.

It is narrated that some of the believers stayed behind from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Among them were some who had a change of heart, disliked their position, and then caught up with him (ﷺ).

From al-Hasan (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: It reached me that one of them had an orchard worth more than a hundred thousand dirhams. He said, "O orchard! Only your shade and the waiting for your fruit kept me back. Go, for you are in the way of Allah." Another had only his family, and he said, "O family! Nothing delayed or held me back except the trials [caused] by you." So, by Allah, I will surely endure hardships until I catch up with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he took up his provisions and caught up with him (ﷺ). Al-Hasan (may Allah be pleased with him) said: Thus, by Allah, the believer repents of his sins and does not persist in them.

And from Abu Dharr al-Ghifari: his camel was slow, so he carried his goods on his back and followed the trail of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on foot. When the Prophet (ﷺ) saw his figure, he said: "Be Abu Dharr!" The people said, "It is he." He (ﷺ) said: "May Allah have mercy on Abu Dharr: he walks alone, dies alone, and will be raised alone."

And from Abu Khaythamah: he reached his orchard, and he had a beautiful wife who spread out bedding for him in the shade, spread the mat for him, and brought him dates and cold water. He looked at it and said, "Cool shade, ripe dates, cold water, and a beautiful woman, while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is in the heat and the wind. This is not good." He stood up, saddled his she-camel, took his sword and spear, and set off like the wind. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) cast his gaze toward the road, and suddenly there was a rider whom the mirage was lifting up. He (ﷺ) said, "Be Abu Khaythamah!" And he was. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) rejoiced at him and asked forgiveness for him.

Among them were those who remained and did not catch up with him (ﷺ), including the three. Ka'b (may Allah be pleased with him) said: When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned from the expedition, I greeted him, and he returned the greeting in the manner of one who is angry, after which he mentioned me and said, "I wonder what kept Ka'b back." It was said to him, "Only the beauty of his two cloaks and the looking at his own sides kept him back." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I know of him nothing but virtue and Islam." He forbade us, the three of us, from speaking, and the people turned away from us; no one spoke to us, near or far. When forty nights had passed, we were ordered to keep away from our wives and not approach them. When fifty nights were completed, suddenly I heard a voice from the summit of Sal': "Rejoice, O Ka'b ibn Malik!" I fell down prostrate to Allah. I was as my Lord described me: ﴿the earth became narrow for them despite its vastness, and their souls became narrow for them﴾. Good news kept following one another. I put on my clothes and set out toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and found him sitting in the mosque with the Muslims around him. Talhah ibn 'Ubaydullah got up, hurrying toward me until he shook my hand, and said, "May the acceptance of Allah of your repentance be a blessing to you." I will never forget that for Talhah (may Allah be pleased with him). The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), his face shining with a glow like the moon, said: "Rejoice, O Ka'b, in the best day that has passed over you since your mother bore you." Then he recited the verse to us.

From Abu Bakr al-Warraq, who was asked about sincere repentance (al-tawbah al-nasuh) and said: It is that the earth becomes narrow for the one who repents despite its vastness, and his soul becomes narrow for him, as with the repentance of Ka'b ibn Malik and his two companions.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 119:

﴿O you who believe﴾ is a general address that includes those who repent by primary inclusion. It was also said that it is specifically addressed to the Tulaqa' (those freed, i.e., those who embraced Islam after the conquest of Makkah) who stayed behind from the ghazwa (military expedition) of Tabuk. ﴿Be mindful of Allah﴾ in everything you do and everything you leave undone. This includes, by primary inclusion, dealing with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) concerning matters of the campaigns (maghazi). ﴿And be with the truthful﴾ in their oaths and their covenants, or in the religion of Allah in intention, speech and action, or in every matter, so that what was mentioned is included. Or it refers to their repentance and turning back to Allah. In that case, the intended people are then these three (who stayed behind) and their likes.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them) that it is an address to those among the People of the Book who believed. That is: be with the Muhajirun (Emigrants) and the Ansar (Helpers), and join their line in truthfulness and all other fine qualities. It has also been recited as (مِنَ الصّادِقِينَ) (min al-sadiqin, "from the truthful ones").

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 120:

﴿It was not for the people of Medina﴾0 It was not right (ma sahha) nor fitting (wa-ma istaqama) for them, ﴿and for those Bedouins around them﴾ such as Muzayna, Juhayna, Ashja', Ghifar and their like, ﴿to lag behind the Messenger of God﴾ when he set out for the raid (ghazw), ﴿nor to care for their own selves above his self﴾. That is, they should not withhold their selves from his noble self, nor protect themselves from what he did not protect himself from, but rather they should endure with him what he endures of terrors and calamities. The statement is in the meaning of a prohibition (nahy), even though it takes the form of a report (khabar).

﴿That﴾ refers to what the context indicates of the obligation of accompanying him (al-mushaya'a). ﴿Because﴾, because of the fact that ﴿they are not afflicted by thirst﴾, that is, a slight thirst, ﴿nor fatigue﴾, nor any weariness, ﴿nor hunger﴾, that is, any famine in which the forbidden things are not made lawful (la yustabah 'indahu al-muharramat) at their levels. For if slight thirst and fatigue are not without reward, then it is more fitting that these should not be without it. So there is no need to emphasize the negation by repeating the word la (not). It is possible that by hunger (makhmasa) is meant that level, and the order would then follow the frequency of occurrence and its rarity: thirst occurs more often than fatigue, and fatigue occurs more often than hunger in the sense mentioned. Thus the placement of the word la in the middle is not for emphasizing the negation, but to indicate that each one of them is independently a virtue and is counted as such.

﴿In the way of God﴾ and in exalting His word. ﴿Nor do they tread a path that enrages the disbelievers﴾, that is, they do not trample with their feet, the hooves of their horses, or the soles of their mounts, any trampling or any place that is trodden. ﴿Nor do they inflict on an enemy any infliction﴾, nayl being a verbal noun (masdar) like qatl (killing), asr (capture) and nahb (plunder), or a direct object (maf'ul), that is, something inflicted by them. ﴿Except that there is written for them thereby﴾, that is, for each one of the matters enumerated, ﴿a righteous deed﴾ and an accepted good act, merited by the decree of the gracious promise of a beautiful reward and attainment of nearness (zulfa). The tanwin (nunation) of "a righteous deed" is for magnification (li-l-tafkhim). The fact that what is written is the very thing they did does not prevent the entry of the particle bi (thereby), for difference in the aspect (al-'unwan) suffices for that.

﴿Indeed God does not waste the reward of the good-doers﴾ for their good, as a causal reason (ta'lil) for what preceded regarding the recording (al-katb). By "the good-doers" (al-muhsinin) is meant either those under discussion, and placing the apparent noun in place of the pronoun serves to praise them and bear witness that they are included in the category of good-doers, and that their deeds are of the kind of good, and to indicate that the ground (al-ma'khadh) of the judgment is its causal reason ('illiyya); or it is the general class of good-doers, and they are included in it by primary inclusion (dukhulan awwaliyyan).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 121:

﴿And they do not spend any small expenditure﴾ even a date or the lash of a whip, ﴿nor a large one﴾ like what 'Uthman (may Allah be pleased with him) spent. The ordering is in terms of how frequently each of the mentioned things occurs and how rarely it does. The placement of "wa la" (and not) in between is to specify that each of the two is independently recorded and rewarded, not to emphasise the negation, as in His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿and they do not cut across﴾, meaning, they do not pass through in their journey ﴿a valley﴾ (wadi). It originally means every opening through the mountains and hills that serves as an outlet for floodwater; it is an active participle from "wada", meaning it flowed, and then it became common usage for any valley in general.

﴿except that it is written for them﴾, meaning, that which they did of spending and crossing is recorded for them ﴿so that Allah may reward them﴾ for it ﴿with the best of what they used to do﴾, meaning, the best reward for their deeds, or the reward for their best deeds.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 122:

﴿It is not for the believers to go forth all together.﴾ That is: it is not right or proper for them to all go forth together for something like a military expedition or the pursuit of knowledge, just as it is not proper for them all to hold back together, for that would disrupt the affairs of livelihood. ﴿Why should not a group from every division among them go forth?﴾ That is: why does a large group not go forth, such as the people of a town or a great tribe, ﴿a party﴾, that is, a small company, ﴿so that they may gain understanding of the religion﴾, that is, that they may exert themselves to acquire fiqh (deep juristic understanding) of it and undertake the hardships of attaining it, ﴿and so that they may warn their people﴾, that is, so that they make the goal of their striving and the aim of their purpose from this the guidance and warning of their people, ﴿when they return to them﴾. Its specific mention is because it is the more important matter. In this there is evidence that acquiring fiqh of the religion is a fard al-kifaya (communal obligation, which is discharged when enough people fulfil it), and that the aim of the one seeking knowledge should be uprightness and steadfastness, not exalting himself over the servants of God or spreading himself throughout the lands, as is the habit of the people of this age. And God is the One sought for help.

﴿So that they may be cautious﴾, meaning the intention that they may take heed of what they warn against. It has been cited as evidence that khabar al-ahad (reports transmitted by a single person or a few, not reaching the level of mass transmission) are authoritative proof, because the generality of ﴿every division﴾ requires that a party go forth from every three who are alone in a village to gain fiqh, so that they may warn their division, in order that they may remember and be cautious. If reports were not accepted unless they were mutawatir (transmitted by so many narrators that their agreement on falsehood is impossible), this would not benefit anything.

It has also been said that the verse has another sense: when the believers heard what was revealed concerning those who stayed behind, they hastened to go forth out of desire and fear, and they ceased from seeking fiqh. So they were commanded that a party from every division should go forth to jihad, and that their successors should remain seeking fiqh, so that fiqh, which is the greater jihad, would not be cut off, because argument by proof is the foundation and the purpose of the mission. Thus the pronoun in ﴿li-yatafaqqahu﴾ (so that they may gain understanding) and ﴿li-yundhiru﴾ (so that they may warn) refers to the remaining divisions after the parties that went forth for the raid, and the pronoun in ﴿rajaʿu﴾ (they return) refers to the parties. That is: the remainder should warn their people, those who went forth, when they return to them with the knowledge they acquired during their absence.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 123:

﴿O you who have believed, fight those adjoining you of the disbelievers﴾ They were commanded to fight the nearest of them, then the nearest after them, just as the Prophet (ﷺ) was first commanded to warn his own clan, for the nearer deserves more compassion and efforts at reform. It was said: they are the Jews around Madinah, such as Banu Qurayzah, al-Nadir, and Khaybar. It was also said: they are the Romans, for they inhabited al-Sham, which is near Madinah in relation to Iraq and other regions.

﴿And let them find in you harshness﴾ That is, severity and steadfastness in fighting. It is also recited with a fatha on the ghayn, like sakhtah, and with a damma; both are dialectal forms of it. ﴿And know that Allah is with the God-fearing﴾ with protection and support. By "the God-fearing" is meant either the addressees, where the apparent noun is placed in the position of the pronoun to specify that faith and fighting in the manner mentioned are from the category of piety and that they are attested to belong to the company of the God-fearing; or it means the category in general, into which they enter primarily. By "being with" is meant constant guardianship. The reason for using ma'a (with) before the one followed has been mentioned in the saying of the Exalted: "Indeed Allah is with us."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 124:

﴿And when a surah is sent down﴾ from the surahs of the Qur'an, ﴿among them﴾, i.e., among the hypocrites, ﴿is one who says﴾ to their companions, in order to confirm them in hypocrisy, or to the common believers and the weak among them, in order to turn them away from faith, ﴿"Which of you has had its increase in faith?"﴾ And it has been read with the accusative "ayyukum" (which of you), on the assumption of a verb that the mentioned one explains, meaning: "This surah has increased which of you in faith?"...

The attribution of increase, although they have no faith at all in reality from the standpoint of the belief of the believers, is as expressed by His words, exalted is He: ﴿The believers are only those who, when Allah is mentioned, their hearts tremble, and when His verses are recited to them, they increase them in faith﴾. As for ﴿those who believed﴾, it is a response from Him, glorified is He, and a confirmation of the truth and a specification of their state, both in this world and the next. That is, as for those who believed in Allah, exalted is He, and in what came from Him, ﴿it has increased them in faith﴾ through an increase in certain knowledge resulting from reflecting upon it and understanding the realities contained in it, and the joining of their faith in what it contains to their earlier faith, ﴿and they rejoice﴾ at its descent and at the religious and worldly benefits it contains.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 125:

﴿As for those in whose hearts is a sickness﴾ i.e., disbelief (kufr) and corrupt belief (su' al-'aqidah), ﴿it adds to them uncleanness upon their uncleanness﴾ i.e., disbelief in these (verses) joined to disbelief in other than them, and false beliefs and blameworthy characters likewise; ﴿and they die while they are disbelievers﴾, and that becomes firmly established in them until they die upon it.

﴿Will they not see?﴾ The hamza (هَمْزَة, the interrogative particle) here expresses denunciation and reproach, and the waw (واو, conjunction) is for coordination with an understood clause, meaning: "Will they not look and not see" ﴿that they﴾, that is, the hypocrites, ﴿are tested every year﴾ of the years ﴿once or twice﴾. The intended meaning is mere multiplicity, not a statement of the exact number of occurrences. That is, they are afflicted with the various kinds of calamities, such as sickness, hardship, and other things that remind them of their sins and of standing before the Lord of Might. This should lead them to faith in Him, the Exalted, or to striving alongside the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so that they bear what is revealed to him of signs, especially the striking verses that increase faith and expose the shameful vices within them. ﴿Then they do not repent﴾: this is coordinated with "will they not see" and falls under the denunciation and reproach. The same applies to His words, exalted is He: ﴿nor do they take heed﴾. The meaning is: Will they not see their being tested, which should lead them to faith, and then they do not repent of the hypocrisy they are upon, nor do they take heed through those trials, which call for remembrance and repentance? It is also read with the letter ta' (تاء, second-person prefix), in which case the address is to the believers and the hamza expresses wonder (لِلتَّعْجِيبِ): "Will you not look and not see their wondrous condition, which is their being tested in succession, without heeding it?" Thus His words, ﴿then they do not repent﴾, and what is coordinated with it, are coordinated with (﴿they are tested﴾).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 127:

﴿And when a surah is revealed﴾ is an explanation of their state at the time of its revelation, when they were in the gathering where the revelation was being conveyed, just as the first (verse) explains their statements when they were absent from it. ﴿They look at one another﴾: they signal to each other with their eyes, denying it (the surah), or mocking it, or out of rage at what it contains of their disgrace. ﴿"Does anyone see you?"﴾ That is, saying: "Does any one of the Muslims see you?" (so) "let us slip away," showing that they cannot endure listening to it, and laughter overcomes them so that they are exposed; or they exchange glances, consulting over arranging the departure and slipping away stealthily (liwa'an). They say: "Does anyone see you if you rise from the assembly?" The use of the second-person pronoun (in "does anyone see you") is to rouse the addressees to earnestness in seizing the opportunity, for a person is more concerned with his own affair than with the affair of his companions, as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿"And let him be gentle and let him not make anyone aware of you"﴾ (18:19). It has also been said that the meaning is: "And when a surah is revealed concerning the faults of the hypocrites."

﴿Then they turned away﴾ is a conjunction with (they "looked at one another"), and the delay (in expression) is in view of finding the opportunity and ascertaining that none of the believers could see them. That is: they all turned away from the gathering of revelation, fearing exposure or for some other reason. ﴿God has turned their hearts﴾ That is: away from faith, in accordance with their turning away from the assembly. The sentence is either informative or supplicatory. ﴿because they are a people who do not understand﴾ That is: because of their poor comprehension, or because of their failure to reflect.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 128:

﴿Indeed there has come to you﴾ The address is to the Arabs. ﴿a Messenger﴾ — what a Messenger, a Messenger of great standing — ﴿from among yourselves﴾ — of your own kind, an Arab of the Quraysh like you. It is also read with a fatha on the fa' (anfusikum → anfasikum), meaning: the most noble and most excellent of you. ﴿It grieves him greatly that you suffer﴾ — meaning: your suffering and your encountering of what is disliked is burdensome and severe for him; he fears for you a bad end and falling into punishment. This is one of the results of the kinship mentioned before (al-mujanasah). ﴿He is ardently concerned for you﴾ — for your faith and the rectitude of your condition. ﴿Towards the believers﴾ — from among you and from among others — ﴿he is full of compassion and mercy﴾. The more emphatic of the two has been placed first, namely ra'fah (compassion), which is an expression for intense mercy, in order to preserve the rhyme (fawasil).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 9, verse 129:

﴿Then if they turn away﴾ is a shift in address (talwin lil-khitab) and a redirection of it towards the Prophet (ﷺ) as consolation for him; that is, if they turn away from believing in you, ﴿then say: "Allah is sufficient for me"﴾, for He suffices you and helps you against them. ﴿There is no god but Him﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) affirming the content of what precedes it. ﴿In Him I have put my trust﴾, so I hope in none and fear none but Him. ﴿And He is the Lord of the Mighty Throne﴾, that is, the Mighty Dominion, or the greatest, all-encompassing body from which decrees and destinies descend. It is also read as "al-'Azim" in the nominative (bi'l-raf').

And from Ubayy: that these two verses were the last to be revealed.

And from the Prophet (ﷺ): "The Qur'an was revealed to me only verse by verse and letter by letter, except for Surat Bara'a and Surat Qul Huwa Allahu Ahad, for these two were sent down to me accompanied by seventy thousand rows of angels."
